Posture

Formal discovery has started.Defendants served Demand for Production, Set One on 9/28/2026. It formalizes 8 of Cunningham's 9 informal requests and adds 9 vendor and insurance demands. (S-38; A-81)
The informal requests were rated insufficient.Cunningham, 9/2026: items 1–3 and 5 insufficient, 6–9 no response, 4 resolved; no second mediation day before the CMC; they plan to file an answer and cross-complaint. (Kit §0 (Gmail 1a0e8bb75c0a0a1c))
Defendants have not answered the Complaint, as far as the record shows.As of 8/18/2026 there was an open-ended extension. No answer or cross-complaint has been located since. (Briefing §2; no later source)
Settlement positions are far apart.Ours $5,705,257.43 (7/2/2026). Theirs $7,359,766 plus 2025 profit and lease credits (6/19/2025). The partnership value itself is agreed at $1,162,612.50 before the 90% factor. (Briefing §§2–3; S-2)
The biggest dollar question is legal.Post-death profit share (theirs) vs. the contract's 4% interest (ours). Han v. Hallberg stands; whether § 16601(8) can be varied by agreement is the open question. (OI-30; briefing §5)

Mandatory buyout and the price

Core dispute
  • Hazel's death is a defined “Dissociating Event.” The 7/2018 Amended and Restated Partnership Agreement requires a buyout at 90% of appraised value on a 20-year, 4% note (Art. XIII.B). (governing-instruments-extract, addendum)
  • Four levers decide the number: real-property basis, minority discount, post-death compensation, offsets. Ours $5,705,257.43 vs. theirs $7,359,766 + 2025 profit + leases. (Briefing §§2–3; S-2)
  • Their counsel (Esraelian) proposed and engaged Stan Xavier for the buyout in 2023; Moss Adams found “no obvious errors or omissions in either report.” (Briefing §4 (Ex. G, Ex. Q))

CMC PREPARATION PACKAGE — COVER NOTE

ATTORNEY WORK-PRODUCT SUPPORT — NOT FILINGS — NOT LEGAL ADVICE

To: Brandon M. Ormonde, Ormonde Rascon Re: Manuel Stephen Leal v. Ashley Garabedian, et al., Tulare County Superior Court Prepared: August 18, 2026 · Counsel deadline: September 15, 2026 · CMC: October 13, 2026

ADDED 10/3/2026 — counsel team and dashboard. Brandon Ormonde remains lead; Erika Rason (same office) is co-counsel (client, 10/3/2026). The quickest way into everything below is the attorney dashboard, 07-attorney-dashboard/leal-case-dashboard.html: download it and open it in a browser. It holds status, issues, the discovery tracker, open items, red team, timeline, documents and every memo. It is work product; share it with counsel only.

ADDED 10/1/2026 — formal discovery has started. Defendants served a Demand for Production, Set One, on Steve on 9/28/2026 (18 demands). Read rfp-set-one-response-map.md first. It maps each demand to the record, both ways. Ormonde asked the client for documents by about 10/14/2026 (OI-92). New exposures: A-81 to A-83, plus the A-68 update.

Read in this order

  1. open_items.md — start here. Several things need action outside this workspace, and two are time-critical.
  2. governing-instruments-extract.md — the operative clauses of the three agreements, as actually written. Several conclusions in this package changed once these were read.
  3. complaint-extract.md — the operative pleading, read in full. Ten causes of action, punitive damages, and the exhibit list.
  4. verified_facts_memo.md — every factual assertion graded, with a citation or an explicit "no source."
  5. adverse_analysis.md — the case against us. Written to be uncomfortable.
  6. chronology.csv + timeline-exhibit.html — 100 events; the exhibit prints to one page.
  7. research_memos/ — read 00-READ-FIRST-research-reliability.md first. See the warning below.
  8. source-register.md — what was and was not reviewed, and the citation convention.

Four things to know before you read anything else

1. The § 998 offer has multiple defects, all confirmed on the face of the documents

The proof of service recites January 3, 2018 — over eight years before the July 2026 cover letter. Separately, the offer itself is undated, states no monetary term, the POS envelope block has no street address, and the caption reads VCU3627028 against VCU327028 elsewhere. Every candidate acceptance window has already expired. → verified_facts_memo.md §6; adverse_analysis.md A-2, A-3; open_items.md OI-1.

2. The $45,064 question does not have the answer it was framed to have

$45,064 is Manuel Leal's annual "Personal" withdrawal category total for FY2000 — a column subtotal in a reviewed financial statement. It is not a dated draw. No draw date exists in the record, and no Kaweah Drive purchase or recording document exists either. No day-count gap is computed or reported, because any number would be invented. → verified_facts_memo.md §1.

3. FY2014 is a serious problem and it is in our own reviewed financials

Steve drew $167,503 against Manuel/Hazel's $110,081 — $57,422 more. In the "Personal" category alone it is $120,155 vs. $7,333, a 16:1 ratio. FY2011 also runs against us by $612. Both figures come from our own accountants' statements. → verified_facts_memo.md §4; adverse_analysis.md A-1.

4. ⚠️ The legal research is NOT verified authority

All legal-research domains — leginfo, CourtListener, courts.ca.gov, Justia, Casetext, Google Scholar — were blocked by this environment's network egress proxy, and no CourtListener MCP was available. No judicial opinion was read in its original source. No pin cite is confirmed in any memo. Some statutory text was verified verbatim via the Legislative Counsel's own database export; the case law was not.

Treat R1–R4 as a research roadmap, not as research. Everything must be re-run and Shepardized in Westlaw or CoCounsel before it is relied on or cited. → research_memos/00-READ-FIRST-research-reliability.md; open_items.md OI-18.

What changed mid-preparation, and why it matters

The three governing instruments were initially recorded as "not located." They were then found attached as Exhibits A–C to the defendants' January 21, 2026 mediation brief, along with the Complaint (Exhibit E). Reading them reversed two working assumptions:

  • The 2017 release is narrow. ¶13 releases only claims relating to "the division of the real property," and ¶15 states "the only issues resolved… is [sic] the division of identified real property and the valuation of the improvements." Accounting and fiduciary claims appear NOT released. This was recorded as our strongest structural answer to the record-gap problem. It is withdrawn, and R4's proportionality analysis loses its premise.
  • Both agreements contain a complete three-appraiser fallback mechanism that neither side used, and whose clocks expired in early 2023. The contract may already supply the remedy we filed suit to obtain.

⚠️ The defendants' brief is marked "CONFIDENTIAL SETTLEMENT COMMUNICATIONS — EVIDENCE CODE § 1152" and was addressed to the mediator. Please assess mediation confidentiality (Evid. Code §§ 1115–1128) before using the brief or anything sourced only to it. The instruments themselves are contracts between the parties — please obtain clean executed copies from the client file rather than relying on the mediation-brief attachments.

Two exposures that were not on the original list

  • OI-14 — Settlement Agreement ¶8 required a MONTHLY accounting to Hazel (by the 15th of each month), for roughly 58 months to her death. No evidence of a single one was found. ¶11 caps borrowing at $100,000 per 30-day period and capital expenditures at $100,000 without both partners' approval. This — not the appraisal dispute — is the case defendants are actually building.
  • OI-15 — Our client was a co-trustee of the Manuel C. Leal Bypass Trust, and ¶5 entitled Hazel to all Bypass income monthly from March 25, 2015. Our own July 2026 letter offers $327,427.02 for "earned but undistributed" Bypass income. That figure may measure our liability rather than our claim. Please consider how it is characterized in correspondence.

Scope limits — stated plainly

  • The master case brief claims list was never provided. Claims in it that are not addressed in verified_facts_memo.md remain ungraded.
  • No forensic ledger extraction CSVs exist. All financial findings rest on annual reviewed statements and one document marked "DRAFT — FOR INTERNAL DISCUSSION PURPOSES ONLY." The .QBX file has never been extracted (OI-2).
  • No property records of any kind were located — no Kaweah Drive deed, refinances, HELOC, ARM, or 2016 gift deed; no Shell Beach purchase or remodel record (OI-3, OI-6).
  • The Complaint has now been read (complaint-extract.md). Its 21 exhibits have not — only A, B and C, and those via defendants' brief. Retrieving Exhibits D–U from the client file is the fastest way to document the 2023–2025 chronology (OI-20).
  • 1994–1996 ledgers are recorded as "not located in available records." This workspace makes no assertion that anything was withheld, concealed, or destroyed — no document supports one.
  • Nothing in this package has been sent to any party. No correspondence was generated, drafted, or transmitted.

Added after reading the Complaint (Exhibit E)

The October 13, 2026 CMC is a CONTINUED date. The clerk's stamp on the Complaint set the original CMC for February 2026. Please pull the docket for the continuance and any scheduling order — this workspace was built assuming October 13 was the first CMC, and any existing case-management deadlines are untracked. OI-19.

We pleaded punitive damages, and nothing else in the file mentions it. Counts 3, 6 and 9 each seek § 3294 punitives on a breach of implied covenant theory, alleging "fraud, oppression and/or malice." No tort is pleaded anywhere in the Complaint. Defendants have not responded under the open-ended extension, so no motion to strike has been filed — but it is available at any time. Worth deciding proactively. OI-22, A-18.

Complaint ¶45 may be the best fact in the case. It pleads that Moss Adams — the neutral defendants retained — reviewed both real property appraisals, found both valid, and "specifically found that there were no errors or an improper appraisal performed by Correia Xavier." That directly defeats defendants' stated reason for rejecting the Xavier appraisal. The document is Complaint Exhibit Q and is not in this workspace. Please get it first. OI-20.

Two things in the Complaint cut against us, both quotable by defendants from our own pleading: ¶¶73 and 96 plead the Xavier appraisal was commissioned for an IRS Form 706 filing rather than on the buyout parameters (A-20), and ¶37 pleads that Jace Leal agreed with defendants to use Dustin at Moss Adams — while four counts rest on defendants having engaged Moss Adams unilaterally (A-21, OI-21).

The prayer asks the court to order defendants to "employ" Correia-Xavier and Moss Adams — neither a party. R2 flags Civ. Code § 3390(b) and (d) against exactly that form of relief. The statute's text was read verbatim; its case-law gloss was not. Please verify before the CMC and before any amendment deadline. A-19.

Added after reading Complaint Exhibits D–U (all 21 exhibits, all 27 emails)

Correction first: an earlier note in this package said Exhibits D–U were not in the workspace. They were — bound into the same PDF after the Complaint body. All have now been read. email-exhibits-extract.md supersedes the retrieval list in OI-20.

Exhibit G is the best document in the case. On March 21, 2023 Robyn Esraelian — defendants' own counsel — emailed Stan Xavier, copying you, and attached the Tenants in Common Agreement:

"Attached is the Tenants in Common Agreement that sets forth the terms of the buy-out… We are seeking an appraisal of the properties for purposes of the Tenants in Common Agreement Buy out provisions and for the Dairy Partnership valuation… Brandon: please confirm the properties are correct…"

She also proposed Xavier in the first place (Ex. E, 2/15/2023: "do you have any thoughts about using Xavier-Correrria?"). Defendants proposed the appraiser, engaged him, gave him the buy-out terms, and asked you to confirm scope. That is the joint-appointment evidence, and it is theirs.

Two adverse items are withdrawn or reduced as a result. A-20 — which treated the Complaint's "IRS 706" allegation as an admission against us — is withdrawn; the emails show a two-stage engagement defendants interrupted before buy-out scope was set. A-21, on Jace and Moss Adams, is downgraded: the retention decision came six days before any conversation with Jace, and you objected twice the same day.

The "negative capital account" problem is solved — it is a mislabel, not a missing fact. Exhibit R (your March 3, 2025 letter) shows the adjustment is $262,592.00 of excess distributions during Hazel's lifetime plus $194,352.65 after her death = $456,944.65, and the arithmetic to $3,950,565.28 checks exactly. It is not a negative capital account, which is what the Complaint pleads three times and what our own financials contradict. Worth correcting the label. Frazer's capital-account summary — Exhibit B to that letter — is still missing.

Three new adverse facts you should see before the CMC:

  1. $850,894.54. Exhibit J (9/26/2023): Esraelian asserts "there was an agreement as to the amount of the profit distribution owed to Hazel from 2015 through 2021 in the amount of $850,894.54," and demands payment. No response appears in the record. OI-25.
  2. Exhibit Q is more qualified than ¶45 says. Moss Adams did find no errors and gave Correia-Xavier a slight advantage — but it also concluded "it is not possible to conclude to a supportable indication of value as both reports are equally credible," recommended a jointly hired third appraiser, and described CX as "hired by the potential buyer" coming in lower on every component. Exhibit G refutes that last point. Our May 23, 2025 letter says Moss Adams "validated the findings" — that overstates it. A-24.
  3. BioGas and Feedstock leases. Their June 2025 counteroffer claims a pro-rata share of credits from leases that appear nowhere else in this entire record. Unquantified. OI-27.

One procedural item: every page of Exhibit Q reads "FOR CLIENT USE ONLY. NOT TO BE RELIED UPON BY THIRD PARTIES," and it says the signatories need not testify. We attached it to a publicly filed Complaint. Worth addressing — we may need Klett. OI-26.

The gap is narrower than it looks. Their partnership figure — $1,162,875 — is identical to ours. The dispute reduces to four items: the real property basis (Correia-Xavier alone vs. the two-appraisal average), the minority discount (30% vs. 15%), their profit claim, and our $456,944.65 offset. That may be a more useful frame for the CMC than the appraiser fight, which drives only the first.

Highest-priority missing document: Stan Xavier's May 8, 2023 email, quoted in Exhibit K as showing he was "waiting for us to define the scope for appraising the property for purposes of buyout." It is not an exhibit. It should be in the firm's archive. OI-28.

The post-death profits claim — post-death-profits-issue.md

Their position is that Hazel's Trust remains a partner entitled to profits after 9/23/2022: $1,617,761 through December 2024, plus 2025 profit, plus BioGas/Feedstock credits. Their brief makes it a gating issue — "the buyout of the Dairy cannot be completed as the unpaid profits need to be paid prior to the sale."

The contract text is good for us. Article XIII.B.1 defines Hazel's death as a "Dissociating Event" in express words; B.2 says the Partnership "shall purchase" her interest; and B.2 and Settlement ¶7(b) both supply 4% interest on the deferred balance — the parties' own answer to what the selling side gets while it waits. Article XIII.D shows they knew how to say an interest passes by estate plan and is not bought out; they said it for you and Marla, not for Hazel. Article I.B also fixes the percentages: Bypass 7.5% / Steve 30% / Hazel's Trust 37.5% / Steve & Marla 25%.

Two things cut hard against us, and you should see both before the CMC.

1. Their best legal argument. The named partner is the Trust, not Hazel personally. R4 reports Corp. Code § 16601(7) dissociates a trust-partner on distribution of its entire interest, "but not merely by reason of the substitution of a successor trustee." Our answer is that the Agreement's PARTIES clause defines "Hazel" to include "Trustee of THE HAZEL J. LEAL REVOCABLE TRUST," so the parties contracted around the default. That statute is UNVERIFIED and needs to be run first — it decides the largest dollar issue in the case. OI-30.

2. Our own books allocate profits to her after death. The FY2024/2023 reviewed statements carry a column headed "ESTATE OF HAZEL LEAL" and allocate 37.5% of profit and loss every post-death year, with a capital account of $3,218,795 at 12/31/2024 — and we made distributions to it ($73,192 in 2024, including $70,441 "Personal"). That is practical construction, in our own accountants' work, against the position we are taking. Worth asking Frazer why the account was maintained and on whose instruction before treating it as an admission.

But the arithmetic helps. If she shares profits she shares losses, and FY2023 was a $(888,608) loss year — her allocation was $(333,228). Against FY2024's $759,997, the net for both years is $426,769. Check whether their $1,617,761 nets the FY2023 loss. OI-31.

Two incidental findings worth your attention. Note 8 records that "the Manuel Leal Bypass Trust was dissolved" and its partnership interest "transferred to Steve Leal" on 1/1/2023 — $821,249, to the surviving co-trustee who is also the managing partner, with nothing in this record showing defendants were told (OI-34). And the FY2024 review carries a Qualified Conclusion on two GAAP departures, one expressly "at the request of the Dairy's management" (OI-35).

One thing this resolves in our favour. Article VI.E provides that a drawing-account debit balance from "drawings in excess of his share of Partnership profits" is "a liability of that Partner to the Partnership" and "shall not reduce his interest in the capital of the Partnership." That is exactly our $262,592.00 offset — and it explains why the capital account stayed positive. The substance is supported by the Agreement; only the Complaint's "negative capital account" label is wrong. Correcting the pleading to track Article VI.E would fix it.

5. The law, verified vs. open (details: 02-legal-research/verification-report-courtlistener.md)

Verified against opinion text this month (CourtListener; KeyCite still required):

  • Han v. Hallberg (2019) 35 Cal.App.5th 621 — trustee substitution ≠ dissociation (§ 16601(8)); review granted then DISMISSED 8/31/2020 — the opinion stands. Their best case. Our distinction: their buyout keyed to "death of a partner"; ours keys to "Hazel's death" by name and labels it a Dissociating Event. Note the published split with Presta (2009) 179 Cal.App.4th 909; Tulare (5th Dist.) is bound by neither.
  • Rappaport v. Gelfand (2011) — § 16701(b) verbatim: buyout price carries interest from the dissociation date — matches the contract's 4% answer.
  • Poster (1990) 52 Cal.3d 266 — § 998 + § 1013 = 35 days (our July offer is expired).
  • Gorobets (Cal. 8/6/2026) + Mostafavi fn. 6 — § 998 terms/alternatives must be in the offer itself, offeror's burden. Both cut against the old offer's cover-letter structure.
  • Bewick (1945) 26 Cal.2d 92 (Traynor) — when a party's refusal breaks the agreed appraisal mechanism, the court fixes the price and decrees specific performance; Petrolink (2018) — court-appointed Evid. Code § 730 appraiser. This is the cure for the Complaint's § 3390 problem (Woolley: no specific performance of personal services — the current prayer asks the court to order defendants to "employ" two named non-parties).

The dispositive open question: whether the agreement's express "Dissociating Events" definition contracts around § 16601(8) — i.e., § 16103(b)'s non-waivable list. One Westlaw session: KeyCite Han, pull §§ 16103/16601/16603/16701 and § 16404's limits on Art. III.

05-for-brandon/action_plan.md · 25,528 characters

CONSOLIDATED ACTION PLAN

ATTORNEY WORK-PRODUCT SUPPORT — PREPARED FOR COUNSEL — NOT A FILING — NOT LEGAL ADVICE

Manuel Stephen Leal v. Ashley Garabedian, et al. · Tulare County Superior Court Prepared August 18, 2026 · Counsel deadline September 15 (28 days) · CMC October 13 (56 days)

This plan is support for Brandon Ormonde's strategic decisions, not a substitute for them. Nothing here predicts what a court will do. Nothing here gets sent to any party.

1. WHAT "WINNING" ACTUALLY LOOKS LIKE ON THIS RECORD

Both sides want the buyout to close. Defendants' own mediation brief treats the buyout as inevitable — their fight is price, profits, and leverage. The realistic win is therefore: close the buyout at a defensible number, without letting the fiduciary/accounting counterattack metastasize into its own case. A trial "victory" ordering defendants to employ two specific appraisers is the weakest version of winning — the relief as pleaded has a possible Civ. Code § 3390 problem (unverified), Moss Adams is now Baker Tilly, and the § 998 vehicle built on the same structure is defect-laden.

The gap, decomposed (rough demonstrative arithmetic — not opinions of value)

Our July 2026 offer: $5,705,257.43. Their June 2025 demand: $7,359,766 + 2025 profit + lease credits. The ~$1.65M+ gap is four levers, each worth roughly half a million to a million dollars:

Lever Our position Theirs Rough swing
1. Real property basis Correia-Xavier ($14.05M adjusted) Average of both appraisals ($16.0M net) ~$0.5–0.7M
2. Minority discount 30% 15% ~$0.8–0.9M
3. Post-death compensation 4% interest ($677,830) 37.5% profit share ($1,617,761 + 2025 + leases) ~$0.9M+
4. Offsets −$456,944.65 excess distributions $0 ~$0.5M

Strategic observation for counsel: the appraiser-identity fight (lever 1) is the smallest lever, yet it is what the Complaint is built around. Levers 2 and 3 are where the money is, and on both of those the contract text is our strongest asset — the TIC/Settlement formula contemplates identified discounts (the prior Xavier work used 20–30%), and Art. XIII.B expressly prices the post-death wait at 4% interest.

The three pillars of the affirmative case

  1. The contract already decides the big questions. Hazel's death is a defined "Dissociating Event" (Art. XIII.B.1); the buyout is mandatory ("shall purchase"); delay compensation is 4% interest, not profits (Art. XIII.B.2, Settlement ¶7(b)); Steve/Marla's interests pass by estate plan while Hazel's is bought out (Art. XIII.D) — a deliberate asymmetry.
  2. The joint-appointment record is theirs. Esraelian proposed Xavier (Ex. E), engaged him with the TIC Agreement attached "for purposes of the… Buy out provisions" (Ex. G), Xavier was waiting on joint scope (his 5/8/2023 email, quoted in Ex. K), and defendants revoked before scope was set. Every element is in writing, mostly in their counsel's words.
  3. Their own neutral undercut their "errors" story. Moss Adams found "no obvious errors or omissions" and gave Xavier's report a "slight advantage" (Ex. Q) — while also declining to pick a number and recommending a jointly hired third appraiser.

The decision counsel should make first (framed, not made, here)

Whether to keep fighting for "Xavier's number binds" or to pivot to "complete the valuation now" via the contract's own three-appraiser fallback / a court-appointed appraiser.

  • Hold the Xavier line: maximizes lever 1, keeps the breach narrative clean — but our own pleading concedes the appraisal omitted the contractual discounts, Exhibit Q declined to endorse the number, the fallback clocks expired unused on both sides, and the pleaded relief has the § 3390 problem.
  • Pivot to completion: accept a jointly appointed third appraiser (or court appointment), which instantly moots their "errors" narrative, aligns us with Moss Adams' own recommendation and the contract's fallback — and concentrates the fight on levers 2 and 3, where our text arguments are strongest. Cost: gives up part of lever 1.

Either way, the case theory should stop being "make them use our appraiser" and become "enforce the buyout the contract mandates, priced the way the contract says."

Where we can lose

Honestly: not on the buyout — on the counterattack. Their theory is covenant breach and information suppression by the managing partner (A-13), and our exposed flanks are real:

  • ~58 months of ¶8 monthly accountings with no evidence of compliance
  • the unanswered 9/26/2023 demand asserting an "agreed" $850,894.54
  • the Bypass Trust dissolved and its 7.5% transferred to our client on 1/1/2023, with no notice shown (A-14 / OI-34)
  • our own books carrying an "Estate of Hazel Leal" profit column post-death
  • the LOC/capital-expenditure covenants we cannot yet prove we honored
  • pre-2017 record gaps, restatements, and a qualified accountants' conclusion

They are running a forensic review. We have served no discovery. Closing that asymmetry is as important as any argument.

🔴 OI-2 — QBX extraction status

Status: NOT STARTED. No extraction exists.

File: QB_Manuel_Leal_Dairy 10.5.2009 (QuickBooks2013 Acct Transfer Jan 29,2014 05 48 PM).QBX Drive 1ePWvKVpIsBy3exr2eqQ2ZPVi2Bcq5evS — 18.4 MB Also present: Manuel Leal AJEs.QBJ (Drive 1tDO8Mge-bV_MUKUfwPxWZDpR_M3kWqcF, 126 KB) and Manuel Leal AJEs.xlsx (Drive 1yqjmNBGZ_PbNaBoQ478OJ8j07tUevz4F) — adjusting journal entries.

What a .QBX is. An Accountant's Transfer File — a proprietary, encrypted QuickBooks format. It is not a database that can be read directly. Converting it requires a QuickBooks Desktop installation of a compatible vintage (2013-era or a version that will migrate it), typically QuickBooks Accountant/Enterprise. It cannot be extracted by script, and it cannot be extracted in this environment.

Why it matters — this is the file that unblocks the transaction-level questions:

  • It is the only candidate source of dated transaction detail in the record.
  • Without it, we have no general ledger and no check register at all — every financial finding in this workspace rests on annual reviewed statements. See adverse analysis A-8.
  • It is the only realistic path to a dated draw underlying the FY2000 $45,064 figure (see OI-6).

Important limitation counsel should know before spending money on this. The file is dated 10.5.2009 with a transfer stamp of January 29, 2014. It is unlikely to contain FY1994–FY1996 data and may not reach back to FY2000. Counsel should confirm the earliest transaction date in the file before commissioning any broader reconstruction.

Recommended action: engage the partnership's accountants (Frazer LLP appears in the record — Drive 1Ql1d-B-SfuLQMtSYg6ED1N232Rdpc48l) or a QuickBooks forensic specialist to open the file and export: (a) the general ledger by date, (b) the partner draw/equity accounts by transaction, (c) the check register, (d) the earliest and latest transaction dates. Ask for the date range first — it is a cheap question that determines whether the rest is worth doing.

🔴 OI-14 — Did we comply with Settlement Agreement ¶ 8 and ¶ 11? Answer this first.

This has displaced the appraisal dispute as the most urgent factual question in the case. Defendants' brief builds its theory on covenant breach, not on draw disparity.

¶ 8 — monthly accounting. "…an accounting of the Partnership operations will be provided to Hazel on the 15th of each month… the Partnership shall respond with answers to any questions raised by Hazel on or before the 25th of each month."

→ Were monthly accountings delivered from December 2017 to Hazel's death on September 23, 2022 — roughly 58 months? Counsel needs a month-by-month answer and the transmittals. This workspace found no evidence of a single one.

¶ 11 / ¶ 11(a) — borrowing and capital-expenditure caps. Steve may draw on an established credit line without approval up to $100,000 in any 30-day period; capital expenses of $100,000 or more need both partners' approval; no loans to any partner and no borrowing without approval of all partners.

→ Did any 30-day window exceed $100,000? Requires the line-of-credit statements for December 2017 – September 2022. → Did any capital expenditure reach $100,000 without Hazel's written approval? Requires the capital-expenditure schedule and any approval correspondence. → Counter-fact worth developing: ¶11(a) also binds Hazel — approval "is not to be unreasonably withheld and an approval decision must be made within ten (10) days." 🔴 OI-30 — Verify the dissociation statutes. This decides the largest dollar issue in the case.

Defendants claim the Hazel J. Leal Revocable Trust remains a partner entitled to profits after September 23, 2022. The claim is $1,617,761 through December 2024, plus 2025 profit, plus BioGas/Feedstock credits.

The contract text is good for us:

  • Art. XIII.B.1 defines Hazel's death as a "Dissociating Event" in express words.
  • Art. XIII.B.2: "the Partnership shall purchase her Partnership Interest" — mandatory.
  • Art. XIII.B.2 and Settlement ¶7(b) supply 4% interest on the deferred balance — the parties' own answer to what the selling side receives while waiting.
  • Art. XIII.D shows the parties knew how to say an interest passes by estate plan and is not bought out — they said it for Steve and Marla, not for Hazel.

The statutory overlay is the risk, and it is UNVERIFIED:

  • Corp. Code § 16601(7) reportedly provides that a trust-partner is dissociated on distribution of its entire transferable interest, "but not merely by reason of the substitution of a successor trustee." The named partner is the Trust, not Hazel personally. If that is the text, the default rule favours them.
  • Our answer is that the Agreement's PARTIES clause defines "Hazel" to include "Trustee of THE HAZEL J. LEAL REVOCABLE TRUST," so Art. XIII.B.1 makes her death the Dissociating Event for the Trust's interest — the parties contracted around the default.
  • Corp. Code § 16103 (extent to which the partnership agreement governs) must be confirmed, including the non-waivable list.
  • Corp. Code §§ 16603 and 16701 — R3 and R4 both report RUPA's buyout remedy is value at the dissociation date plus interest, not post-dissociation profits. Confirm.

Run this first in Westlaw/CoCounsel. Everything else on this issue is downstream of it.

✅ OI-63 UPDATE (8/19/2026) — Treas. Reg. § 1.736-1 now READ IN FULL (client upload of the Cornell LII text)

Source: 26 CFR § 1.736-1 [T.D. 6500, 25 FR 11814 (Nov. 26, 1960), as amended by T.D. 6832 (July 7, 1965)], client-uploaded PDF, read 8/19/2026. Key text VERBATIM:

  • (a)(1)(ii): "A partner retires when he ceases to be a partner under local law. However, for the purposes of subchapter K, chapter 1 of the Code, a retired partner or a deceased partner's successor will be treated as a partner until his interest in the partnership has been completely liquidated."
  • (a)(6): "A retiring partner or a deceased partner's successor in interest receiving payments under section 736 is regarded as a partner until the entire interest of the retiring or deceased partner is liquidated… the partnership shall not be considered to have terminated upon the death of the partner…"
  • ⚠️ (a)(1)(i) — the honest caveat: "Section 736 and this section do not apply if the estate or other successor in interest of a deceased partner continues as a partner in its own right under local law."

REFINED BRIDGE (stronger than the original): because of (a)(1)(i), the K-1s are NEUTRAL, not an admission — under OUR theory (dissociation + pending buyout) § 736 required partner-treatment on the returns until liquidation; under THEIR theory (continuing partner) ordinary rules produce the identical K-1s. The reporting is the same under both stories, so the returns prove neither. Argue A-40's cross-examination problem as NON-PROBATIVE reporting, not as affirmative proof of dissociation. Do not over-claim "§ 736 required it" standing alone — defendants can invoke (a)(1)(i) + Han to say § 736 never applied.

Two bonuses for settlement architecture:

  1. (b)(1): "Generally, the valuation placed by the partners upon a partner's interest in partnership property in an arm's length agreement will be regarded as correct." (Same for goodwill formulas, (b)(3).) Tax law respects the contract's 90%-of-appraisal price — supports the Art. XIII.B framework end-to-end.
  2. (b)(5)(iii): the § 736(a)/(b) allocation of payments "may be made in any manner to which all the remaining partners and the withdrawing partner or his successor in interest agree" — tax character is NEGOTIABLE. § 736(b) = capital treatment to the Trust / no deduction to us; § 736(a) = ordinary income to them / reduces our shares. A real lever for bridging dollar gaps in settlement — put it on the Frazer agenda.

Currency caveat for Frazer/counsel: the uploaded reg text is the 1960/1965 version; the § 736 STATUTE was amended in 1993 (limiting § 736(a) treatment of goodwill/unrealized- receivables payments where capital is a material income-producing factor — it is, for a dairy), so most buyout payments here likely fall under § 736(b). Frazer applies current law; nothing in this update changes the DO-NOT-AMEND recommendation, which stands.

OI-65 FOURTH UPDATE (9/26/2026) — limitations map for the JT-TEN claim (Estate of Yool VERIFIED via CourtListener)

Estate of Yool (2007) 151 Cal.App.4th 867 read in relevant part (CourtListener cluster 2257154). Verbatim anchors: CCP §366.2 "pertains to actions on the 'liability of the person'"; a resulting trust "does not implicate the personal liability of a decedent"; Prob. Code §9000(b) expressly EXCLUDES from creditor claims "a dispute regarding title of a decedent to specific property," resolved instead under §850; the resulting-trust statute is the four-year catch-all (CCP §343, per McCosker), and it "does not begin to run ... in the absence of repudiation by the trustee, that is, until demand has been made upon the trustee and the trustee refuses" (Berniker, quoted in Yool).

THE MAP (framework for counsel; Yool text verified, statutes and application NOT):

  1. Dead framing — damages claim against HAZEL (breach of spousal fiduciary duty / improper gift): CCP §366.2 gave ONE YEAR from her death — expired ~9/22/2023. Any version of this claim pleaded as Hazel's personal liability is time-barred on the statute's face.
  2. Live framing — equitable ownership of specific property held by SUSAN (Manuel's community half never validly passed; Susan holds it as resulting/constructive trustee; Prob. Code §850 petition): per Yool, §366.2 does not apply to title-to-specific- property disputes; the four-year §343 clock governs and, under the Berniker rule, arguably has NOT STARTED because no demand has ever been made and nothing was repudiated. Counsel must map our void-gift/constructive-trust theory onto Yool's resulting-trust holding (analogous, not identical — Yool involved bare title accommodation; citing treatment/KeyCite required) and weigh the discovery-rule fight (knowledge of the ACCOUNT vs knowledge of the community character of its funding).
  3. Fam. Code §1101 spousal route: keys to Manuel's ACTUAL knowledge of the transaction (3-year from actual knowledge; death/dissolution provisions — statute UNVERIFIED from here, Westlaw item); as a claim against Hazel it likely collides with §366.2 regardless. Secondary.
  4. Laches applies to the equitable route no matter what — every year of delay from TODAY is on us; the eleven years before now are explainable (nobody knew the facts' legal significance; no demand, no repudiation, no adverse holding asserted until survivorship vested in 9/2022 at the earliest). CLIENT CONTEXT RECORDED: the family (Manuel, Hazel, Steve, Susan) did not understand community-property law. Legal relevance: ignorance of LAW tolls nothing, but the operative clocks here key to FACTS (actual knowledge; discovery; demand-and-refusal) — and family-wide ignorance corroborates that no written spousal consent ever existed and that no demand/repudiation ever occurred, which is what keeps framing 2 alive. SEQUENCING: a demand on Susan STARTS the Berniker clock — do not send one until the Morgan Stanley subpoena returns and counsel has chosen the tier (plead / price / hold).

🔴 OI-72 — COUNSEL DECISION: pay or formally tender the undisputed amount, with no conditions

Why this is on the list: every offer so far was a settlement offer with conditions. That includes 3/3/2025, 7/2/2026 ("a release of all other claims by all parties (Civ. §1542)") and the 998. VERIFIED (Mission Ins. Group v. Merco Construction Engineers (1983) 147 Cal.App.3d 1059, 1067, read in full via CourtListener): "the conditional tender did not stop the running of interest," under Civ. Code §§ 1504 and 1494. If the contract's 4% rate applies, interest has kept running even on the amount our side concedes. On our own $3,950,565.28 that is $158,022.61 per year, about $13,168.55 per month. Whether 4% applies, and to what base, is itself disputed. Statutory text as quoted in the opinions read. Current text and later case treatment (KeyCite) are not confirmed:

  • Civ. §1504: an offer of payment "duly made… stops the running of interest on the obligation" (Mission, fn. 1).
  • §1494: an offer "must be free from any conditions which the creditor is not bound, on his part, to perform" (Mission, fn. 1).
  • §1495: an offer "is of no effect if the person making it is not able and willing to perform according to the offer" (Turner v. Seterus, Inc. (2018) 27 Cal.App.5th 516, 542; passage read, not the whole opinion).
  • §1500: a money obligation "is extinguished by a due offer of payment, if the amount is immediately deposited in the name of the creditor, with some bank… and notice thereof is given" (Hicks v. E.T. Legg & Associates (2001) 89 Cal.App.4th 496, fn. 4, read in full). An offer "under Section 1500" with no deposit could be found ineffective (id. at p. 510).
  • §1525: where part of the money is conceded, "the debtor may pay, without condition, the amount conceded to be due, leaving to the other party all remedies…" (Mission, p. 1068).
  • CCP §2076: whoever receives a tender must state any objection at the time, "or be precluded from objecting afterwards" (Hicks, fn. 10). Considerations for counsel, both ways:
  • For: paying or tendering may stop interest on that portion, if counsel concludes it does. It turns "we'd love to pay them" into something a court can see. It answers the "they've been paid nothing in four years" argument (post-death-profits-issue §5.2). It fits §1525's stated policy. It makes defendants state their objections on the record (CCP §2076).
  • Against / risks: (a) Which amount is "conceded"? Our own figures run from $3,950,565.28 (3/2025) to $5,705,257.43 (7/2026, which includes interest and bypass income). Tendering less than our latest offer invites a "lowball" framing. (b) Title (OI-68). Paying before record title is confirmed is risky. A §1500 deposit in the creditor's name, escrow, or a deposit in court each leaves the funds in different hands; counsel chooses the mechanics. (c) Tax. A payment by the partnership to the Trust as successor starts a §736 liquidation (S-18; A-40's (a)(1)(i) trap), so structure it with the CPA first. (d) Who pays. Art. XIII.B.2 says the Partnership pays for the partnership interest; TIC §7(b) says the Purchaser (a remaining Owner) pays for the land. (e) Ability (§1495). Have the financing commitment in hand first (OI-71). (f) Could a payment be characterized as an election, or affect the specific-performance claim? That is counsel's call. (g) A tender on the contract's own terms (10% down plus notes) at our price needs far less cash. However, it may be treated as conditioned on accepting our disputed price.

Response map: Defendants' Demand for Production, Set One, to Manuel Stephen Leal (served 9/28/2026)

ATTORNEY WORK-PRODUCT SUPPORT — PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL. This map is for counsel. It maps each demand to the record, flags what helps and what hurts, and lists what the client must pull. It is not a draft response. Objections, privilege calls, the response deadline and what gets produced are counsel's decisions. Nothing here has been sent to any party.

Source document (S-38): "DEMAND FOR PRODUCTION OF DOCUMENTS, SET ONE, TO MANUEL STEPHEN LEAL", 12 pages, dated 9/28/2026, signed for Whitney, Thompson & Jeffcoach (Thompson, Cunningham). Propounded by both co-trustees under "Sections 2031.010, et seq." (as recited, p.1). Proof of service: served 9/28/2026 on Ormonde by mail and by email (p.12). Caption: Hon. David C. Mathias, Dept. 1; action filed 10/16/2025; trial date "None Set" (p.1). Preserved as 01-verified-facts/2026-09-28_defendants-RFP-set-one-to-manuel-stephen-leal.pdf (chat upload 10/1/2026; also attached to Gmail 1a0ef9a945712acd).

Register figures below come from the Citizens QuickBooks register 2009–9/30/2026 (S-29; 33,364 lines, running balance unbroken). Split deposits show only "-SPLIT-", so the register cannot identify the payer of a deposit.

0. The short version

  1. What it is. There are 18 demands. Demands 1–3 and 5–10 formalize items 1–3 and 5–9 of Cunningham's informal nine-item list (kit: nikki-9-requests-kit.md). Item 4 (5Leal / Kings) is not repeated; Cunningham called it resolved. Demands 11–18 are new. Each targets a payee or insurance line and asks whether the expense was really a dairy expense. Three of them list specific check numbers.
  2. Counsel's ask of the client. Ormonde, 9/29/2026 (Gmail 1a0ef9a945712acd, S-39): "You must produce all documents responsive to the request in your possession or easily attainable. If we fail to produce items that are available, we can be barred from using them in trial." He asked for the documents "within 15 days from today", which is about 10/14/2026. That is counsel's working date, not a court deadline. The formal response date is counsel's to calendar. It is not computed here.
  3. Their side now holds the cash-rent / hoof-trimming statement. Demand 6 asks for the "cash rental income YOU claim was used directly for hoof trimming." A-68 said no transmission outside counsel had been located. This wording says the statement reached them. The channel is not established; ask Ormonde. See A-81 and OI-93.
  4. Their CPA is working entry by entry, with data past February 2026. The demands cite check numbers dated as late as 6/15/2026 (Built Wright #42341). The full QuickBooks backup went to their CPA on 2/12/2026. How they hold later entries is not established (no source). Possibilities include the AgWest loan file reviewed 7/29, the 7/10/2026 export or other production.
  5. Two answers are better than we thought:
    • Demand 10 (the balloon): the books show the AgWest money was deposited into Citizens.
    • Demand 11 (Built Wright): the partnership's own CPA called it "the new freestall" in writing.
  6. Two new exposures surfaced while mapping:
    • Ormonde & Rascon fees, including entries memo'd "plus Jace Bill", are now expensed by the partnership (A-83).
    • The partnership bought and installed a mobile home in 2017. That bears directly on whose cash rent it is (A-68 update).

1. "They're still looking for stolen funds." Is that what this is? Both ways.

Yes, in substance, the demands are built around a diversion theory. They fall into three groups:

Group Demands The question behind it
Income that might not reach the books 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; 6 (cash rent) Were sales or rent taken in cash or deposited somewhere other than Citizens?
Partnership money spent on non-dairy things 11–18 Construction, insurance, life insurance, hardware, fuel, vehicle repair, electrical: where, and for whose property?
Capital-account entries that move value between partners 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 Were Hazel's draws overstated, Steve's contributions overstated, the Bypass transfer proper, the balloon a partnership debt?

The demands are specific: check numbers, invoice-level detail, "location of services rendered," "confirmation that the expense was a DAIRY expense." So their CPA has picked entries that look personal on their face. That is the groundwork for the answer and cross-complaint Cunningham said is coming (kit §2.6).

But the demands do not, by themselves, show they believe Steve stole money. Counsel should expect them to give, and a court to hear, these other reasons, all ordinary:

  • Valuation. When a business interest is valued, personal expenses run through the business are usually added back to income ("normalization"). Higher income means higher value. Demands 11–18 feed that adjustment whether or not anyone calls it theft.
  • Capital accounts. Every offer since 3/3/2025 nets a $262,592 excess-distribution offset (OI-60). Demands 6–8 test the numbers behind it, as we would.
  • Post-death profits. If they claim a share of post-death profits (post-death memo), every post-death expense lowers that share. Built Wright and the legal fees bear on it.
  • Their role as trustees. Trustees arguably have to investigate the trust's main asset. That is a legal point, UNVERIFIED, for counsel.
  • Our own record invited several of these:
    • the 5/1/2026 draft saying rent cash "bypasses the formal ledger" (A-68);
    • the 3/6/2026 answer admitting the dairy insures Steve's two rental houses, Jace's house and personal vehicles, and pays "some personal fuel" (kit §2.4);
    • "no cash hay sales" against $121,148 of 2024 crop sales (kit item 1).

Bottom line for Jace: treat this as an audit, not an accusation. The best answer to a "funneling" story is clean, complete, third-party records. That means vendor statements, policy schedules, bank images and a permit. Where the dairy did pay something personal, our side should be the one to identify it and say how it was charged. Late or partial production feeds the story, and Ormonde has already warned that withheld documents can be barred at trial.

2. Demand by demand

Format: asks (key words verbatim) → record → helps / hurts → pull → counsel flags.

Demand 1 — Hay sales, 2015 to present

  • Asks: "all hay sales made by the DAIRY from 2015 to the present, including … receipts, invoices, journal ledgers, and deposits."
  • Record: kit item 1. The 3/6/2026 answer said "We do not have any cash hay sales." "Hay Cash Sales" has two inconsistent explanations: an expense label (3/6) and a revenue label (5/1 drafts). The FY2024 statements show $121,148 of crops sold to third parties. There is a "688000 · Feed sales" account. Frazer's 2020 entries name a customer, "Caleb Garcia." Also: Frazer, 2/3/2026: "I saw you got $100,000 for hay fire insurance" (Gmail 19c244dd811a1b04, S-40). That was an insurance recovery, not a sale. It is hay-related money, so be ready to explain it.
  • Helps / hurts: no evidence of off-book hay sales has been found. The risk is the inconsistent explanations, not a known diversion.

Deposition outline: working draft for counsel

ATTORNEY WORK-PRODUCT SUPPORT — PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL — DRAFT. Not to be served, shared, or used without counsel's review.

Started 10/1/2026 at the client's request. Each block lists:

  • the purpose (the fact we want on the record);
  • the foundation (the document that proves it if the witness denies it);
  • the questions, short and one fact each, in the order a lawyer might ask them;
  • ⚠️ risks: where the answer can hurt us.

Counsel decides who is deposed, in what order, and which questions survive. Some witnesses may be off-limits or need special handling; those are flagged. No discovery has been served by either side yet (incoming-counsel briefing §2). Depositions follow counsel's discovery plan.

Witness list (proposed):

3 Lauren Ruff / The Garabedian Group "Hazel's CPA" (Esraelian, 12/29/2020) Third party; subpoena

1A. The buyout is mandatory and was meant to be valued at death

Purpose: lock in the contract structure they cannot dispute.

Foundation:

  • Partnership Agreement Art. XIII.B.1–2 and XIII.J (post-death-profits-issue.md §3);
  • TIC ¶11 and Settlement Agreement;
  • defendants' mediation brief p.4 ("the buyout of the Dairy cannot be completed as the unpaid profits need to be paid prior to the sale").

Questions:

  1. You've read the July 2018 Amended and Restated Partnership Agreement?
  2. You understand it says that on Hazel's death "the Partnership shall purchase her Partnership Interest"?
  3. You agree the partnership is required to buy the trust's 37.5%?
  4. The price is 90% of appraised value, 10% down, and a 20-year note at 4%?
  5. The agreements say the valuation is "as of the date of Hazel's death"?
  6. Your side is asking for 37.5% of the profits after that date?
  7. And interest on those profits from the date of death? (Ex. U: $1,617,761 "includes a reasonable rate of interest… from the date of Hazel's passing.")
  8. And 90% of the date-of-death value as well?
  9. Where in the agreement does it say the trust receives profits after Hazel's death in addition to the purchase price and 4% interest?

⚠️ Risk: Q9 is an open "why/where" question. Use it in deposition only. Their answer will be §5.1 (the trust is the partner and did not die; Han v. Hallberg). Better to hear it now.

04-adverse-analysis/adverse_analysis.md · 207,495 characters

ADVERSE ANALYSIS — RED-TEAM OF OUR OWN RECORD

⚠️ ATTORNEY REVIEW DRAFT ⚠️

ATTORNEY WORK-PRODUCT — PREPARED FOR COUNSEL — NOT A FILING — NOT FOR DISCLOSURE TO ANY PARTY

Matter: Manuel Stephen Leal v. Ashley Garabedian and Hazel Susan Leal, Successor Co-Trustees Prepared: August 18, 2026 · For: Brandon M. Ormonde, Ormonde Rascon

How to read this document

This memo is written from the chair of Niki (Nikole E.) Cunningham of Whitney Thompson & Jeffcoach. Everything below is the strongest honest version of the other side's case. Where our documentary response is weak, this memo says so. Where we have no response, it says that too.

This memo is only useful if it is uncomfortable. Nothing has been softened for narrative fit. Every adverse fact carries the same citation discipline as the verified facts memo.

Ranking is by documentary strength available to the opponent, not by how much we dislike it.

A-1. FY2014: Steve drew $57,422 more than Manuel/Hazel — and it is in our own reviewed financials

Severity: HIGHEST. This is the single strongest documentary fact against us.

What Cunningham has. Our own reviewed financial statements:

Year ended December 31, 2014 — Total withdrawals: Manuel Leal $110,081 · Steve Leal $167,503 Of which "Personal": Manuel $7,333 · Steve $120,155 — Equity Accounts 1997-2015.pdf (Drive 1O7OGL798JcaTXginVNMIUgKtNV-ckK0l), FY2015/2014 statement

How she uses it. Any argument that Hazel's side over-drew from the partnership is met with a single page from our own accountant's statements showing that in FY2014 Steve took 16 times as much in the "Personal" category as Manuel did. She does not need an expert. She needs one exhibit.

She also has FY2011: Steve $42,119 vs. Manuel $41,507. Smaller ($612), but it makes FY2014 look like a pattern rather than an outlier, and it lets her say "in the two most recent years before Manuel's death, Steve out-drew his father."

Our best documentary response:

  1. Composition, not amount. Manuel's FY2014 draw was dominated by Medical: $59,962 (against Steve's $3,015) — 54% of Manuel's total. Medical withdrawals in a partner's final years are not discretionary consumption. On a discretionary basis the gap narrows considerably. This is a real point and it is documented in the same statement.
  2. Income taxes are pass-through, not benefit. Of Steve's $167,503, $41,333 was income taxes — tax on partnership income allocated to him, not personal enrichment. Netting taxes from both sides: Steve $126,170 vs. Manuel $72,972. The gap narrows from $57,422 to $53,198 — this response is weaker than it first appears and counsel should not lean on it.
  3. The 20-year aggregate still runs the other way, substantially. See the full series in verified_facts_memo.md §4.1.

Honest assessment: response (1) is genuinely good. Response (2) is thin. Response (3) invites the reply that we are averaging away the years that matter. Counsel should expect to concede FY2014 and fight on composition rather than deny the number.

A-2. The § 998 proof of service is dated January 3, 2018

Severity: HIGH — and it is our own offer, so the defect is ours to explain.

What Cunningham has.

"On January 3, 2018, I served the foregoing OFFER TO ALLOW JUDGMENT (CCP § 998)…" "…Executed on January 3, 2018, at Tulare, California." — Georgia Davidson — 998 offer FINAL.pdf (Drive 11VQh2jHIMvTnhVQr2bcIVZjoXcwrudYB), Proof of Service

The cover letter is dated July 2, 2026. The POS is off by eight years, five months and twenty-nine days.

How she uses it. She does not have to prove prejudice to make this hurt. She argues the offer was never validly served, that the § 998 clock never started, and that no cost-shifting under § 998(c) can attach. She may also argue the POS — a document executed under penalty of perjury — is unreliable on its face.

It gets worse, and counsel needs all of it:

  • The offer is UNDATED. "Dated: ______" is blank on both the offer and the Request to Enter Judgment. Counsel should treat this as potentially more serious than the POS date: a defective POS may be curable by evidence of actual service; an offer with no date on its face may be harder to fix, and it complicates computing the acceptance window from the document itself.
  • The POS envelope block has no street address. It names Thompson, Cunningham, and the firm — then stops. No 970 W. Alluvial Avenue, no city, no ZIP.
  • The case number in the 998 caption is VCU3627028 — one digit longer than the VCU327028 used in our own mediation brief and cover letter.
  • The plaintiff's name is wrong in the body of our own offer: caption reads "MANUEL STEPHEN LEAL," body reads "PLAINTIFF, STEVEN MANUEL LEAL."
  • Counsel's own name is misspelled twice: "BRANDON M. OMRMONDE."
  • The cover letter's page-2 header reads "January 2, 2024."

Our best documentary response:

  1. The defects are template artifacts, not misrepresentation, and there is a pattern proving it. Plaintiff's Mediation Brief (Drive 1bAo0s_6EL-Jc60VPzOCoCNDwlkiqDkzO) is also undated ("Dated: January ___, 2026"), its POS is also blank ("On January ___, 2026"), no service box is checked, and the execution line reads "20263." This office demonstrably leaves date fields unexecuted across documents. That supports "unfilled template," not "false statement."
  2. Actual notice is not in dispute. Cunningham received the July 2, 2026 cover letter, which expressly states "Concurrent with this offer, we are delivering a C.C.P. 998 offer." If she responded to or acknowledged the offer, actual receipt is established independently of the POS.
  3. Legal analysis of curability, substantial compliance, and § 998(c) consequences is in R1.

Honest assessment: response (1) cuts both ways and counsel must decide whether to deploy it. It rebuts intentional misdating, but it hands Cunningham the argument that this office's proofs of service are systemically unreliable — which is worse in a case where service dates control a cost-shifting statute. Recommend counsel weigh this carefully before putting the mediation-brief POS in front of anyone.

Response (2) is our strongest line and depends entirely on obtaining the as-served proof of service — which is not in this record. See OI-1.

A-3. The § 998 offer contains no monetary term

Severity: HIGH — structural, and largely unaddressed in our file.

What Cunningham has. The § 998 offer asks only that defendants employ Correia-Xavier and Moss Adams to appraise. No dollar figure appears anywhere in it. The $5,705,257.43 lives only in the cover letter.

How she uses it. § 998(c)(1) turns on whether the party who rejected the offer failed to obtain a "more favorable judgment." Cunningham argues that an offer with no monetary term cannot be compared to a judgment, so cost-shifting cannot attach as a matter of law — and that placing the money in a cover letter rather than the offer was a choice we made. She may add that the offer is too uncertain to be capable of valuation.

She has a further point that is genuinely awkward: our § 998 offer directs defendants to employ Moss Adams to appraise the partnership — but on our own account, Moss Adams already completed that valuation on November 18, 2024 ($2,840,000) (Mediation Brief p.7). The offer asks for work our own brief says is done.

Our best documentary response:

  1. The offer tracks the specific performance relief pleaded in the Complaint — which is the point of a § 998 offer in a specific-performance action. An offer that mirrors the prayer is not defective merely because the prayer is non-monetary.
  2. The Settlement Agreement, TIC Agreement, and Partnership Agreement supply the price formula (90% of appraised value with identified discounts). The offer is therefore arguably certain-by-reference even without a stated sum.
  3. Legal authority on non-monetary § 998 offers is in R1.

Honest assessment: response (2) is the real argument and it depends on instruments we have not reviewed. The Settlement Agreement, TIC Agreement, and Partnership Agreement are not in this record — only our brief's characterization of them. Until counsel reads the actual buyout clauses, we do not know whether the formula is self-executing enough to make the offer certain. This is a documentary gap, not a legal one. See OI-4.

On the Moss Adams point we have no good documentary response in this record. Counsel should clarify the intended scope of ¶2 of the offer before the CMC.

Severity: MEDIUM-HIGH — this is where we are the record-keeper and the gaps are ours.

What Cunningham has. Our client is the managing partner who kept the books. The Litigation folder contains a 1Citizens Statements 10623 folder, and pre-2017 Citizens statements are reported missing. ⚠️ CORRECTION — August 18, 2026

This item previously identified the 2017 release as our strongest structural answer, flagged that we had not read it. We have now read it. It does not do what we hoped.

Settlement Agreement ¶13 releases only claims "which in any way arise out of or relate in any way to the division of the real property owned jointly by the Partnership, Hazel, Steve and Marla." ¶15 then states expressly: "The only issues resolved by this Settlement Agreement is [sic] the division of identified real property and the valuation of the improvements identified in the Agreement," and that the agreement is "not intended to affect the rights or defenses among them with respect to any of the future divisions."

The release is narrow and appears not to reach accounting, draw, distribution, or fiduciary claims. Counsel should not rely on it to bar pre-2017 accounting discovery, and research memo R4's proportionality analysis loses its central premise.

What remains: responses (1) and (2), plus burden and proportionality arguments that now have to stand on their own. This is a materially worse position than this memo previously recorded, and counsel should plan on the pre-2017 period being discoverable.

A-13. The $100,000 borrowing covenant and the monthly accounting duty — defendants' actual theory

Severity: HIGHEST alongside A-1. This is the case they are actually building.

Their brief does not lead with draw disparity. It leads with covenant breach and information suppression, and the covenants are in the contract:

¶11(a) "…Steve may borrow from an already established credit line without approval of the Partners up to $100,000.00 in a thirty (30) day period." ¶11 "…any capital expenses of $100,000 or more, will be approved by both partners… no loans shall be made to any partner without approval of all partners; no borrowing… without approval of all partners." ¶8 "…an accounting of the Partnership operations will be provided to Hazel on the 15th of each month… the Partnership shall respond with answers to any questions raised by Hazel on or before the 25th of each month."

Their allegations, in their words:

  • "records confirm Steve has been in breach of the Settlement Agreement which prohibits him from drawing more than $100,000 from the Dairy's line of credit in a 30 day period. Not only has Steve routinely breached this covenant…"
  • "…whether Steve has used this line of credit to funnel profits to himself under the guise of expenses so that he could withhold profit distributions to Hazel/the Trust."
  • "…whether Steve inappropriately reinvested profits… into capital expenditures exceeding $100,000… thereby increasing the value of the company for his benefit."
  • "a forensic review of the Dairy's books reveal[s] irregularities in the expenses and profit distributions."
  • Footnote 1: "Steve has breached the Settlement Agreement on multiple occasions."

Why this is worse for us than the draw analysis. These are bright-line contractual covenants with numeric thresholds, not fuzzy fiduciary standards. Compliance is provable or disprovable from the line-of-credit statements and the capital-expenditure records. And ¶8 is a monthly obligation — roughly 58 months between December 2017 and Hazel's death on September 23, 2022. Every missed month is a discrete alleged breach.

Our best documentary response:

  1. ¶11(a) permits borrowing up to $100,000 per 30-day period without approval, and expressly deems it "part of the day-to-day operations." Ordinary operating draws on the line are contractually authorized. The question is only whether any 30-day window exceeded the cap — a countable question.
  2. ¶11(a) also constrains Hazel: approval of borrowing over $100,000 "is not to be unreasonably withheld and an approval decision must be made within ten (10) days." If requests were made and not answered within ten days, that is a defense, and potentially a counter-breach.
  3. TIC ¶1(b) obliged the Partnership to pay "any [and] all expenses related to the property" — so property-expense payments are performance, not diversion.

Honest assessment: we cannot currently answer point 1 at all. We have no line-of-credit statements and no capital-expenditure schedule in this record, and the pre-2017 Citizens gap compounds it. We also have no evidence of a single monthly accounting having been delivered under ¶8. Counsel should treat "did we comply with ¶8 and ¶11?" as the first factual question to answer, ahead of anything about the appraisals. New open item: OI-14.

A-14. The Bypass Trust: our own $327,427.02 offer may be an admission of OUR liability

Severity: HIGH. This is the most dangerous item added today.

The chain, entirely from documents:

  1. The Settlement Agreement identifies "STEVE M. LEAL and HAZEL J. LEAL, Co-Trustees of THE MANUEL C. LEAL BYPASS TRUST, dated February 14, 2005." — Our client was a co-trustee of the Bypass Trust.
  2. Recital F: on Manuel's death (March 25, 2015) "Hazel and Steve became successor Co-Trustees of the Trust."
  3. ¶5: "Hazel shall be entitled to receive all income from the account in the Manuel C. Leal Bypass Trust on a monthly basis from the date of Manuel's death. Any unpaid amounts of income… shall be paid to Hazel within 30 days of execution of this Agreement."
  4. Our own July 2, 2026 offer letter includes "a payment of $327,427.02 to satisfy all earned but undistributed income from the Manuel C. Leal Bypass Trust through Haze[l]'s date of death."

How Cunningham uses it. Our own settlement letter concedes that $327,427.02 of Bypass Trust income was earned and not distributed to a beneficiary who was contractually entitled to receive it monthly from March 25, 2015 — a period of roughly seven and a half years to her death. Our client was a co-trustee with the duty to make those distributions. She reframes our offer as an admission of a trustee accounting failure, and the defendant co-trustees, as Hazel's successors, are the counterparty.

She may add: ¶5 required "any unpaid amounts of income" to be paid within 30 days of execution of the Settlement Agreement — so the failure post-dates and breaches the settlement itself.

Our best documentary response:

  1. We are offering to pay it. The sum is in our offer precisely to resolve it. Voluntary tender is not the posture of a party concealing a shortfall.
  2. ¶5 conditioned the account division on "a payment of approximately eighty-five thousand dollars ($85,000)… to the Partnership to cover expenses paid by the Partnership" — there was a contemplated offset, and its status is unknown on this record.
  3. Hazel was herself a co-trustee of the Bypass Trust alongside Steve until her death. A co-trustee's own inaction bears on any claim by her successors.

Honest assessment: response (3) is the strongest and it is genuinely strong — the distribution duty ran to Hazel from a trust she co-trusteed. But counsel must establish who actually controlled the Bypass Trust account and whether the $85,000 offset was ever paid, before making any argument here. New open item: OI-15. Until then, counsel should be careful about how the $327,427.02 figure is characterized in correspondence — it currently reads as a concession.

A-15. The three-appraiser fallback mechanism nobody used

Severity: HIGH — and it may reshape the whole case.

Both the TIC Agreement (¶11) and the Partnership Agreement (Art. XIII §J) contain a complete, self-executing fallback: if the parties cannot agree on a single appraiser within 30 days of the triggering event, each side appoints one within 15 days; if those two cannot agree on value within 30 days, they appoint a third; and "the decision in writing of any two (2) of the three (3)… shall be binding and conclusive."

How Cunningham uses it. The contract already answers the question we filed suit over. Defendants proposed a weighted average or "jointly selecting a third appraiser" — which is much closer to the contractual mechanism than our demand that the first appraisal bind. She argues we are asking the court to rewrite a dispute-resolution clause we simply did not follow.

Two further problems, both in our own papers:

  1. Our own mediation brief concedes the Xavier appraisal did not comply with the contract: it "was performed on 100% ownership and did not identify discounts as required by the Settlement Agreement and TIC Agreement." We are asking the court to make binding an appraisal our own brief says omitted a contractually required term.
  2. The clocks expired. The windows run from "Hazel's dissociation or death" — September 23, 2022. The 30/15/30-day periods lapsed in early 2023. Neither side invoked the mechanism.

Our best documentary response:

  1. If Xavier was validly "jointly appointed," the text is excellent for us: his decision is "binding and conclusive," full stop — and defendants' dissatisfaction with the result would be irrelevant. Our brief documents mutual agreement through counsel (Feb–Mar 2023) and a joint scope call (April 6, 2023). This is a better argument than our brief makes it look.
  2. Cost allocation is contractual and favors us: jointly appointed appraisers split equally; unilaterally appointed appraisers are borne by the appointing party. Defendants engaged J. Hower & Associates unilaterally — on the face of ¶11, that is their cost.
  3. Defendants' own conduct — engaging a second appraiser rather than invoking the fallback — is equally a departure from the mechanism.

Honest assessment: our answer to the "did not identify discounts" concession is weak, and it is a concession in our own brief. Counsel should decide whether to reframe: the omission of discounts may be a correctable computational gap in an otherwise binding appraisal, rather than a failure of the appraisal itself. That framing needs to be settled before the CMC. Whether this clause is an appraisal-as-arbitration provision is R2's central question and is UNVERIFIED — see the research warning.

A-16. The 1983 promissory note, the 25% share, and the $350,000 payment

Severity: MEDIUM-HIGH.

What Cunningham has, from the Settlement Agreement's own recitals:

Recital A: "…on or about March 10, 1983, Steve and Marla executed a Promissory Note… as the purchase price for Steve's acquisition of a twenty-five percent (25%) share of the Partnership in the amount of $212,035, at nine percent (9%) interest." ¶6: "Steve and Marla will pay to Hazel, $350,000 on the Note, on or before six (6) months from December 7, 2017."

Her brief asserts "Steve also failed to repay the Note, which had amassed considerable unpaid interest that was due to Hazel/the Trust."

How she uses it. Two ways. First, Recital A is an executed acknowledgment that Steve bought in at 25% — which supports the 75/25 allocation and undercuts the 50/50 position our Capital Analysis leans toward (A-10). Second, ¶6 is a hard-dated payment obligation, and non-payment is a discrete post-settlement breach with nine percent interest running.

Our best documentary response:

Their interest was one community-property block, which bears on how the remaining 75% is characterized between Manuel's estate and Hazel individually.
  2. The FY1993 reviewed statement allocates net income equally — Manuel $106,101 / Steve $106,101.   3. Note the date discrepancy in their favor and against them: their brief says "March of 1993"; the Settlement Agreement says "March 10, 1983." Ten years of interest turns on which is right. Counsel should pin this down.

Honest assessment: point 2 is a real and useful distinction — it explains how both the 25% recital and the 50/50 income allocation can be true. But it needs the 1983 Partnership Agreement, which is not in this record. New open item: OI-16. On ¶6, counsel must simply determine whether the $350,000 was paid.

Defendants' brief states: "the parties agreed to an open-ended extension to respond to the Complaint, no discovery has taken place, and no trial date has been set."

A-18. We pleaded punitive damages on contract counts, and nobody in this file has mentioned it

Severity: HIGH — and it is entirely self-inflicted.

What Cunningham has. Counts 3, 6 and 9 — each a breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing — each allege verbatim:

"Defendants' fraud, oppression and/or malice was a substantial factor in causing Plaintiff's harm and as such Plaintiff requests this court award… punitive damages against Defendants pursuant to California Civil Code 3294."

Neither our mediation brief, nor the § 998 offer, nor the July 2026 cover letter mentions punitive damages anywhere. This appears to have dropped out of the file's working narrative while remaining in the operative pleading.

How she uses it. A motion to strike, and she has three angles:

  1. Breach of the implied covenant sounds in contract, and § 3294 punitive damages generally require a tort. The Complaint pleads no tort at all — no fraud count, no conversion, no breach of fiduciary duty. Counsel should evaluate whether the punitive prayer can survive without one.
  2. The allegation is bare recitation of the statutory elements with no supporting facts. Fraud ordinarily requires particularity.
  3. Defendants are sued solely as successor co-trustees. Against whom would punitives run, and out of what assets?

Our best documentary response. We have none on this record, and this workspace cannot supply the legal answer — the research environment could not verify authority.

Honest assessment: this is the kind of thing that gets stricken and costs credibility on everything else in the pleading. Because defendants have not responded under an open-ended extension, the motion has not been filed — but it is available to them at any time. Counsel may prefer to decide proactively whether to amend rather than defend it, and to do so before the CMC rather than in response to a motion. See open_items.md OI-22.

A-19. The prayer asks the court to make defendants "EMPLOY" two non-parties

Severity: HIGH — structural, and it now runs through the pleading, the § 998 offer, and the relief.

Adverse item A-3 previously flagged this as a § 998 problem. Having read the Complaint, it is broader than that. Every specific-performance count seeks "an order from the court to employ Correia-Xavier" or "to employ MOSS ADAMS jointly," and the declaratory counts seek a declaration that the parties "are required to jointly use" them, with discounts "as determined in his/their professional opinion."

Neither firm is a party. Defendants' brief notes Moss Adams is "now Baker Tilly."

Research memo R2 flags Civ. Code § 3390(b) — no specific enforcement of "an obligation to employ another in personal service" — and § 3390(d) — no order compelling a party "to procure the act or consent of… any other third person." The statutory text was read verbatim; the case law was not, and this is UNVERIFIED.

How she uses it. If § 3390 reads the way its words read, our primary relief — pleaded four separate ways — may be unavailable in the form requested, and the § 998 offer built on the same structure inherits the defect.

Our best response: R2's alternative framings — judicial valuation, appointment under CCP § 1281.6 (court "shall appoint" where the agreed method fails), or Evid. Code § 730. Any of these gets a valuation without ordering a party to employ a stranger to the action.

Honest assessment: counsel must verify § 3390's gloss before doing anything — but the fit between the statute's words and our prayer is close enough that it should be checked before the CMC and before any amendment deadline passes. See open_items.md OI-18 item 6.

A-20. Our own Complaint says the Xavier appraisal was commissioned for a different purpose

Severity: MEDIUM-HIGH — and it damages our best contractual argument.

What Cunningham has, from our own pleading:

¶73, ¶96. "Defendants then unilaterally had Correia-Xavier perform a real estate appraisal for purposes of filing for a IRS 706 filing but refused to perform a Real Property appraisal to include the parameters as defined in the Settlement Agreement…"

How she uses it. Adverse item A-15 identified our best contractual argument: Xavier was "jointly appointed," so under TIC ¶11 and Art. XIII §J his decision is "binding and conclusive," and defendants' dissatisfaction with the number is irrelevant.

Our own Complaint undercuts that. If, as we plead, the Xavier appraisal was commissioned for estate-tax purposes and not on the buyout parameters, then it is not the appraisal the buyout clauses call for — and defendants can say so by quoting us. Paired with our other concession that it "was performed on 100% ownership and did not identify discounts as required" (¶41), we have pleaded two independent reasons the Xavier appraisal is not the contractual one.

Our best documentary response:

  1. ¶45 is the counterweight, and it is strong: Moss Adams — a neutral defendants retained — reportedly found "no errors or an improper appraisal performed by Correia Xavier," and found both appraisals valid. Obtain Complaint Exhibit Q.
  2. The discount omission may be a correctable computational step rather than a defect in the appraisal — Xavier could supply discounts on the same underlying valuation.
  3. Defendants controlled the scope instruction. Our ¶42 pleads the appraisal "was performed… based on instructions from Defendants' attorney to Xavier without input from Plaintiff." If the scope was wrong, defendants set it.

Honest assessment: response (3) is the coherent theory and counsel should lead with it — the appraisal is the contractual one, defendants mis-scoped it, and the cure is to have Xavier complete it, not to start over. But it requires abandoning any argument that the existing Xavier number is already binding as-is. Those two positions are not compatible, and the Complaint currently gestures at both.

A-21. Jace Leal, not counsel, was the channel — and our own pleading says he agreed to Moss Adams

Severity: MEDIUM-HIGH.

What Cunningham has, again from our own pleading:

¶37. "On July 16, 2024, Defendants attorney responded stating that the Defendants and Plaintiff's son, Jace Leal, had agreed to use Dustin at Moss Adams to perform the Partnership Appraisal." ¶38. Defendant Ashley emailed Jace Leal directly with the appraisals and Moss Adams analysis (9/26/2024). ¶39. Defendant Ashley emailed Jace Leal the appraisals and valuation (1/17/2025). ¶30. Defendants' counsel emailed Jace Leal, copying plaintiff's counsel (6/20/2023).

How she uses it. Our theory is that defendants unilaterally engaged Moss Adams without plaintiff's input — that is the Second, Eighth, Ninth and Tenth Causes of Action. Our own Complaint records that our side, through Jace Leal, agreed to the Moss Adams engagement. She argues consent, or at minimum ratification, and points out that we pleaded it ourselves.

Our best documentary response:

  1. Jace Leal is not the plaintiff and not a party. He is the plaintiff's son. Whether he had authority to bind Steve on the appointment of a contractual appraiser is a real question, and the agreements require the appraiser be "jointly appointed by all the parties."
  2. ¶37 also pleads what happened next: plaintiff's counsel "immediately responded requesting a joint meeting with Dustin Schneider… After that time, Defendants' attorney refused to respond to phone calls." Even if there was agreement on who, there was refusal on scope — and scope is what the Complaint actually complains about.
  3. Defendants' choice to route substantive matters to a non-party while declining counsel's calls is itself the conduct pleaded in the implied-covenant counts.

Honest assessment: response (2) is the right frame and counsel should sharpen the pleading around it — the grievance is exclusion from scope, not from selection. As currently pleaded, the Complaint says both, and the "unilateral engagement" allegation is in tension with our own ¶37. See open_items.md OI-21.

A-22. Nearly a year has passed with no discovery and no response to the Complaint

Severity: MEDIUM — a posture problem, and it is a CMC issue.

Timeline from the documents: Complaint filed October 16, 2025 → original CMC set for February 2026 → mediation January 28, 2026 → § 998 offer July 2026 → CMC now October 13, 2026.

Defendants' brief states "the parties agreed to an open-ended extension to respond to the Complaint, no discovery has taken place, and no trial date has been set."

How she uses it. She does not need to. The posture speaks for itself: roughly twelve months from filing, defendants have not answered, we have served no discovery, and we made a § 998 offer — whose acceptance window has already expired — into a record where no discovery has been taken. Meanwhile defendants describe a "forensic review of the Dairy's books" already underway.

Our best documentary response: the extension was consensual and the parties were mediating in good faith, which explains the pause.

Honest assessment: that explains the period through January 2026. It does not explain February through August. Counsel should arrive at the CMC with a discovery plan and a position on terminating the open-ended extension. See open_items.md OI-17.

⛔ A-20 — WITHDRAWN

A-20 held that Complaint ¶¶73 and 96 — pleading the Xavier appraisal was commissioned "for purposes of filing for a IRS 706 filing" — was an admission that undercut our binding-appraisal theory.

The email record shows it is not an admission. It is an accurate description of a two-stage engagement that defendants interrupted:
