⚠️ THE ORIGINAL CMC WAS SET FOR FEBRUARY 2026, NOT OCTOBER 13, 2026

The clerk's stamp on page 1 sets a CASE MANAGEMENT CONFERENCE for 02-1?-2026 at 9:30 a.m. (day digit illegible; the year reads 2026).

The October 13, 2026 date in the workspace tasking is therefore a continued date, not the original. Counsel should confirm against the docket what happened to the February 2026 CMC, whether it was continued by stipulation (consistent with the January 28, 2026 mediation and the "open-ended extension to respond" that defendants describe), and whether any case-management order, scheduling order, or continuance order carries obligations we have not tracked. See open_items.md OI-9 and OI-19.

2. Ten causes of action — three parallel sets

Our mediation brief described the pleading loosely. The actual structure is ten counts, running the same three theories against each of the three agreements:

# Cause of action Instrument Provision pleaded Relief
1 Breach of contract Settlement Agreement § 7(a) (real property) Specific performance — order defendants to employ Correia-Xavier; damages
2 Breach of contract Settlement Agreement § 7(b) (partnership) Specific performance — order defendants to employ Moss Adams jointly; damages
3 Breach of implied covenant Settlement Agreement — Damages + punitive damages, Civ. Code § 3294
4 Declaratory relief Settlement Agreement — Declaration that parties must jointly use Xavier and Moss Adams
5 Breach of contract TIC Agreement § 7(b) and § 11 Specific performance — employ Correia-Xavier; damages
6 Breach of implied covenant TIC Agreement — Damages + punitive damages, § 3294
7 Declaratory relief TIC Agreement — Declaration re Xavier
8 Breach of contract Partnership Agreement Art. XIII, § B.2 Specific performance — employ Moss Adams jointly; damages
9 Breach of implied covenant Partnership Agreement — Damages + punitive damages, § 3294
10 Declaratory relief Partnership Agreement — Declaration re Moss Adams

As to all causes of action the prayer seeks general, compensatory, economic and non-economic damages; attorney's fees "pursuant to contract, law, or statute"; pre-judgment interest; costs; and further relief.

3. ⚠️ PUNITIVE DAMAGES ARE PLEADED — this was not mentioned anywhere else in the file

Counts 3, 6 and 9 each allege, in identical language:

"Defendants' fraud, oppression and/or malice was a substantial factor in causing Plaintiff's harm and as such Plaintiff requests this court award Plaintiff… punitive damages against Defendants pursuant to California Civil Code 3294."

Neither our mediation brief nor the § 998 offer nor the July 2026 cover letter mentions punitive damages at all. Counsel should be aware this is in the operative pleading.

Why counsel should evaluate this early — three concerns, stated as questions, not conclusions:

  1. Each punitive count is pleaded on breach of the implied covenant, which in California generally sounds in contract. Counsel should evaluate whether § 3294 punitive damages are available on these counts absent an independently pleaded tort. No tort cause of action is pleaded anywhere in the Complaint — there is no fraud count, no conversion count, no breach of fiduciary duty count.
  2. The "fraud, oppression and/or malice" allegation is conclusory. It recites the statutory elements without supporting facts, and fraud ordinarily requires particularity.
  3. Defendants are sued solely in their representative capacity as successor co-trustees. Counsel should consider against whom punitive damages would run and from what assets they would be satisfied.

Practical exposure: these three counts are a natural target for a motion to strike or demurrer. Because defendants have not yet responded under an open-ended extension, that motion has not been filed — but it is available to them at any time, including in the run-up to the CMC. Counsel may wish to decide proactively whether to amend rather than defend them. This is a legal question this workspace cannot answer — the research environment could not verify authority (see ../02-legal-research/00-READ-FIRST-research-reliability.md).

4. ⚠️ The prayer asks the court to order defendants to "EMPLOY" two non-parties

Every specific-performance count asks for "an order from the court to employ Correia-Xavier" or "to employ MOSS ADAMS jointly." The declaratory counts ask for a declaration that the parties "are required to jointly use" those firms, with "discounts applied as determined in his/their professional opinion."

This is the exact structure research memo R2 flagged against Civ. Code § 3390(b) (no specific enforcement of "an obligation to employ another in personal service") and § 3390(d) (no order compelling a party "to procure the act or consent of… any other third person"). Neither Correia-Xavier nor Moss Adams is a party. Defendants' brief further notes Moss Adams is "now Baker Tilly."

R2 suggests an alternative framing — judicial valuation, appointment under CCP § 1281.6 (court "shall appoint" where the agreed method fails), or Evid. Code § 730.

⚠️ R2's § 3390 analysis is UNVERIFIED. The statutory text was read verbatim; the case-law gloss was not. Counsel must confirm in Westlaw/CoCounsel before acting. But the fit between the statute's words and this prayer is close enough that it should be checked before the CMC, and before any amendment deadline.

Note the same structure carries into the § 998 offer, which offers judgment requiring defendants to "employ Stanley Xavier" and "employ MOSS ADAMS." If the pleaded relief is problematic, the § 998 offer inherits the problem. See adverse_analysis.md A-3.

5. Facts pleaded that are NOT in either mediation brief

These are new to the workspace and several are useful.

5.1 — The prior Xavier appraisal used a 20%–30% discount range

¶17. "For valuing the Real Property at that time, the Hazel and Steve agreed to use real estate appraiser Stan Xavier… In the appraisal, Xavier discounted minority interests in the Real Property between 20%-30%, depending on the property characteristics."

⚠️ Our three stated discount positions do not match each other:

Source Minority discount
Complaint ¶17 (prior Xavier appraisal) 20%–30%, varying by property
March 3, 2025 offer ($3,950,565.28) 30%
July 2, 2026 cover letter ($5,705,257.43) 25% — described as "consistent with the discounts applied by Stan Xavier when valuing the real property in 2017"
Defendants' June 19, 2025 counteroffer 15%

Counsel should reconcile these before the CMC. The July 2026 letter's characterization of 25% as "consistent with" the prior Xavier work is defensible against a 20–30% range, but it is not the 30% we demanded in March 2025, and the movement is documented in our own correspondence.

5.2 — Moss Adams found NO errors in the Xavier appraisal (Complaint Exhibit Q)

¶45. "Moss Adams also provided a review letter as it pertains to the two Real Property appraisals. In their summary, Moss Adams found that both appraisals were valid and that the two appraisers used different approaches. Notably, Moss Adams specifically found that there were no errors or an improper appraisal performed by Correia Xavier."

This is the strongest fact in the Complaint and it goes directly to the heart of defendants' case. Defendants' whole justification for rejecting the Xavier appraisal is that it "contained errors" — they attach a schedule of them as their Exhibit D. A neutral they themselves retained reportedly found otherwise.

Action: obtain Complaint Exhibit Q (the Moss Adams review letter) and read it directly. It is not in this workspace. If it says what ¶45 says it says, it is a centerpiece document. See open_items.md OI-20.

5.3 — The Xavier appraisal was commissioned for IRS Form 706, not for the buyout

¶73, ¶96. "Defendants then unilaterally had Correia-Xavier perform a real estate appraisal for purposes of filing for a IRS 706 filing but refused to perform a Real Property appraisal to include the parameters as defined in the Settlement Agreement…"

Counsel should treat this as double-edged. It explains why the appraisal came back at 100% ownership with no discounts — a 706 valuation would not apply buyout discounts. But it also undercuts our own position that the Xavier appraisal is the binding buyout appraisal under TIC § 11: on our own pleading, it was commissioned for a different purpose. See adverse_analysis.md A-15.

5.4 — A documented promise to release the appraisal, then a two-month silence

¶31. "On August 18, 2023, Defendants' attorney contacted Plaintiff's attorney by email and indicated that the land appraisal by Correia Xavier had been completed and that she would be releasing it to Plaintiff's attorney 'by next week' after reviewing with their clients." (Exhibit I)

¶32. "On or about September 26, 2023 (more than a month later), Defendants' attorney had still not released the appraisal… and acknowledged by email they were still talking to Xavier directly." (Exhibit J)

Hower Associates appraisals were credible despite significant difference in valuations. At that time, Defendant Ashley also suggested averaging the values…" ¶39. Counsel should note this cuts both ways. It supports our narrative that defendants bypassed counsel and controlled information flow. 01-verified-facts/1983-note-capital-shift-1994-96.md · 7,817 characters

The 1983 note and the 1994–1996 capital shift (client hypothesis, tested 10/1/2026)

ATTORNEY WORK-PRODUCT SUPPORT — PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL. This tests a client hypothesis against the documents. It is not a finding.

The hypothesis. Jace (email to Mike Edwards, Frazer, 9/30/2026, Gmail 1a0f3ec7d6bf95e0, subject "Tax returns"; not privileged — an accountant email): "There was some kind of transfer of capital between 1993 and 1997… How else would his capital account go down while manuel's went up?" The client's theory is that this transfer paid off Steve's 1983 buy-in note.

The email's attachments ("attachment 1.pdf" and three photos) could not be opened. The Gmail connector cannot read attachments, and the photos are not in Drive. The same theory appears in Jace's March 2017 letters ("Steve.Hazel adjust letter", 1Oqs1OafCkUSyUNx8TQIgkolo7JGUWFQZ / 1JhY8tTN3QRUIHfio7y7SYGxkEoiqSdsU), which said the principal was "transferred on paper by Adair & Evans… using Steve's partnership income during those years."

1. What the documents show (read 10/1/2026)

The note ("partnership note.pdf", 1g35f55ZeAeJ1zwsFrtI4TWVmTfBImFtW; read in full)

Term What it says
Date, makers, payees March 10, 1983. Makers: Manuel S. Leal and Marla M. Leal. Payable to "MANUEL C. LEAL and HAZEL J. LEAL, husband and wife".
Principal and interest $212,035.00, "with interest from January 1, 1982… at the simple rate of nine percent (9%)"
Interest Interest is payable each December 31 "until such time as both MANUEL C. LEAL and HAZEL J. LEAL have died, except that the undersigned's obligation to pay interest shall not exceed the total amount of his net profits distributed to him from MANUEL C. LEAL & SON DAIRY… interest not paid as a result of the foregoing shall be added to principal."
Principal Principal is not due until both parents have died: 10% then, and the balance over 30 annual installments.
Prepayment "The undersigned shall have the right to make early or additional principal payments on this Note without penalty and without securing the prior written consent of the holders."
Form of payment "Principal and interest is payable in lawful money of the United States of America."
Acceleration At the holders' option, on "the sale or other transfer of all or any of the undersigned's interest in said partnership".
Later assignments Manuel assigned his rights in the note to his Living Trust on 2/14/2005. Hazel assigned her one-half to her trust on 11/10/2017 (trust-instruments-extract).

FY1993 statements (Adair, Evans, Erwin, Taylor & Gross; "equity 1992-1993.pdf", 1NlzMqhAQBaAkdGyF63wjo42tTWkPCuwI, pp. 3–4, read visually)

  • Printed: net income $212,202. Withdrawals $122,063. Partners' capital at year-end $373,027 (1992: $282,888). Manuel C. Leal $180,568 / Steve Leal $192,459 at 12/31/1993.
  • Handwritten on this copy, not printed by the accountants. The handwriting is apparently the client's: the same arguments appear in the 2017 letters.
    • 1/1/1993 balances: Manuel $156,897 / Steve $125,991.
    • 50/50 net income: $106,101 each.
    • Withdrawals: Manuel $82,430 / Steve $39,633.
    • The note "$66,468 is more than 25% of profits, so profits were obviously split 50/50 in 1993."
  • The partner split of 1993 income and withdrawals is therefore a derivation that assumes 50/50, not an accountant's figure. Chronology row 1993-12-31 is corrected by note, not by a silent edit.

FY1997 Exhibit C (printed; "equity 1997.pdf", 1O_MAgX6PGY98uluyxkDYt7KZwPCYVamG, read visually)

Total Manuel Leal Steve Leal
Balances 1/1/1997 $517,438 $451,069 $66,369
Capital contributions $21,856 $21,856 —
Net income $80,298 $40,149 $40,149 (printed 50/50)
Withdrawals $17,714 $16,231 $1,483
Balances 12/31/1997 $601,878 $496,843 $105,035

FY1994, FY1995 and FY1996 statements, returns and ledgers: NOT LOCATED (source register; chronology 1994-01-01).

2. The arithmetic (calc)

From 12/31/1993 to 1/1/1997, which covers 1994, 1995 and 1996:

Partner Change in capital
Manuel +$270,501 ($180,568 → $451,069)
Steve −$126,090 ($192,459 → $66,369)
Total +$144,411

If profits were split 50/50 (as printed in 1997 and inferred in 1993) and nothing else happened, the swing would require Steve to have withdrawn $396,591 more than Manuel over the three years. For comparison, Steve's withdrawals were about $40K in 1993 and $1.5K in 1997, and Manuel's were the larger in both years. That is implausible. A reallocation of capital from Steve to Manuel is the natural reading.

The implied transfer T is (396,591 + Manuel's withdrawals − Steve's withdrawals) ÷ 2:

Assumption about 1994–96 withdrawals Implied transfer
Equal withdrawals ≈ $198,296
1997 pattern (Manuel +$14,748/yr) ≈ $220,418
1993 pattern (Manuel +$42,797/yr) ≈ $262,491

The note's principal, $212,035, falls inside that range. Unpaid interest at 9% simple is $19,083 a year, about $286K over 1982–1996 if none was ever paid.

A competing explanation that also fits. The 1983 Partnership Agreement set initial capital at 75/25 (Manuel $636,105 / Steve $212,035). If the accountants allocated 1994–96 profits 75/25, or made a catch-up reallocation to the agreement's percentages, much of the swing is explained without any note payoff. For example, with roughly $600K of three-year income the implied transfer drops to about $60K–$137K. The 1994–96 profit split is unknown.

3. Grade and significance (both ways)

Grade: PARTIAL / INDETERMINATE. The capital shift is SUPPORTED by printed figures. That it was a payoff of the note is NOT ESTABLISHED. It is consistent with the numbers but not documented.

If it is proven, it helps:

  • The note allowed prepayment without consent, so a voluntary 1990s payoff needed no one's sign-off.
  • The value went to the payees' side. A transfer credited to Manuel's capital moved value to the community of Manuel and Hazel, the note's payees. That capital later passed to Hazel's trust and the Bypass column. So any renewed claim on the note's full balance (Thompson's 2017 P&I figure was $879,945.25) would be a double recovery.

What cuts against it:

  • There are no 1994–96 records. The 75/25 reallocation explanation is live.
  • The note requires payment "in lawful money". Whether a book transfer counts as payment is a question for counsel (UNVERIFIED).
  • The same theory was raised in March 2017, before the 12/7/2017 Settlement Agreement. ¶6 then compromised the note at $350,000. The settlement likely governs whatever happened in the 1990s (accord, novation and release effects are UNVERIFIED; counsel decides).
  • The live exposure is still A-56: no proof the $350,000 was ever paid. This hypothesis does not answer that.

4. What would prove or disprove it

  1. Partnership Forms 1065 with K-1s for 1994, 1995 and 1996. The K-1 capital-account analysis (beginning, contributed, share of income, withdrawals, ending) would show the transfer and its label. Check whether the 9/30 email's "Tax returns" attachments are these.
  2. Steve's and Marla's personal returns for 1994–96, which would include the partnership K-1s. The 2017 letter says Steve's returns back to 1983 exist.
  3. Manuel's and Hazel's 1994–96 returns: Schedule B interest income from the note shows whether interest was paid.
  4. Adair, Evans financial statements and adjusting entries for 1994–96 (from the firm or its successor; unlikely after 30 years).
  5. Any writing by Manuel or Hazel acknowledging payment, or a cancelled or marked note.

⚠️ THIS RESOLVES THE APPARENT CONTRADICTION IN OUR OWN PLEADING — AND REVERSES ADVERSE ITEM A-20

adverse_analysis.md A-20 treated Complaint ¶¶73 and 96 — pleading the Xavier appraisal was done "for purposes of filing for a IRS 706 filing" — as an admission that undercut our binding-appraisal theory.

On the full email record it is not an admission. It is an accurate description of a two-stage engagement that defendants interrupted:

  1. Xavier was jointly selected for both purposes (Exs. E, F, G, H).
  2. He completed the estate-tax appraisal (Ex. I, Aug. 18, 2023).
  3. He was waiting for the parties to jointly define buy-out scope (Stan Xavier's email of May 8, 2023, quoted in Ex. K).
  4. Before that scope was set, defendants revoked and retained J. Hower (Ex. K).

The buy-out appraisal was never completed because defendants walked away before the scope was defined — not because Xavier was the wrong appraiser or the appraisal was the wrong kind.

A-20 is withdrawn. The theory counsel should carry is the one already stated in our own March 3, 2025 letter (Ex. R), quoted at §6 below.

The Complaint pleads three times (¶¶46, 64, 107) that the valuation "failed to consider the negative capital account of HAZEL," and our mediation brief repeats it. It is $456,944.65 of asserted excess distributions ($262,592.00 during Hazel's lifetime plus $194,352.65 after her death). Those are different concepts. A partner can take distributions exceeding her profit share while her capital account remains positive.

The fact is supportable. The label in the Complaint is wrong. Counsel should consider correcting the characterization rather than defending "negative capital account," which our own reviewed statements contradict.

⭐ THE PARTNERSHIP NUMBER IS ALREADY AGREED

Defendants' partnership figure — $1,162,875 — is identical to ours (Ex. R). Both sides derived it the same way: Moss Adams' $3,101,000 business value net of double-counted land, × 37.5%.

The dispute is therefore narrower than it looks. The gap is four items:

  1. Real property basis — CX alone ($14,220,000) vs. the two-appraisal average ($16,160,000)
  2. Minority discount — 30% vs. 15%
  3. Their profit claim — $1,617,761, plus retains, interest, 2025 profit, and BioGas/Feedstock credits
  4. Our excess-distribution offset — $456,944.65

Counsel may find it useful to frame the CMC around those four items rather than the appraiser dispute, since the appraiser dispute drives only item 1.

⚠️ New issue: BioGas and Feedstock leases. Item 5 raises partnership revenue streams that appear nowhere else in this workspace — not in the financial statements reviewed, not in the capital analysis, not in either mediation brief. New open item OI-27.

A.2 Whether the year is split at 9/23/2022 (Hazel's date of death)

The FY2022 Exhibit C does NOT split the year at September 23, 2022. It presents each year as a single period: one net-income allocation line and one set of withdrawal lines for all of 2022, all in a column still headed "HAZEL LEAL." There is no interim balance at any date, no "Estate of Hazel Leal" column, and no pre-death/post-death sub-periods. (By contrast, the client-prepared workbook in Section C does split 2022 at the death date — see C.2.)

Consequence for the $194,352.65 reconciliation test: the FY2022 statement shows total withdrawals charged to the "HAZEL LEAL" column for calendar 2022 of $171,285 (Medical $148,871 + Personal $21,844 + Donations $570), but it does not state how much of that fell before versus after 9/23/2022. The pre/post-death split of Hazel-column 2022 withdrawals — including whether roughly $112,563 of post-death 2022 distributions occurred (i.e., $194,352.65 less $8,598 charged to "Estate of Hazel Leal" in the FY2023 statement and $73,192 in the FY2024 statement) — cannot be derived from this statement. Note also that the full-year Hazel-column withdrawals ($171,285) exceed $112,563, so the statement neither confirms nor excludes that quantum; monthly partnership ledgers or bank records would be required. No line in the FY2022 statement matches $194,352.65 or $112,563: not found.

01-verified-facts/lol-equity-age-retirement-2005-2007.md · 4,470 characters

Land O'Lakes equity "age retirement" checks to Manuel and Hazel, 2005–2007 (read 10/1/2026)

ATTORNEY WORK-PRODUCT SUPPORT — PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL. Extract of a client-saved document. It is not a finding of ownership.

Source: "Leal age retirement payouts.pdf" (Drive 1Cr2YBKQtc0PJRCwLUe7Y3c6_kJO78SP8, saved by the client to the litigation folder 10/1/2026; 13 pages; an image scan with no text layer, read visually page by page).

  • Six Land O'Lakes, Inc. cover letters (Jim Fife), each with its check stub and check face.
  • One page is a copy of Hazel's California driver license. That page holds personal identifiers; it is not transcribed here.

What the checks show

Every letter reads, in substance: "your Land O'Lakes equity age retirement check, which reflects Land O'Lakes commitment to return 100% of the equity investment held by member-owners who have reached age 75… your equity ownership… is now redeemed in full."

Date Payee LOL member no. Check no. Stub Amount
2/24/2005 Manuel C. Leal 2017201 14465258 R001052 IND_RET $86,534.70
4/7/2005 Manuel C. Leal 2041468 14477101 R001085 IND_RET $12,541.61
4/6/2006 Manuel C. Leal 2017201 14571322 R001197 IND_RET $5,800.81
2/22/2007 Manuel C. Leal 2017201 14645390 R001292 IND_RET $29,088.18
4/5/2007 Manuel C. Leal 2017201 14654723 R001319 IND_RET $14,732.93
6/21/2007 Hazel Leal 2017201 14670580 R001383 IND_RET $137,197.24
Total (calc) $285,895.47

All checks are payable to the individual at 21127 Road 68, Tulare, not to the partnership.

Grade and significance (both ways)

The payments are SUPPORTED by the checks and letters (copies; negotiation and deposit not shown). Three things are INDETERMINATE:

  1. Whose equity it was. Land O'Lakes patronage equity normally accrues on the milk a member ships.
    • If member no. 2017201 was the account the dairy shipped under after 1983, much of this equity was earned by partnership milk. It was paid out to Manuel and Hazel personally, and to Hazel at a time she was not a partner.
    • If it was Manuel's pre-1983 sole-proprietorship equity, or the membership was his personally, it was theirs.
    • No. 2041468 is a second membership, also unexplained.
  2. Whether the books recorded it. The reviewed statements (S-4) show large "Personal" withdrawals for Manuel in exactly these years:
    • 2005: $243,256, against Steve's $10,124;
    • 2007: $220,838, against Steve's $74,360. That is consistent with the checks having been run through the partnership as Manuel's withdrawals. It is not proof. If they were recorded, they are already in the parity numbers and favor our side. If they were not, they are unrecorded distributions of a partnership asset.
  3. How the client came to hold it. The scan's metadata (eCopy ShareScan) suggests a law-firm copier. It may be an enclosure to the 2016 Gin letters. Ask the client.

What helps: about $286,000 of cooperative equity went to Manuel and Hazel personally in 2005–2007, including $137,197 to Hazel individually. If it was partnership equity, it bears directly on the draw-parity comparison and on any "Steve took more" narrative (A-1, A-60).

What cuts against it:

  • Age-retirement redemptions are paid to the member of record. LOL's records name Manuel and Hazel as the owners, so the other side will say the equity was theirs.
  • This is 2005–2007, before the 2017 Settlement. Whether accounting claims for that period survive is a question for counsel (UNVERIFIED; see the Settlement ¶13/¶15 release scope).
  • It cannot be used without the partnership's LOL membership and equity statements.

To close it out (OI-82)

  1. The LOL membership records for no. 2017201 and no. 2041468: member name and entity type, and the equity allocation history by year. Source: Land O'Lakes member services; any 1099-PATR forms in the Drive tax folders.
  2. The partnership balance sheets for 2004–2008: an "Investment in Land O'Lakes" or patronage equity line, and whether it fell by about $286,000 in 2005–2007. The Adair, Evans / reviewed statements are already on Drive (S-4 covers Exhibit C only).
  3. Whether the checks were deposited to the dairy account (pre-2010 bank statements; the Citizens QuickBooks export starts 12/31/2009).
01-verified-facts/mary-visit-2026-10-04-transcript-extract.md · 8,507 characters

Visit with Mary, Hazel's sister (10/4/2026): transcript extract and grading

ATTORNEY WORK-PRODUCT SUPPORT — PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL. For counsel only.

Sources:

  • S-44: "Mary transcript" (Google Doc, Drive 1-r7jJAIkxn6Eyy5UJ70gcDVjZYG0LTzieF1-jMfs62E, created 10/5/2026 03:25 UTC by the client). It is an automatic phone transcript of S-43. Read in full.
  • S-43: the recording, 2026-10-04_visit-with-mary-hazels-sister_recording.m4a (15:00).

Limits of the transcript:

  • It has no speaker labels, many mis-heard names ("Janelle" is likely Danielle; "Robinson" possibly Robyn), and it starts mid-conversation. That is consistent with a trimmed 15:00 file.
  • Speaker attributions below are inferred from context (for example, the speaker who says "my mom" about Hazel is taken to be Steve). They are not established.
  • Nothing in the transcript shows that Mary was told about, or agreed to, the recording. Consent is NOT ESTABLISHED (A-85).

1. Who Mary is (from the transcript; CLIENT-ATTESTED / inferred)

  • Hazel's sister; Steve's aunt (client, 10/4/2026).
  • Age: about 90. "I'm gonna be 91 in December" (inferred Mary).
  • Competence indicators, in her own words:
    • "I still take care of all the books… I do all the booking";
    • "assistant to the Super[intendent] of Schools for 45 years";
    • "sold real estate for about 35 years";
    • she still owns three properties and has sold two on carry-back paper.
  • Widow of "Louie." She attends "the Pacheco stuff" and is close to "Louie's brother… Gabe." Her surname may be Pacheco (inference only; confirm).
  • "Eddie" went with her to see Hazel (relationship not stated).
  • Most of the 15 minutes is family genealogy (Pereira, Mendes, Rebello, Fagundes, Pacheco) and is not case-relevant.

2. Case-relevant passages (verbatim from the auto-transcript; errors as in source)

A. Hazel's move to a care home, and who controlled visits. Inferred Steve:

"when … they [] put my mom in that home … And Sue had to okay anybody to visit. … my mom was, oh, I'm going to go home. I want to go home"

"there's no reason for Hazel to be there because we were paying the same … for that fancy deal as we did for Consee … around the clock care in her house by people she liked … Same price … It was 14 … what we paid … for all four. Around the clock here, it was about 14 a month."

Checked against the books (register S-29, 504000 Medical–Hazel):

  • Quail Park Shannon Ranch (assisted living): 27 payments, 7/17/2020–9/1/2022, $258,712.74, running $9,687.50–$10,554.13 a month.
  • Private caregivers continued alongside: Maria Cardosa to 12/2021; Jennifer Sousa to 10/2021.
  • Monthly care spending ran about $13,000–$14,000 in 2021 and $13,000–$20,000 in 2019 before the move.

Grade: the cost statement is SUPPORTED in substance ("about 14 a month" fits 2021). The "same price as home care" comparison is roughly supported. "Sue had to okay anybody to visit" is CLIENT-ATTESTED (a party's statement on tape); no facility record has been reviewed.

B. Mary was refused a visit before Hazel died. Inferred Mary:

"Just before she died, she left a message with Eddie that something was going … So, Eddie called and tried to get an appointment for us to go see her before she died. And they wouldn't let us."

Grade: CLIENT-ATTESTED (witness statement). Who refused, and when, is not stated.

C. Hazel asked Mary for her banker and stockbroker; the confrontation with Danielle; police called. Inferred Mary:

"[Hazel] called me up and she wanted the name of her banker and of the stockbroker. … I tried to call her and I couldn't get through. And so Eddie and I … I'll tell her the information. Well, when I got there, before you know it, Danielle was there. That's because the nurses had instruction … to call … They started arguing with me … And then they called the police … It was a fiasco. They're the ones that asked me for the number. Hazel said Susan was messing with her bank account and Susan was messing with her stock account."

"They said I was there to attack … I didn't touch anyone. I didn't do anything. … they call the cops … And that's when they went to the attorney and filed this whatever it was. I'd like to show you that."

The date is not stated. It is likely during the Quail Park period, 7/2020–9/2022 (inference).

Grade: CLIENT-ATTESTED. What Hazel told Mary is hearsay within a witness account. Whether any of it is admissible is counsel's question (UNVERIFIED). The police call and any filing could be checked in public or agency records (§4).

D. The trust side's statements about Mary. Inferred Steve:

"Sue told my mom [you assaulted Danielle] … she and Sue convinced my mom that you attacked Danielle … that put a wedge between my mom and you. And I guess that was the intention, because maybe you were going to get to the bottom of something they didn't want to."

Grade: CLIENT-ATTESTED. Steve's speculation about motive is on tape, in his words (A-85).

E. Letters from the trust's attorney. Inferred Mary:

"The attorney she got was Ashley's … They were the ones who sent me a [letter]" / "I've got letters like that [from] that nasty witch for 10 years."

This points to documents in Mary's hands: attorney letters, possibly from Esraelian ("Robinson" may be "Robyn"), over about ten years, and "this whatever it was" that was filed. They are not seen.

F. Other:

  • "Sue got those houses." Speaker unclear; general knowledge only. It is consistent with the client's account (OI-83) but is not title evidence.
  • "Danielle was living in her house … she moved with my mom and put Jamie on the house" (unclear).
  • Mary on Susan: "If I died and Susan is there, you tell her to get her ass out."
  • Mary on the attorney: "she's a nasty woman."

3. Both ways

For us:

  1. A witness who was in Hazel's circle in 2020–22, who says Hazel sought her own banker/stockbroker information and said Susan was "messing with" her accounts, and that facility staff were instructed to call Danielle. That bears on who controlled Hazel's finances and access in her last years. The Morgan Stanley and account questions (A-54, OI-59, OI-62) sit nearby.
  2. Corroborates the care-cost record, and that Hazel's draws in 2020–22 were overwhelmingly her care. That is useful for Demand 6 and the $262,592 offset story.
  3. Mary presents as mentally sharp in this excerpt: dates, ages, finances, her own bookkeeping. If her testimony matters, her age argues for counsel acting soon.

Against us, or limits:

  1. Relevance to the buyout case is indirect. Nothing in the excerpt touches the partnership, the buyout, valuation, post-death profits or Hazel's intentions about the dairy. A fight over Susan's handling of Hazel's money risks looking like a trust contest. Hazel's trust has a no-contest clause, and Steve was disinherited by the 11/10/2017 restatement (A-79). How that interacts is counsel's call (UNVERIFIED).
  2. Mary is not neutral. She was in a police-involved confrontation with Danielle. She has received attorney letters accusing her. She calls the trust attorney a "nasty witch" and says Susan should be put out if Mary dies. Cross-examination would center on bias. Her age invites memory questions despite the competence indicators.
  3. The tape captures Steve feeding a theory to the witness ("I guess that was the intention… get to the bottom of something they didn't want to"). If produced, it supports a "plaintiff shaped her account" argument.
  4. Hearsay. Most of what matters is Hazel's words relayed by Mary.
  5. Consent to record is not shown (A-85). If Mary did not consent, the recording itself is a problem, separate from her live testimony (Penal Code § 632, UNVERIFIED).

4. What would make it evidence (OI-101)

  • Mary's own documents:
    • the attorney letter(s) and anything "filed";
    • her phone records or notes of Hazel's call asking for the banker/stockbroker names.
  • The police call: the agency (Visalia PD or Tulare County Sheriff), date and incident number.
  • The facility: Quail Park Shannon Ranch's visitor-authorization instructions and incident notes. Counsel obtains these by subpoena or authorization, not the client.
  • The date: when Hazel called Mary, and when the incident happened.

"ht" Cash checks 42 checks, $49,300.10, 5/2009–1/2018 51 checks, $67,710.00, 7/2010–1/2018

01-verified-facts/post-death-profits-issue.md · 43,990 characters

THE POST-DEATH PROFITS CLAIM — DOCUMENTARY ANALYSIS

ATTORNEY WORK-PRODUCT SUPPORT — PREPARED FOR COUNSEL — NOT A FILING — NOT LEGAL ADVICE

Issue: Defendants contend the Hazel J. Leal Revocable Trust remains a partner and is entitled to partnership profits for the period after Hazel's death on September 23, 2022. Prepared: August 18, 2026. This is the largest dollar issue in the case.

⚠️ This memo analyses the CONTRACT TEXT only. It states no legal conclusion. The California statutory and case-law overlay — principally Corporations Code §§ 16601, 16603 and 16701 — could not be verified in this environment (see ../02-legal-research/00-READ-FIRST-research-reliability.md). Every statutory reference below is flagged and must be confirmed by counsel in Westlaw/CoCounsel before it is relied on.

1. What they are claiming, and what it is worth

Source Claim
Ex. J (9/26/2023, Esraelian) "There was an agreement as to the amount of the profit distribution owed to Hazel from 2015 through 2021 in the amount of $850,894.54… this amount is only the profit through 2021 … it doesn't include Hazel's share of the profit since January 2022!"
Ex. U (6/19/2025, Esraelian) — item 4 "Hazel's share of unpaid Partnership Profit through December 2024, due to her from her Partnership interest in the Bypass Trust as well as her own interest in the Partnership, along with unpaid retains, in the amount of $1,617,761, which includes a reasonable rate of interest on account of non-payment of these amounts due from the date of Hazel's passing."
Ex. U — closing "plus Hazel's 2025 profit distribution to be calculated as of the date of final settlement"
Ex. U — item 5 "credits due to the Partnership on account of the BioGas and Feedstock leases… Hazel's trust should receive its pro-rata share"
Defendants' mediation brief, p.3 "He also disputes the payment of profits from the date of Hazel's death until the buyout is completed, claiming falsely that alleged delays… somehow absolves him of his obligation to pay an owner of the company its share of profits pursuant to its ownership interest."
Defendants' mediation brief, p.4 "the issue of unpaid profits has yet to be finalized. As a result, the buyout of the Dairy cannot be completed as the unpaid profits need to be paid prior to the sale of the Dairy."

Note the structure of their position: unpaid profits must be paid before the buyout closes. That makes the profits question a gating issue, not a side issue — which is why it belongs at the CMC.

UPDATE 8/18/2026 — the $850,894.54 "agreement" is now documented. Esraelian's email of August 30, 2022 (client-produced; native copy to be pulled) agrees with Jace's calculation of $850,894.54 for 2015–2021 — covering Hazel personally and as Bypass beneficiary — and directs payment annually, capped at basis, via Mike Edwards, to avoid capital gains tax. The amount is agreed; the schedule their counsel prescribed was multi-year; Hazel died 24 days later. See OI-25 (answered) and A-23 (updated).

Note also that their claim bundles at least four distinct things, which counsel should insist on separating:

  1. Pre-death partnership profit (2015 – 9/23/2022)
  2. Post-death partnership profit (9/23/2022 forward) ← the issue in this memo
  3. Bypass Trust income (a trust claim, not a partnership claim — see §6)
  4. Milk retains, and now BioGas/Feedstock lease credits

2. Who the partners are, and in what percentages — now established

Amended and Restated Partnership Agreement, Article I.B (Ex. C to defendants' mediation brief):

"Partnership Interest: The percentage interest owned by each Partner as shown on the books of the Partnership as follows:

Partner Interest
THE MANUEL C. LEAL BYPASS TRUST 7.5 percent
STEVE M. LEAL 30 percent
THE HAZEL J. LEAL REVOCABLE TRUST 37.5 percent
THE STEVE AND MARLA LEAL LIVING TRUST 25 percent

This resolves several open questions at once:

  • Hazel's Trust holds 37.5% — matching Esraelian's own description in Ex. D ("we need to value Hazel's 37.5% interest in the dairy") and the 37.5% used in every valuation.
  • Steve's side holds 55% (30% + 25%) and the Bypass Trust holds 7.5%.
  • The 50/50-vs-75/25 question in our Capital Analysis (adverse_analysis.md A-10) is answered for the post-June-2018 period by an executed instrument. It remains open only for the pre-2018 period.
  • On Hazel's death, Steve became sole surviving co-trustee of the Bypass Trust, so he now directs 30% + 25% + 7.5% = 62.5%, against Hazel's Trust's 37.5% pending buyout.

And critically — the defined term. The Agreement's PARTIES clause provides:

"Second Party: HAZEL J. LEAL, Co-Trustee of THE MANUEL C. LEAL BYPASS TRUST, Dated: February 14, 2005; Trustee of THE HAZEL J. LEAL REVOCABLE TRUST, Dated: November 3, 2008 (hereinafter collectively 'Hazel')."

"Hazel" is a defined term that expressly includes her capacity as trustee of Hazel's Trust. Counsel may consider this significant, because it is the answer to the most obvious statutory objection — see §5.1.

3. What the Agreement says happens on Hazel's death

Article XIII — "WITHDRAWAL OR DEATH OF A PARTNER"

B.1. "Sections B.1-3 of this Article … specifically apply to Hazel. Hazel cannot sell her Partnership Interest to anyone who is not a member of the Partnership. If Hazel dissociates from the Partnership, either by sale or other transfer of some or all of Hazel's Partnership Interest for consideration, as a result of Hazel's death or desire to sell (the 'Dissociating Events'), then the Partnership shall purchase her Partnership Interest at a price determined and payable in the same manner as set forth in Article [XIII].B.2."

B.2. "In the event of the death of Hazel, the Partnership shall continue and will not be dissolved. The Partnership shall purchase her Partnership Interest at ninety percent (90%) of the appraisal value of her Partnership Interest including any discounts identified in the appraisal (the 'Value'). At the time of purchase, the Partnership shall pay ten percent (10%) of the Value on the note to purchase the Partnership Interest. The note will be amortized over a twenty (20) year term, at four percent (4%) interest. The Partnership note will be due in ten (10) years."

Three features counsel may consider decisive on the contract text

(a) The Agreement itself calls Hazel's death a "Dissociating Event." Art. XIII.B.1 defines the term that way in express words: "If Hazel dissociates … as a result of Hazel's death … (the 'Dissociating Events')." Art. XIII.J repeats it — "within thirty (30) days of Hazel's dissociation or death." The parties contracted for the characterisation defendants now dispute.

(b) The buyout is mandatory, not optional. "the Partnership shall purchase her Partnership Interest." It is not an option Steve may exercise; it is an obligation triggered by the Dissociating Event.

(c) The Agreement supplies its own compensation for deferred payment — 4% interest, not profits. Art. XIII.B.2 prescribes 10% down and a note "amortized over a twenty (20) year term, at four percent (4%) interest," due in ten years. Settlement Agreement ¶7(b) is identical. The parties expressly addressed what the selling side receives while it waits to be paid, and what they chose was interest at 4%.

Counsel may consider framing it this way: on defendants' reading, the Trust would receive (i) 90% of appraised value, (ii) 4% interest on the deferred balance, and (iii) a continuing 37.5% profit share — three returns on one interest, for a period during which the Agreement says the Partnership "shall purchase" that interest.

(d) The asymmetry in Article XIII.D is deliberate and worth noting

D. "In the event of the death of Steve or Marla, the Partnership shall not be dissolved and his or her interest in the Partnership shall transfer according to the terms of his or her Will, Trust, or by intestacy, and shall not be subject to any buy out provision of this Amended Agreement."

Steve's and Marla's interests pass by estate plan and are expressly NOT bought out. Hazel's is mandatorily bought out. The Agreement treats the two sides differently on purpose. Counsel may consider that this supports reading Art. XIII.B as an exit mechanism — Hazel's side was always intended to leave the Partnership on her death, while Steve's side continues.

4. Article VI.E answers the "excess distributions" question too

Article VI.E. "A credit balance in a Partner's Drawing Account shall be treated as a liability of the Partnership to that Partner… A debit balance in a Partner's Drawing Account, whether occasioned by drawings in excess of his share of Partnership profits or by charging him for his share of Partnership loss, shall be treated as a liability of that Partner to the Partnership and shall not reduce his interest in the capital of the Partnership."

⚠️ THIS VINDICATES THE SUBSTANCE OF OUR OFFSET AND CONFIRMS THE LABEL IS WRONG

Our March 3, 2025 letter (Ex. R) deducts $262,592.00 of "excess distributions above her partnership share during Hazel's lifetime" plus $194,352.65 of post-death distributions. The Complaint (¶¶46, 64, 107) calls this a "negative capital account," and our own reviewed financials show a positive capital account — which this workspace flagged as a contradiction (adverse_analysis.md A-4).

Article VI.E explains why both are true and which label is right. Excess drawings create a debit balance in the Drawing Account, which the Agreement makes "a liability of that Partner to the Partnership" and which "shall not reduce his interest in the capital of the Partnership."

So the capital account is supposed to stay positive while a drawing-account debit accumulates. They are separate ledgers by contract. Our offset is not a negative capital account — it is a drawing-account debit balance owed by the partner to the partnership, and the Agreement says so in terms.

Counsel should consider amending the Complaint's characterisation to track Article VI.E. As pleaded it is contradicted by our own financials; as Article VI.E describes it, it is supported by the Agreement.

Still needed: Frazer's capital-account summary — Exhibit B to the March 3, 2025 letter (open_items.md OI-5, OI-28).

5. The counterarguments — stated at full strength

This section is written against our own position. Counsel should not go to the CMC without it.

5.1 — "The partner is a TRUST, and a trust is not dissociated by a trustee's death"

This is their best argument. The partner named in Article I.B is "THE HAZEL J. LEAL REVOCABLE TRUST" — an entity, not Hazel personally. Hazel's death substituted Ashley and Susan as successor co-trustees; the Trust itself did not die.

Corporations Code § 16601 — UNVERIFIED, counsel must confirm. Research memo R4 reports that § 16601(7) treats a trust-partner as dissociated on "distribution of the trust's entire transferable interest in the partnership, but not merely by reason of the substitution of a successor trustee." If that is the statutory text, the default rule is that this Trust remains a partner.

Our answers, in order of strength:

  1. The Agreement's defined term reaches the Trust. "Hazel" is defined to mean Hazel "Trustee of THE HAZEL J. LEAL REVOCABLE TRUST." Art. XIII.B.1 makes "Hazel's death" the Dissociating Event for that defined party — i.e. for the Trust's interest. The parties contracted around the default.
  2. Partnership agreements generally govern relations among partners — counsel should confirm the scope and the non-waivable list (Corp. Code § 16103 — UNVERIFIED).
  3. The Agreement was drafted with this exact structure in view. Every partner is a trust or a trustee. The drafters knew Hazel would hold through a revocable trust and still keyed the buyout to "Hazel's death."
  4. Art. XIII.D confirms the parties knew how to say "passes by trust and is not bought out" — they said it for Steve and Marla and did not say it for Hazel.

Honest assessment: argument 1 is strong on the text, but it is a contract-versus-statute question and counsel must verify § 16601 and § 16103 before relying on it. This is the single most important item to run in Westlaw.

5.2 — "The buyout never closed, so nothing converted"

Art. XIII.B.2 says "At the time of purchase, the Partnership shall pay ten percent (10%) of the Value." There has been no purchase, no 10% payment, and no note. Defendants will argue the Trust cannot be treated as a paid-out seller when it has received nothing, and that a party carrying the risk of an unliquidated interest for four years should share in the returns.

Our answers:

  1. Interest is the contractual answer to delay (Art. XIII.B.2; Settlement ¶7(b)) — and it runs at 4%, which is what our own July 2026 offer tendered.
  2. The valuation date is fixed at death by the Settlement Agreement, TIC ¶11 and Art. XIII.J ("as of the date of Hazel's death"). If value is fixed at death, counsel may argue the economic position was fixed at death too.
  3. Corp. Code § 16701 — UNVERIFIED. R4 and R3 both report that RUPA's buyout remedy is value as of the date of dissociation plus interest from that date. If so, the statutory model matches the contract: interest, not profits.

Honest assessment: the equitable pull of "they haven't been paid anything in four years" is real, and a court may feel it. Counsel should be ready with the delay chronology (§5.3) and with the fact that we tendered interest.

[CORRECTION 9/26/2026 — see adverse analysis A-67.] "Tendered" above means offered in a settlement letter. The 7/2/2026 offer required "a release of all other claims by all parties (Civ. §1542)". VERIFIED: a conditional tender does not stop the running of interest under Civ. Code §§ 1504/1494 (Mission Ins. Group v. Merco (1983) 147 Cal.App.3d 1059, 1067). The point that we consistently proposed the contract's 4% stands. The suggestion that interest was stopped by our offers does not. For the unconditional-tender option, see OI-72.

5.3 — "Steve caused the delay, so he cannot benefit from it"

Defendants' brief: "Steve's unlawful conduct, secrecy, and breaches… are the cause of the present dispute." Our position is the reverse — they revoked the agreed appraiser and withheld the reports.

This is a genuinely contested factual question and it is the one the post-death profits issue may actually turn on. Our documentary record here is now strong (see email-exhibits-extract.md):

  • Esraelian proposed Correia-Xavier (Ex. E) and engaged him for the buyout (Ex. G)
  • Xavier was waiting on the parties to define buyout scope (Stan Xavier's 5/8/2023 email, quoted in Ex. K)
  • Esraelian promised the appraisal "by next week" on 8/18/2023 (Ex. I) and had not produced it on 9/26/2023 (Ex. J)
  • Defendants unilaterally retained J. Hower and then Moss Adams (Exs. K, N)
  • Ashley routed reports to Jace with a stated preference they not go to counsel (Ex. P)

Against us: the $850,894.54 demand of 9/26/2023 went unanswered in this record; no monthly accountings under Settlement ¶8 have been located; and defendants say they were waiting on information from the Dairy's CPA.

5.4 — ⭐ THE STRONGEST ARGUMENT AGAINST US: our own reviewed financials allocate profits to Hazel after her death

This is not an argument they have to construct. It is in our own books, signed off by our own accountants, every year since she died.

Manuel Leal & Son Dairy, Statements of Partners' Capital, FY2024 and FY2023 (Frazer LLP, Independent Accountants' Review Report dated February 18, 2025 — Drive 1cqN3Cp2t9pMFiql2mXOYYZFZTxsSVZRm). The statement carries a column headed "ESTATE OF HAZEL LEAL" and allocates to it, in every period after her death:

Total Steve Leal Estate of Hazel Leal Bypass Trust
Balances 1/1/2023 $9,201,369 $5,506,304 $2,873,816 $821,249
Transfer of capital (Note 8) 0 +821,249 0 (821,249)
Capital contribution 360,000 360,000 0 0
Net loss 2023 (888,608) (555,380) (333,228) 0
Withdrawals 2023 (155,638) (147,040) (8,598) 0
Balances 12/31/2023 8,517,123 5,985,133 2,531,990 0
Net income 2024 2,026,658 1,266,661 759,997 0
Withdrawals 2024 (148,063) (74,871) (73,192) 0
Balances 12/31/2024 $10,395,718 $7,176,923 $3,218,795 $0

The allocation ratio is exactly 62.5% / 37.5% in both years — precisely the Article I.B percentages, with the Bypass Trust's 7.5% rolled into Steve's column as of 1/1/2023.

How Cunningham uses this, and counsel should assume she will lead with it:

  1. Practical construction. The party now arguing that Hazel's side ceased to be a partner on September 23, 2022 has, for three consecutive fiscal years, had its own accountants allocate 37.5% of profit and loss to her estate and carry a capital account for it — $3,218,795 at December 31, 2024.
  2. We also distributed to her after death. The same statements show withdrawals charged to the Estate of Hazel Leal of $8,598 in 2023 and $73,192 in 2024 — including "Personal" of $70,441 in 2024. A dissociated non-partner does not take personal withdrawals. (These are presumably part of the $194,352.65 our March 2025 letter deducts.)
  3. The books are ours. Our client manages the Dairy and engages Frazer. This is not defendants' characterisation; it is our own reviewed financial statement.

Our best documentary responses — and counsel should weigh them honestly:

  1. Bookkeeping convention is not legal entitlement. Where a mandatory buyout is triggered but unclosed, an accountant may reasonably keep the exiting partner's account open until the purchase settles. Frazer prepared these statements; counsel should ask Frazer why the account was maintained and on whose instruction before treating the presentation as an admission.
  2. Allocation is not distribution. Art. VII.C provides that "All Profits and Losses allocated to the Partners shall be credited or charged … to their Capital Accounts." The statements show allocations to a capital account, not cash distributions of profit. A capital allocation that is later extinguished in the buyout is not the same as an entitlement to be paid profit.
  3. ⭐ If she shares profits, she shares losses — and 2023 was a big loss year. The Dairy's net loss in FY2023 was $(888,608), of which the Estate of Hazel Leal was allocated $(333,228). Net across FY2023 and FY2024 the allocation to Hazel's side is $759,997 − $333,228 = $426,769 — not the seven figures their letter implies for the same period. Counsel should test whether defendants' $1,617,761 nets the FY2023 loss. If it does not, the claim is overstated on our own books.

Honest assessment: response 3 is strong and quantified; responses 1 and 2 are real but they are explanations of our own conduct, which is a weaker posture than pointing at theirs. Counsel should decide early whether to (a) argue the accounting presentation is a convention that does not control the legal question, or (b) accept the allocation framework and litigate the amount — pressing the FY2023 loss, the offsets, and the valuation date. These are different cases and the choice should be deliberate.

5.5 — "Article VII allocates profits to Partners, full stop"

Art. VII.A/B. "Partnership Profits, Losses, gains and credits shall be allocated among the Partners in accordance with their respective Partnership Interest… The balance to be distributed to the Partners in accordance with their respective Partnership interests."

Defendants will read this as unqualified. Our answer is that it turns entirely on whether the Trust is still a "Partner" after the Dissociating Event — which is §5.1. Article VII does not independently answer the question; it just restates it. Counsel should not over-rely on Art. VII in either direction.

6. What is genuinely SEPARATE and probably survives regardless

Counsel should concede these rather than defend them, and insist they be unbundled from the partnership-profits claim.

6.1 — Bypass Trust income (a trust claim, not a partnership claim)

The Bypass Trust is a separate partner holding 7.5%. Settlement Agreement ¶5:

"Hazel shall be entitled to receive all income from the account in the Manuel C. Leal Bypass Trust on a monthly basis from the date of Manuel's death. Any unpaid amounts of income… shall be paid to Hazel within 30 days of execution of this Agreement."

Steve was a co-trustee of the Bypass Trust and became sole surviving trustee on Hazel's death. Our own July 2026 letter offers $327,427.02 for "earned but undistributed income from the Manuel C. Leal Bypass Trust through Hazel's date of death."

This is a trustee-accounting claim owed to Hazel as income beneficiary. It is not affected by Article XIII at all, and the dissociation argument does not reach it. See adverse_analysis.md A-14 and open_items.md OI-15 — this remains our most dangerous exposure.

⭐ What happened to the Bypass Trust's 7.5% is now answered — by our own financials.

Note 8 — Transfer of capital. "In 2022, Hazel Leal passed away and the Manuel Leal Bypass Trust was dissolved. On January 1, 2023, the partnership interest of the Manuel Leal Bypass Trust was transferred to Steve Leal." — FY2024/2023 Statements, Note 8

The Bypass Trust's $821,249 capital moved to Steve's column effective 1/1/2023, and the Bypass column reads $0 from that date.

Two consequences, pulling in opposite directions:

  • For us: defendants' Ex. U claims profit due to Hazel "from her Partnership interest in the Bypass Trust." The Bypass Trust dissolved on her death and its partnership interest went to Steve. There is no post-death Bypass partnership interest for her estate to claim.
  • Against us: the transfer was to our own client, recorded by our own accountants, effective the January 1 after Hazel died — and defendants were not told, so far as this record shows. Counsel should expect them to ask by what authority the Bypass Trust was dissolved and its 7.5% partnership interest transferred to the surviving co-trustee, who is also the managing partner. Obtain the Bypass Trust instrument's termination and remainder provisions before this comes up. This connects directly to adverse_analysis.md A-14 and open_items.md OI-15, and it makes those items more urgent, not less.

The boundary on the income claim: ¶5 entitles Hazel to Bypass income during her life. The pre-death claim (our $327,427.02 offer) is unaffected by any of this and remains live.

6.2 — Milk retains

Settlement Agreement ¶9. "Hazel shall be paid the sum of at least three thousand dollars ($3,000) each year for milk retentions commencing on December 15, 2017 and continuing annually thereafter."

Ex. U claims "unpaid retains." The clause has no stated death cutoff. Counsel should determine what was paid and when. The annual amount is small; the point is that it is a separate contractual obligation and should not be conflated with profit share.

6.3 — Pre-death profits (2015 – 9/23/2022)

Nothing in the dissociation analysis touches profits earned before Hazel died. The $850,894.54 asserted "agreement" (Ex. J) covers 2015–2021 and sits squarely in this period. This is a real claim and counsel should assume it is owed in some amount — the questions are the number, the offset, and whether an agreement on $850,894.54 exists. OI-25.

7. How the two positions compare, in numbers

Our position (as offered 7/2/2026) Their position (Ex. U, 6/19/2025)
Real property $3,653,412.50 $5,198,366 (pre-10%)
Partnership $1,046,587.50 $1,162,875 (pre-10%) → both sides agree at $1,162,875
Compensation for the wait $677,830.41 interest at 4% "from the dissociation to present" $1,617,761 profit + retains + interest through Dec 2024, plus 2025 profit, plus lease credits
Bypass income $327,427.02 bundled into the $1,617,761
Offsets $456,944.65 excess distributions (in the March 2025 offer) none
Total $5,705,257.43 $7,359,766 + 2025 profit + BioGas/Feedstock credits

Our own offer already stakes out the dissociation position. The July 2, 2026 letter tenders "$677,830.41 in interest (4% per annum) covering the period from the dissociation to present." We have used the word "dissociation" and paid the contract's 4% rate. That is a coherent position consistent with Art. XIII.B.2 — counsel should keep it consistent.

Counsel should confirm the $677,830.41 computation. 4% on $4,700,000 from 9/23/2022 to 7/2/2026 (≈3.77 years) is approximately $709,600, so the figure appears to run from a later start date or a different base. Whatever the basis, it should be stated, because opposing counsel will reconstruct it.

The practical shape of the dispute: the parties already agree on the partnership value ($1,162,875 pre-discount). The gap is (1) real property basis, (2) minority discount, (3) this issue — profits vs. interest for the post-death period, and (4) our offset. Item 3 is worth roughly $940,000 on the face of the two letters, before 2025 profit and the lease credits.

8. What counsel needs — new open items

  1. ⭐ Verify Corp. Code §§ 16601(7), 16603 and 16701, and § 16103 in Westlaw/CoCounsel. The whole issue turns on whether the Agreement's "Dissociating Events" definition displaces the default rule that substituting a successor trustee does not dissociate a trust-partner. → open_items.md OI-30.
  2. FY2024/2023 statements have now been read (see §5.4). 9. Two drafting defects in the Agreement, noted for completeness

  • Article cross-references are wrong throughout Article XIII. The text repeatedly says "this Article XII" and "Article XII.B.2" where it plainly means XIII. Art. XIII.B.1 refers to "Article XII.B.2" for the price mechanism; the mechanism is at XIII.B.2. Counsel should be ready to address this if defendants argue ambiguity — and note that the Complaint's ¶105 citation to "Article XIII, Section B.2" is CORRECT, as is ¶22's citation to §J. They govern different things (the buyout right and the appraiser mechanism respectively). This corrects the flag raised at complaint-extract.md §6, item 4.
  • Article XIII.I cites "Sections 15672-15673 of the California Corporations Code" for an assignee's rights. Those are limited partnership provisions, and this is a general partnership formed "pursuant to the Uniform Partnership Act." Counsel should confirm the correct current sections before quoting the clause.
  • Preamble dates the Original Agreement March 16, 1983; the Settlement Agreement Recitals A and C say March 10, 1983. A six-day discrepancy in our own instruments. → OI-16.

10. Other findings from the FY2024/2023 reviewed statements

Recorded because they bear on other items in this workspace.

10.1 — The accountants' conclusion is QUALIFIED, on two GAAP departures, one at management's request.

"Basis for Qualified Conclusion — Under generally accepted accounting principles, all loans due within one year of the balance sheet date should be shown as current liabilities. At the request of the Dairy's management, debt amounting to $1,391,112 is shown as long-term even though the loans are due within one year. Additionally … the Company has presented its results of farming operations on a net basis … [not] in accordance with … GAAP."

Counsel should expect this to be used alongside the restatements already recorded at adverse_analysis.md A-9: our financial presentation departs from GAAP in a way the accountants attribute to management's request, and management is our client.

10.2 — Line-of-credit activity is substantial, which sharpens OI-14. The AgWest Farm Credit lines allow maximum borrowings of $1,700,000 (secured by the dairy herd) and $300,000 (feed inventories), at 8.30%. The line-of-credit balance moved from $913,420 at 12/31/2023 to $0 at 12/31/2024, and the Dairy ran a $99,279 bank overdraft at 12/31/2024 with $0 cash. Settlement Agreement ¶11(a) caps draws at $100,000 in any 30-day period. Movement of that size cannot be assessed from annual statements. The monthly line-of-credit statements are essential — open_items.md OI-14.

10.3 — No BioGas or Feedstock lease appears anywhere in the FY2024/2023 statements. The only lease disclosed (Note 5) is a solar equipment finance lease from Farm Credit Leasing, ten-year, expiring October 2026. Defendants' Ex. U claims credits from "BioGas and Feedstock leases." "Note 6 — Related party transactions. JL Ag is a related party that provides harvesting services for the Dairy. During the years ended December 31, 2024 and 2023, the Dairy paid harvesting expenses totaling $22,102 and $13,330, respectively, to JL Ag."

Small in amount, but it is a disclosed related-party payment by a partnership whose management is accused of self-dealing. Counsel should know who owns JL Ag and be ready on it. → OI-33.

10.5 — Acreage, again. Note 1 states the Dairy "farms approximately 584 acres." Moss Adams' Exhibit Q says 565.12 acres; the Settlement Agreement and Complaint say 652.02 acres. Three figures. Counsel should reconcile — adverse_analysis.md A-26.

LEAL REVOCABLE TRUST." Minor, but counsel should note that our own books do not use the partner's contractual identity — and that "estate" is closer to defendants' framing than to ours.

Full detail: financials-2022-2025-extract.md. Four findings, two of them serious:

12. UPDATE — the FEDERAL K-1s are now read (tax/banking sweep, 8/18/2026)

Source: partnership Forms 1065 on Drive, 2015–2022 and 2024, read in full; per-year table in drive-sweep/financials-tax-banking-sweep.md §2. This is the strongest documentary development on this issue in either direction, and both sides of it must be absorbed.

12.1 What the returns show (adverse to the "creditor-only" framing)

  • 2022 (the death year): Hazel's individual K-1 is marked FINAL (37.5% → 0) and the Bypass Trust's K-1 is FINAL (7.5% → 0). In their place, the Hazel J Leal Revocable Trust UDT 11/3/2008 (EIN 88-6746852) enters at 0 → 37.5%, taking a $93,988 income allocation and an $11,172 distribution, and — significantly — a $1,841,569 share of recourse liabilities. Steve moves 55 → 62.5 (absorbing the Bypass 7.5).
  • 2024: the partnership return continues Steve 62.5 / Hazel Revocable Trust 37.5, allocating the Trust $375,483 of ordinary income, $82,441 of cash distributions, and a $1,499,399 recourse-liability share.
  • 2023: the Form 1065 is NOT on the Drive (the "2023.pdf" in the tax folder is a Bankston rent cash-flow). Obtain it from Frazer — OI-48.

The partnership's own federal filings, two tax years after death, treat the Revocable Trust as a 37.5% profit-sharing, liability-sharing partner — not as a dissociated creditor holding a note claim at 4%. Defendants will call this our own admission, on returns our side signed. The absolute "she stopped being a partner on September 23, 2022" framing cannot be squared with these documents; the position must run through the contract (Art. XIII.B: death = Dissociating Event; buyout at 90% + 4% as the exclusive delay compensation) and election/waiver — as the drafts-sweep already forced (adverse analysis A-30), and as the FY2023–24 books already suggested (§5.4 above).

12.2 What the same returns give us (the loss-sharing corollary, now locked)

If the K-1s make the Trust a continuing partner, they make it a continuing partner in the loss year too. The client's Partnership Income Summary shows 2023 book income of ($888,608) — and 37.5% of that is ($333,228), exactly the FY2023 Estate-column allocation in the reviewed statements (§5.4). 37.5% of 2024's $2,026,658 is $759,997 — again exact. The missing 2023 return matters precisely here — it is the document that forces the netting.

Hazel received guaranteed payments every year 2015–2022: $62,000 (2015–16) rising to $84,000 (2020), $78,000 (2021), $54,000 in the partial 2022 year — then none. Defendants: "you treated her as a partner entitled to compensation; the payments stopped only because you cut them off." Us: the payments track Art. VI.B's guaranteed care payments (paid "even if Hazel's capital account is negative"), i.e., contract performance, not evidence of open-ended partner status — and they ceased with her death because they were personal to her. The characterization fight is predictable; the payment history itself is now fixed.

The 2018 K-1 line-1 figures (Steve $151,219 / Hazel $134,922 / Bypass $16,985) are not in 55/37.5/7.5 proportion as printed. 13.1 Their own schedule nets the post-death losses. The $1,498,480.05 "net distributions payable" is built from lifetime accrual (3/26/2015–9/22/2022 income $6,293,315 × 37.5%/7.5%, less lifetime distributions → $1,368,326.65 accrued at DOD) PLUS a post-death sequence that includes 2022's post-death loss ($338,044) and 2023's loss ($888,608) alongside 2024's $2,026,658 and a 2025 estimate. 13.2 The lifetime component collides with the agreed $850,894.54. The delta (~$517K) is partial-2022 income plus methodology drift. Reconciling THOSE two numbers — both from their side's pen — is the single most valuable cross-exhibit on the profits claim. (Both are separate from Jace's $1,033,717.15 framework — OI-39/OI-51 still stands.)

13.3 Their asymmetry: "The 7.5% allocation to the Bypass Trust ceased at the time of death." Their schedule stops the Bypass Trust's allocation at Hazel's death while CONTINUING her trust's 37.5% allocation for years afterward. Whatever principle ceases one trust's profit share at death must be tested against their continuing-partner theory for the other. (Their likely answer — the Bypass terminated by its own terms and its interest passed to Steve 1/1/2023 — reopens the Bypass-dissolution documentation gap, A-39/OI list.) §5.2 — new answer (3). The trustees have received $288,000 in cash since the death: 48 automatic $6,000 payments, 10/15/2022–9/15/2026 (Citizens QuickBooks register S-29, coded 725000; calc).

§12.3 — correction note. "Then none" is accurate only for K-1 guaranteed payments. The cash continued at $6,000 a month to 9/2026. The guaranteed-payment label ceased; the payments did not.

ADDENDUM 10/1/2026 (later): the client's "double-dipping" framing, and two additional points for counsel

Client (Jace, 10/1/2026): "How would it be reasonable to suggest that they can sell their share of a business and also share in the profits after that date of appraisal? That's double dipping. I really doubt they would be putting money into the business if we had a losing year." This is the §3(c) argument in plain words: value is fixed at death, and waiting is paid at 4%. It is not a new legal theory.

Two additional points for counsel to test:

  1. Does the date-of-death value already price the future profits?
    • If the Moss Adams business valuation (the agreed $1,162,612.50 pre-90% figure) used an income or going-concern approach, it valued the 37.5% interest by the profits it was expected to earn.
    • Paying that value and the actual post-death profits would then pay for the same earnings twice.
    • Check the Moss Adams method section before using this (the valuation method is not confirmed in this workspace).
  2. The losing-year point needs care.
    • On paper, the estate did share the 2023 loss. The books charged its column $333,228, and defendants' own 6/19/2025 schedule nets the 2022 and 2023 losses (§13.1).
    • In cash, the estate shared none of it. In 2023 it contributed $0 and drew about $72,000, while Steve contributed $360,000 (A-77; OI-88).
    • The accurate version of the client's point: the estate shared losses only as bookkeeping entries, while Steve alone funded them.
    • Expect the reply that no one asked the trustees for capital. Whether the agreement has a capital-call mechanism is NOT ESTABLISHED in this workspace; counsel should check the executed Partnership Agreement.

2.4 Statement about draws / capital accounts (p.18)

"Differences in draws on an annual basis can result in the capital accounts for each Partner to reflect a different percentage as time goes on."

Also, on distributions (p.29): "Distributions from the Partnership have been reasonable, with excess retained in the entity as needed." No partner-specific draw amounts appear anywhere in the report.

2.5 Discounts applied

  • Lack of control: "it is our considered opinion that a 12.5% adjustment to the net asset value should be applied in determining the value of the Subject Interest." (§6.3.0, p.30). Rationale includes: "The Partnership Agreement indicates a 75o/o - 25% split. In addition, the wording of the Agreement appears to also give Manuel C. Leal control over many aspects of the entity. However, as a community property interest in Manuel Leal's interest, this valuation must focus on 50% of that interest. Therefore, it does not unilaterally have control." (p.30). Benchmark data: Partnership Profiles secondary-market discounts, category averages 19%–39% (table, p.29).
  • Lack of marketability: "it is my considered opinion that a 15% lack of marketability adjustment for the Subject Interest applicable in this matter." (§7.3.0, p.33).

  • Assumption 1 (p.6): "While the Partnership tax returns indicate that the Partnership owns the land utilized by the entity, the Partnership's attorney has provided documentation indicating that the land parcels are actually owned by the Partners in various trusts, outside of the Partnership. All improvements to the land beyond bare dirt have been paid for and are owned by the Partnership."
  • p.16–17: "the Partnership does not own the land it utilizes for its operations."
  • Current-value balance sheet (p.24): Land book value $2,970,344 adjusted to $0 — Note B: "According to documents provided, the Land is owned outside of the Partnership."
  • Included at appraised values: improvements per Correia-Xavier, Inc. allocation (p.39 summary): Dairy appraisal total $11,500,000 → Land $8,400,000 / Improvements $3,100,000; Feedlot $1,700,000 → Land $1,350,000 / Improvements $350,000; improvements total $3,450,000 carried onto the balance sheet. Long-term debt of $4,579,685 and total liabilities $6,383,333 kept at book (p.24).

Leal managing partner; "placed limitations on Steve's ability to bind the Partnership in obligations greater than $5,000 without the managing Partners' consent"; transfers of interests need "prior written consent of the other Partner"; buyout formula = net worth of tangible assets less debts "multiplied by the Partner's ownership interest percentage in the partnership."

4.1 Every factual assertion adverse to Steve (with quotes)

  1. Capital accounts switched to 50/50 for tax reasons only (p.2, §II.C): "At some point before 1997, the Capital Accounts on the Dairy partnership tax returns were changed to state the partnership owned 50% by Manuel and Hazel and 50% owned by Steve despite the 75/25% ownership interests outlined in the partnership agreement. Importantly, the partnership agreement was never amended to alter the 75/25% ownership interests in the partnership." And (p.4–5): "Steve previously acknowledged that the capital account change on the tax return was done solely to obtain beneficial tax treatment.   2. Steve's own signature on the 706 confirms 75/25 (p.3): "Importantly, Steve signed the Form 706 for Manuel's … thereby acknowledging the accuracy of the information contained therein regarding ownership interests of the partnership (i.e. confirming that the partnership was owned 75% by Manuel and Hazel and 25% by Steve, not 50/50)."
  3. Steve reconfirmed 75/25 after Manuel's death (p.3): "Even more significantly, Steve, Marla and Hazel all executed an amendment to the partnership agreement in September 2016 after Manuel's death … Therein, Steve again confirmed ownership as follows: 37.5% Hazel Leal / 55% Steve Leal (30% as Steve's separate property inherited from Manuel, and 25% by Steve and Marla's Trust constituting Steve's original acquisition of an interest in the partnership in 1993) / 7.5% Manuel C. Leal Bypass Trust." Dated elsewhere in brief as "the amendment to the partnership agreement dated September 29, 2016. See Exhibit '4'." (p.5).
  4. No consideration ever paid (p.5): "Steve failed to pay/provide any additional consideration (or even pay his initial capital contribution) for his purportedly increased interest in the partnership."
  5. Partnership money bought realty titled to individuals (p.3, §II.D): "partnership funds were used to purchase real property in individual partners' names (or their respective living trusts) over the years … Dairy partnership income was the only funding source used to purchase these additional real [property] assets. Additionally, the real property of the dairy … was used as collateral to finance the acquisitions. Therefore, regardless of title, Hazel contends that such properties are assets of the partnership and should be owned in the same ownership percentages as the partnership (i.e. 75/25)." Steve's contrary position stated at p.5: "Steve contends that the properties were held 50/50% instead of 75/25%."
  6. And: "Prior to and after Manuel's death, Steve undertook efforts to keep Hazel in the dark regarding the Dairy's finances and operation."

4.2 Assertions about the profit split (50/50 vs 75/25)

  • Core position (p.4, §III.A): "The partnership agreement identifies the capital accounts as 75% ownership by Manuel and 25% ownership by Steve. 5. 2017.05.31 Letter from T. Thompson re pending issues / documents
