McCormick Barstow LLP (Timothy L. Thompson; Nikole E. Cunningham), May 31, 2017, to Robert Gin and Michael Johnson, Griswold LaSalle, "Re: Manuel C. Leal Living Trust," "VIA E-MAIL AND U.S. MAIL"; bears Griswold received-stamp "JUN 02 2017." Opening: retained "by Hazel Leal, in conjunction with Robyn Esraelian's office, to represent her interests in the Manuel C. Leal Living Trust, the Leal & Son Dairy, and the promissory note signed by Steve and Marla Leal."

Issue 1 — Partnership Capital Accounts. "The original partnership agreement dated March 10, 1983 identifies the capital accounts as 75% ownership to Manuel and 25% ownership to Steve. However, at some time after … the partnership filed tax returns reflecting capital accounts of 50/50% ownership … Steve previously acknowledged that the capital account change on the tax return was done solely to obtain beneficial tax treatment." Agreed remediation not delivered: "it was agreed that … David Bekedam would re-compute the capital accounts starting from 1997 based on the 75/25% ownership and profit and loss allocation, consistent with the partnership agreement. Although it was promised that the analysis and reallocation would be completed by March 15, 2017, we still have not received the reallocation analysis. Following the re-computation … Mr. Bekedam was also supposed to provide a detailed explanation of all draws taken by the partners from 1997 to present. To date, we have not received this requested information."

Issue 2 — Ownership Interests in Partnership Real Property. Document demand: "we request a list of all real property that was purchased by the partnership or using any partnership funds. The list should identify: the property by APN number and address; a description of the current use of the property; a schedule of income and expenses attributable to the property; the source of funds utilized to pay any expenses related to the property; identification of the recipient of any income received from the property; any improvements made to the property; and a list of any improvements on the property that are owned by a person or entity other than the titled owner." Footnote 2: "the partnership books reflect the real properties as a partnership asset. It is our contention that the properties are owned by the partnership, or at a minimum in the same 75/25% ownership ratio."

Issue 3 — Failure by Partnership to Pay Rent. "the partnership is not paying rent for use of the land and there are no written rental agreements in place. … please provide copies of any written rental agreements between the partnership and the land owners. We also ask for documentation of any and all rental payments made by the partnership for use of the land."

Issue 4 — Promissory Note. "Steve and Marla Leal signed a promissory note in favor of Manuel and Hazel Leal on March 10, 1983 in the amount of $212,035.00 at a rate of 9% interest per annum. … there have never been any payments made on the note. As a result, it is estimated that the balance presently owed on the note is $4,400,000. … the note is secured by the Manuel Leal & Son Dairy cattle, dairy equipment, farm equipment, production base and pool quota, all feed and supplies on hand, all accounts receivable, all DCCA retains and revolving fund credits. … some plan for repayment must be established."

Issue 5 — Failure to Account / Financial Information. "Hazel demands that she be provided with the monthly partnership QuickBooks records (by delivery to the Garabedian Group) from January 1, 2017 to present, and continuing monthly thereafter on an ongoing basis. In addition … copies of all supporting documentation, including but not limited to credit card statements, invoices and receipts for expenses paid, bank statements, and bank reconciliation records. Moving forward, we expect to receive the monthly records within 20 days from the end of the month." Also: "Hazel believes that Steve has intentionally kept her in the dark regarding the partnership operation." [Note for the current case: the letter routes records to "the Garabedian Group."]

Issue 6 — Distributions and Draws. "both Steve and Hazel receive a draw from the partnership to pay personal expenses. However, to date there has been no accounting regarding the total of personal expenses paid on account of Hazel and the total paid on account or attributed to Steve (or his wife and children)." And: "Steve has taken complete control of the partnership and refuses to allow Hazel to have any voice in expenditure of partnership funds. As a result, some of Steve's decisions regarding the partnership benefit Steve to Hazel's detriment (i.e. long term reinvestment decisions which require significant capital contribution but will not produce any meaningful financial returns until after Hazel's death)."

Issue 7 — Partnership and Trust Income Tax Returns. Hazel "is unwilling to sign any additional documents or income tax returns that could subsequently be argued as an admission on her part for the current status of the partnership capital accounts"; requests "an acknowledgement and agreement from Steve and the partnership that Hazel's signature on the tax return will not be later used as any sort of admission."

Closing threat/deadline: absent cooperation, "claims against Steve relating to misuse of the partnership funds, breach of fiduciary duty, and possible foreclosure of the promissory note. We ask for a response to this letter no later than June 7, 2017."

01-verified-facts/steve-temp-loans-512000.md · 32,056 characters

Steve's "temporary loans" to the partnership, and the $100,000 (tested 10/1/2026)

ATTORNEY WORK-PRODUCT SUPPORT — PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL. This tests a client explanation against the documents. It is not a finding, and it states no legal conclusion.

The client explanation (Jace, 10/1/2026; CLIENT-ATTESTED): "The 100,000 was a repayment of a temporary loan to the partnership to maintain ability to pay bills. Robyn Esraelian was stalling our ability to pull funds from our operating line with farm credit. You can see evidence of this in emails."

The explanation answered A-60's question about "the $100,000 check to Steve on 9/30/2014." That description was wrong (§1).

1. Correction: there was no $100,000 check on 9/30/2014

The workspace stated in five places that "check #23074 to Steve Leal, 9/30/2014" was for $100,000. Those places were:

  • A-60;
  • the A-60 10/1 update;
  • gmail-extract §2;
  • trust-admin-sweep §2.6;
  • chronology row 2014-09-30 (repeated in delay-ledger line 260).

The error came from a text extraction that misaligned the register's columns. I re-parsed "personal steve.pdf" (Drive 1wVz1Won1T_ovfpqPGhBB71qOKGoEkPTA, account 515000 Personal-Steve, 1999–11/1/2016) with each row tied to its amount. The running balance ties out on every one of the 230 rows (0 breaks). It shows:

Date Type Memo / split Amount Balance
9/30/2014 Check 23074 Steve Leal −$126.00 −16,336.04
12/31/2014 General Journal, FRAZE "TO CLOSE OUT ACCOUNT" / 102000 −$3,657.36 −21,627.37
12/31/2014 General Journal, FRAZE "TO RECLASS STEVE LEAL WI…" / 512000 · Capital Contribution −$100,000.00 −121,627.37

Frazer's own adjusting-entry report confirms the third line. "Accountant Changes 12.31.14.pdf" (Drive 1f5JGW5GYY4weVMoBqbfqETX3Llgz_VNp; duplicate 1RgKBfuN2P0JTGiiwYf0aP2lBMlA1Qzpa), p. 36 of 37, entry 202:

"Added Journal Entry FRAZE 12/31/2014 · Adjusting Entry yes · Capital Cont. - Steve 100000.00 TO RECLASS STEVE LEAL WITHDRAWALS · Personal - Steve 100000.00 TO RECLASS STEVE LEAL WITHDRAWALS"

What it means (calc). The −$100,000 in 515000 is a debit to Personal-Steve, so the offsetting credit went to 512000 Capital Cont.-Steve. Before year-end, therefore, a $100,000 payment to Steve was booked against his capital-contribution account: that is how a contribution or loan is returned. Frazer's adjustment moved it to "withdrawals." Steve's total capital is the same either way. Only the label changed, and the label is what puts $100,000 into FY2014 "Personal" withdrawals (Steve $120,155 vs. Manuel $7,333; A-1).

Not yet located:

  • The 2014 bank transaction itself: its date, the check or transfer, and the payee account.
  • The 512000 ledger for 2012–2014.

Grade: the reclass is SUPPORTED. The underlying 2014 payment is INDETERMINATE.

2. How the dairy booked Steve's loans, in Frazer's words, sent to the other side

On 2/22/2018, Mike Edwards (Frazer) wrote to Aaron Garabedian, cc'ing Robyn Esraelian, Brandon Esraelian, Tim Thompson, Niki Cunningham and Michael Johnson. This was not privileged; it went to opposing counsel. Gmail 1602be0a88bae639, quoted in Edwards's 8/2/2018 forward to Jace:

"3. Steve's capital contributions are for money Steve loaned the business to cover bills. Jace uses this account to post the money Steve put in and when Steve is reimbursed the payments are also ran through this account. I think the current balance owed to Steve is ~$70,000. When we prepare the F/S I will pull the detail together for the loan activity."

This matches the 2014 entry exactly: a reimbursement run through 512000, then reclassed by Frazer. Grade: the practice (loans booked in 512000, repayments run through the same account) is SUPPORTED by the accountant's contemporaneous statement. That this particular 2014 payment repaid a loan is NOT ESTABLISHED. No 2014 inflow has been tied to it.

Where the 2014 repayment's inflow might be (from the printed statements, S-4 1O7OGL798JcaTXginVNMIUgKtNV-ckK0l):

  • FY2014: no capital-contribution line.
  • FY2013: none.
  • FY2012: "Capital contribution 126,028," of which Steve $125,987.

The FY2012 contribution is the nearest documented inflow large enough to cover a $100,000 return. The link is an inference, not a finding (INDETERMINATE). The 512000 detail for 2012–2014 would settle it.

The client's account does fit a different $100,000. Per Jace's 2/22/2018 email, Steve repaid himself "most of" the $170,000 in January 2018, leaving $70,000. That implies roughly a $100,000 repayment (calc: $170,000 − $70,000). The client may be describing the January 2018 repayment, not the 2014 reclass. OI-80 asks the client to say which.

4. What does not reconcile yet (adverse rigor)

  1. Amounts by year. The emails say $170,000 was outstanding in 11/2017, about $100,000 was repaid in 1/2018, and $70,000 was owed in 2/2018. The statements show contributions of $60,000 (2017) and $93,630 (2018), and a $60,000 debit to 512000 in 2019 (sweep §6). If all $170,000 came in during 2017 and nothing was repaid that year, FY2017 should show $170,000, not $60,000. One possible explanation: Garabedian's "$100,000 Temp Loan" entry may itself be the 2014 item still sitting in 512000. That would fit the draft's "If you remove the Frazer Journal Entries… the balance would show zero." But it cannot be squared with "the current total… is $170,000." INDETERMINATE until the 512000 ledger is read.
  2. Loan or capital? No note, no interest, and the reviewed statements call these "capital contributions." The other side can say every repayment was a draw (kit Item 6 caution, and A-72).
  3. Self-repayment after the Settlement. The January 2018 repayment came after the 12/7/2017 effective date. Settlement ¶11 governs borrowing and partner loans, though its signature blocks are dated 2018 (memo §5.1). Whether repaying a pre-Settlement partner loan needed Hazel's approval is for counsel (UNVERIFIED). Partly mitigating: Frazer disclosed the loan-and-repayment practice and the ~$70,000 balance to opposing counsel on 2/22/2018.
  4. Tone evidence cuts against us.
    • [PRIV] Jace, 11/9/2017: "My Dad just isn't too excited about loaning the partnership to pay for nurses."
    • Non-privileged and in their file: Esraelian's "continued threats to take away or to stop paying Hazel's caregivers," and Jace's own 11/3/2017 tie between the advance and "home care nurse expenses for Hazel… ~$138,000."
    • Expect this used for a control or leverage narrative.
    • Updated 10/1/2026: the "threats" sentence answered a specific non-privileged message (11/9/2017, 9:44 AM, see the sequence above). Read both ways:
      • Helps: it states a cash-timing fact, not a refusal. The nurses were paid from partnership funds, and the partnership was waiting on a signature Hazel's side controlled.
      • Hurts: of all the dairy's bills, it singled out Hazel's caregivers. It was sent after the approval was already given. Johnson moved within the hour to take over the communications and restate it neutrally.
      • The same-day [PRIV] line shows Steve was able to bridge but unwilling to do it for the nurses. That would matter if privilege were ever lost, and it shapes deposition answers to "Could Steve have covered those checks?"
      • Esraelian's word "continued" implies other instances. Search lealdairy before any deposition (OI-81).

5. What helps

  • Contemporaneous, non-privileged disclosure. The other side's CPA asked about the temporary loans in 11/2017. Frazer answered in writing on 2/22/2018 to Garabedian, Esraelian, Thompson and Cunningham. "Concealment" is hard to argue for a practice opposing counsel was told about eight years ago.
  • Hazel's side conditioned partnership borrowing on information demands (11/3–11/9/2017, 12/27/2017, 6/15–19/2018). The other side's own emails show why Steve's bridge money was needed.
  • A-1 symmetry (calc, from printed S-4 figures). If FY2014 counts a $100,000 return of Steve's money as a withdrawal, a fair comparison counts the money Steve put in.
    • Over FY2012–FY2014, withdrawals were Steve $280,587 and Manuel $282,700.
    • Contributions were Steve $125,987 and Manuel $41.
    • Net of contributions: Steve $154,600, Manuel $282,659.
    • Excluding only the reclassed $100,000, Steve's FY2014 withdrawals were $67,503 against Manuel's $110,081.
    • These are arithmetic on printed figures. Whether the 2014 payment was a loan repayment is INDETERMINATE (§2).

6. To close it out (OI-80)

  1. The 512000 Capital Cont.-Steve GL detail, 2012–2019. Two copies already exist as Gmail attachments that the connector cannot open:
    • "512000 - Capital Cont. - Steve.pdf" (Edwards, 12/6/2017, thread 1602be0a88bae639);
    • "Steve Temp Loan to Partner.pdf" (Esraelian, 11/9/2017, thread 15fa1ce3b9f72277). Save both to Drive.
  2. The 2014 payment's check image or transfer record (Citizens), and Steve's bank deposit of it.
  3. Steve's bank records for the inflows: the 2012 $125,987, and the 2017 $70,000 and $100,000.
  4. Whether "Response 11.9.17" was sent, and in what final form (Griswold file / Jace's sent mail).
  5. The client's answer: is "the $100,000" the January 2018 repayment, the 2014 reclass, or both?

7.2 What it proves

(a) The 2014 "$100,000" was the return of Steve's 2012 loans. SUPPORTED (partnership GL plus bank register).

  • 2012: Steve put in $125,000 and took back $25,000, net +$100,000. Memos: "LOAN," "Temporary Loan."
  • 2013: $200,000 in and $200,000 out, net 0. Memo "temp loan."
  • 2014: $50,000 in and $150,000 out, net −$100,000. Memo "Pay back Loan."
  • Over 2012–2014, cash in equals cash out: $375,000 each way (calc).
  • Frazer's 12/31/2014 entry moved exactly that net $100,000 into "withdrawals."
  • The FY2014 "Personal" excess in A-1 is Steve being repaid his own 2012 money.
  • Minor wrinkle: Frazer closed $125,987 to capital at 1/1/2013 when the account held $100,000, then reversed the $25,987 difference at 12/31/2013. So the FY2012 statement's "capital contribution $125,987" overstates Steve's 2012 cash by $25,987.

(b) The 2017 $170,000 were repayments TO Steve of his 2015 loans, not loans outstanding. SUPPORTED.

  • 2015 in: 6/30 "TEMP LOAN" $100,000 + 7/9 $50,000 + 10/6 $20,000 = $170,000.
  • 2017 out: 3/2 $100,000 + 4/25 $70,000 = $170,000.
  • Frazer closed the 2015 loans to capital at year-end. That is why the account shows −$170,000 in 8/2017. Jace's draft ("If you remove the Frazer Journal Entries from the account the balance would show zero") is accurate.
  • Correction to §3–§5:
    • Garabedian's "Temp Loan to Partner" entries are these two 2017 repayment checks. Their memo is "Temp Loan P…," which the bank register gives in full as "Temp Loan Payback."
    • My reading that $170,000 was still owed in 11/2017 was wrong.
  • The client's "$100,000 repayment of a temporary loan" most directly matches check #27872, 3/2/2017, "Temp Loan Payback," $100,000. It repaid the 6/30/2015 "TEMP LOAN" of $100,000.

(c) Esraelian cannot explain the $100,000 items. NOT SUPPORTED for 2012–2017.

  • 2012–2014 was Manuel's lifetime.
  • On 6/30/2015, the day of the $100,000 "TEMP LOAN," the register also shows a $150,000 Farm Credit feed-line advance. Feed-line advances posted throughout 2015: 4/29, 6/5, 6/30, 8/3, 8/11, 9/1, 9/12, 10/6, 11/2, 11/13 and 12/1. The line was being drawn.
  • What does fit the Esraelian account:
    • 10/6/2017, $50,000 from Steve. It came while the FCW renewal documents sat with Esraelian (due 10/1/2017; 9/19 "The form is incorrect").
    • 11/17/2017, $20,000 back to Steve ("Repay loan") four days after a $100,000 deposit on 11/13/2017. The amount and date are consistent with the advance Hazel signed for on 11/10.
    • The book balance was −$111,560.43 just before that deposit and −$258,204.46 on 11/28/2017 (calc from register). The cash squeeze was real.

(d) The nurses were paid every week (OI-81 item 1). SUPPORTED at register level.

  • Weekly caregiver checks (504000 Medical-Hazel) went to Jennifer Sousa, Brailee Scoggin, Maria Trovao, Maria Cardosa, Brittany McGarrah, Rebecca Sousa and Carrie Alvarado.
  • Check dates: 10/6, 10/9, 10/19, 10/25, 11/2, 11/9, 11/16, 11/24, 11/30, 12/7, 12/14, 12/15 and 12/28/2017. Checks #29306–29311 are dated 11/9/2017, the day of the "I will not be able to make checks for the home care nurses" email. They were written against a book balance of about −$155,000.
  • Both ways:
    • No week was skipped, so the statement never stopped Hazel's care.
    • But the checks were written anyway, so the email overstated the constraint.
    • Clearing dates need the bank statements.

(e) 🔴 New, adverse: $220,000 to Steve in 2018, coded as personal draws (A-73).

  • 1/13/2018, check #29635, $150,000, 515000 · Personal-Steve.
  • 6/1/2018, check #30321, $70,000, 515000 · Personal-Steve. The balance afterward was $4,493.98.
  • Jace's 2/22/2018 email calls the January check repayment of "most of" the temporary loans, with "$70,000" still owed. The June check matches that $70,000.
  • But the ledger and register show only about $30,000 of Steve loans outstanding at the time: 10/6/2017 +$50,000, less 11/17/2017 −$20,000. The 2015 loans were already repaid in 2017.
  • So about $190,000 of the $220,000 is not supported as loan repayment by either record (calc). It is booked as Steve's draws. A loan that came in through some other channel is not ruled out (INDETERMINATE).
  • Steve's 515000 checks through Citizens in 2018 total $236,286.53 (26 items, calc).
  • On 6/19/2018, 18 days after the $70,000 check, Johnson told Esraelian "There is not enough money to meet current operating needs" and pressed for loan approval. He mentioned Steve returning a $50,000 tax refund but not the $70,000.

8.2 What changes

§7.2(e) and A-73 were wrong on the key point. Corrected:

  • He then lent again: $10,000 (6/8), $15,000 (7/11) and $43,630.24 (7/16, his FTB refund).
  • That is consistent with Johnson's "he has deposited it back."
  • The timing still reads poorly, but it is explicable as a revolving bridge.

2023: $360,000 in (6/24–8/14/2023), "Deposit" memos, no repayment through 512000 since. Jace's 7/16/2026 "bridge loans" description therefore has no repayment yet for the 2023 money. If it is a loan, it is still outstanding.

9. The 2023 $360,000: the client's account of why Steve put it in (10/1/2026)

Client (Jace, 10/1/2026; CLIENT-ATTESTED): "Steve was under the assumption that the buyout would be calculated as of Hazel's date of death. He put that money into the business assuming he was going to be the sole owner of it during a tight cash flow year."

The record:

  • Deposits: 6/24/2023 $155,000 + $5,000 ("Cash"), 7/20 $100,000, 8/14 $100,000. Frazer closed them to capital as a FY2023 "contribution" of $360,000 (S-32).
  • No repayment through 512000 since.
  • FY2023 was a loss year: $888,608, of which the estate's column bore $333,228 (kit Item 6; FS24 Exhibit C).
  • In 2023 the trustees received $72,000 in $6,000 monthly payments (register; destination CLIENT-ATTESTED, OI-88).
  • The instruments do fix value at the date of death: Settlement, TIC ¶11 and Partnership Agreement Art. XIII.J, "as of the date of Hazel's death" (post-death-profits-issue.md §5.2). Steve's assumption matches the text on valuation. Whether post-death results belong to the estate is the disputed issue (§5.1); counsel decides.

What the statement does:

  • It explains the money as an owner's own investment. That fits the books ("capital contribution") better than the 7/16/2026 "bridge loans" email. Jace wrote there, to Ormonde and Frazer: "temporary cash infusions… Steve never charged or collected a cent of interest on these bridge loans."
  • Whether that email reached Cunningham is not established (OI-73).

Why the label matters (for counsel and Frazer; no legal conclusion here):

If it is… Effect Risk
A capital contribution (books; client's stated intent) Raises Steve's capital account. Under a date-of-death valuation it does not change the estate's buyout price. Their side may argue Steve chose to invest at his own risk while the buyout was open. Mainly a capital-account effect.
A loan (7/16/2026 email) A partnership liability owed to Steve, which would have to be repaid. Settlement ¶11(a) bars borrowing without all partners' approval. Calling a 2023 advance a "loan" invites a covenant-breach argument, the same pattern as A-59. No note, no interest, no approval located.

Strongest use, both ways:

  • In 2023 Steve put $360,000 into the business.
  • The estate took out $72,000 and contributed nothing, while being allocated $333,228 of the loss on the books.
  • If the estate is treated as sharing post-death results, the estate both bore part of the 2023 loss and drew cash while Steve alone funded the shortfall. That is a strong fairness point.
  • It cuts the other way only if counsel's theory relies on Steve treating himself as sole owner before any purchase closed. Defendants will say he assumed the risk.

Benefits to the Trust side: water, insurance and utilities, and the Danielle card incident (tested 10/1/2026)

ATTORNEY WORK-PRODUCT SUPPORT — PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL. This tests three client statements against the documents. Nothing here states a legal conclusion.

The client statements (Jace, 10/1/2026; all CLIENT-ATTESTED):

  1. "we have been supplying water to the three houses that Susan owns with dairy supply water for almost 10 years."
  2. "probably 10 or 15 years ago, Hazel asked me to look into some transactions on her credit card that she didn't recognize. I ended up tracing them back to my cousin Danielle. She was using Hazel's card to order stuff online that was shipped to her house."
  3. "We also pay through the business (under Hazel Personal Draws) many expenses on behalf of her estate from the partnership. Danielle's personal vehicle insurance, home insurance for the 3 homes susan owns, culligan water, waste management etc."

Main source for statement 3: the QuickBooks Citizens checking register, 12/31/2009–9/30/2026 (S-29, Drive 1XhazEklYhxAH27FlpuY6IqHSMEZ1muvR; 0 balance breaks). The figures below are calcs from that register. A payment inside a "-SPLIT-" transaction cannot be assigned to an account from this report.

0. Who owns the "three houses"?

The client says Susan owns them. The written record says otherwise. Ashley wrote on 3/12/2025:

"My mom is under the impression that the insurance for the three houses owned 100% by the Hazel J. Leal Revocable Trust is being paid by the partnership. I wanted to check with you to confirm whether this is accurate."

Jace replied: "Yes that's correct." (Gmail 1958b7b5046d2528; non-privileged).

Grade: the three houses are Trust-owned per the 3/2025 record. Whether any has since been distributed to Susan is NOT ESTABLISHED; get the deeds (OI-83). This matters:

  • if the Trust owns them, water and insurance benefit the Trust, the estate the defendants administer, not Susan personally;
  • it is still the other side, and the email shows the trustees knew in 3/2025 that the partnership was paying the insurance.

1. Water to the three houses

Grade: CLIENT-ATTESTED; no document located. The bank register cannot show it, because water from the dairy's own wells has no payee. Its cost sits inside the dairy's pumping electricity, well and pump repairs, and any groundwater fees.

For us: an uncompensated, roughly ten-year benefit from partnership resources to Trust property. It adds to the "benefits flowed to their side" ledger and to the "continued partner-like treatment" theme (gmail-sweep §2.7).

Against us:

  • Without metering or a written arrangement, it cannot be quantified. A number made up after the fact will be attacked.
  • If Steve chose to supply the water while Hazel was alive, the other side will call it a family accommodation or gift, not a debt. (Any waiver or estoppel effect is UNVERIFIED and for counsel.)
  • It is another informal, off-books arrangement, the same pattern A-68 (mobile-home rent) and A-69 (cash hoof trimmer) expose.

To support it (OI-83):

  • addresses and APNs of the three houses and of the well and service lines;
  • whether the houses have their own wells or meters;
  • a pump-electric meter or usage basis;
  • when it began and who asked;
  • any email about it.

2. The Danielle credit-card incident

Grade: CLIENT-ATTESTED. Not corroborated by any document found.

  • Searches of jaceleal@gmail.com for Danielle together with card, charges or Amazon (before 2018) returned nothing on point.
  • What the mailbox does show: from 2013 to 2016, Bank of America sent Hazel J. Leal's BankAmericard Cash Rewards Visa account emails to jaceleal@gmail.com. That fits Jace helping Hazel monitor her card. (Account digits are deliberately not recorded here.)
  • Who Danielle is. The client says she is his cousin. Hazel's trust names Danielle Pedroncelli in Art. Five (trust-instruments-extract). The link is CLIENT-ATTESTED. Ashley is Susan's daughter (gmail-sweep §2.7); whether Danielle is too is not confirmed.

For us: if documented, it is an account of a Trust-side family member taking Hazel's money, discovered by our side at Hazel's request. It also shows Hazel trusted Jace with her finances.

Against us, and why counsel should handle it carefully:

  • Danielle is not a party, and it was Hazel's personal card, not partnership money. Its relevance to partnership accounting is not obvious, and character evidence is restricted (admissibility is for counsel; UNVERIFIED).
  • "If anyone has been dishonest it's their side" is a narrative, not evidence. Raised without documents, it reads as retaliation and invites a counter-attack.
  • Jace's access to Hazel's card account (the BofA emails) cuts both ways. The other side's "control" and "funneling" theme can use it.
  • Recommendation for counsel to weigh: hold it, document it, and do not lead with it.

To support it (OI-84):

  • the card statements showing the charges and ship-to addresses (Hazel's BofA account; the estate holds those records now);
  • any report, dispute or repayment;
  • whether Hazel or Susan knew;
  • approximate date.

3. Expenses for Trust-side family paid through the partnership

What the register shows (calc; post-death means from 9/23/2022):

Payee (QuickBooks name) Booked to 505000 Personal-Hazel Booked as partnership expense Span
Mercury Insurance {Danielle} 26 payments, $18,999.45 (2020–2026; post-death $12,994.72) 70 payments, $23,735.05 to 760000 Insurance-General (2016–2026; post-death $13,330.59) 4/25/2016–9/7/2026
Culligan Water 18 payments, $3,475.73 (2021–2022) 137, $20,229.22 to 745000 Supplies (2010–2021); 6, $1,652.05 to 748000D Repairs (2026) 2010–2026

Home insurance for the three Trust houses not separately identifiable Possibly inside the farm policy: Nationwide, 73 payments, $309,584.28 to 760000. In 2021 Jace wrote that the "little house" was "the same policy as Hazel's house coverage" (Gmail 17a211afd14cdaa2) —
Other 505000 after death Susan Leal $3,774.33 (10/5/2022, "payment for grave" per the 7/10/2026 export); Jack's Catering $4,271.48 ("Hazel Leal Memorial 10/5/22") — 10/2022

Also found:

  • 12/31/2016: check to Jace S. Leal, $1,171.00, memo "Danielle Ins, Hambys, Agsource," booked to 745000 Supplies.
  • 1/15/2019: Tulare-Kings CWA, "Danielle membership fee," $75, booked to 513000 Donations - Steve.

Grade: the client's statement is PARTLY SUPPORTED and PARTLY CONTRADICTED.

  • Supported: Danielle's insurance and Culligan were paid by the partnership, and some of it was charged to Hazel's draws (Mercury quarterly from 2020; Culligan 2021–22).
  • Contradicted as to "under Hazel Personal Draws":
    • $23,735 of Danielle's insurance (70 payments since 2016) was booked as the partnership's own insurance expense;
    • Waste Management was never charged to Hazel;
    • most Culligan before 2021 was booked to dairy supplies.
    • Whether any Waste Management or Culligan service is for the three houses rather than the dairy is NOT ESTABLISHED. Service addresses are needed.

For us:

  • The benefit to the Trust side is larger than Hazel's draws show. Reclassifying the expensed items would raise the estate's draws and lower its capital, which favors the buyout math.
  • The trustees knew. On 3/12/2025 Ashley asked and Jace confirmed that the partnership paid the houses' insurance. On 12/4/2025 Jace told Susan that Danielle's insurance payments "do go through the business" (Gmail 19aeb39a4de4ac29).
  • Our side disclosed partnership-paid personal expenses in 2017 on a family-by-family basis (STEVE.HAZEL PERSONAL EXPENSES.xlsx, chronology 2015-01-01). Steve's family appeared on it too. That is transparency, not concealment.

🔴 Against us (A-75):

  1. Bookkeeping reliability. Our books, kept by Jace, expensed a non-partner's personal car insurance as partnership insurance for ten years. They also reimbursed "Danielle Ins" to Jace as "Supplies," and charged a Danielle fee to Steve's donations. Defendants' CPAs (Edwards & Barber) will use that to attack every classification in 505000 and the parity analysis, whichever way the dollars cut.
  2. Tax. Personal expenses deducted as business expenses on the partnership's returns (2016 onward) are a tax-exposure question for Frazer, not for us. Raise it with Frazer, privately, through counsel.
  3. The same pattern on our side. The 2017 schedule listed partnership-paid personal expenses for Steve ($49,122.05) and Jace/Jordan ($21,304.82) as well as Hazel ($66,072.53). The other side can say everyone's personal items went through the dairy. That neutralizes the "their side took more" point unless it is measured carefully.
  4. Authority after death. After 9/23/2022 the partnership kept paying Danielle's insurance (64 payments, $26,325.31, calc). Who asked for it, and on whose account? If no trustee instruction exists, charging it to the estate's capital can be challenged. If the trustees asked for it, that helps us.

To support it (OI-85):

  • Mercury policy declarations: the named insured and vehicle, and whether either Mercury series is a dairy vehicle;
  • Waste Management and Culligan service addresses;
  • the Nationwide declarations, schedule of locations;
  • any trustee request for the post-death payments;
  • the "2017.12.06 Jace Leal Draw Reconcilliation.xlsx" Johnson sent Esraelian, Thompson and Garabedian on 12/6/2017 (Gmail 1602de83c0269477; attachment not in Drive).

4. Corroboration in the same register (A-58)

From 11/16/2016 to 9/30/2026, the register shows monthly $1,655 payments to Susan Leal, each charged to Steve's capital account: 510000, or 515600 "Steve Draws - Susan Leal Pmt" in 2019. They end with check #42765, 9/30/2026, "Last Payment," $1,689.19. This corroborates A-58 (ten years of performance on Susan's annuity, paid from Steve's side) at bank-register level.

02-legal-research/00-READ-FIRST-research-reliability.md · 13,666 characters

⛔ READ THIS BEFORE OPENING R1–R4

THE LEGAL RESEARCH IN THIS FOLDER IS NOT VERIFIED AUTHORITY

ATTORNEY WORK-PRODUCT SUPPORT — PREPARED FOR COUNSEL — NOT LEGAL ADVICE Prepared August 18, 2026

What happened

Memos R1–R4 were scoped to be researched using a CourtListener MCP server, with every citation verified by retrieving the source.

That was not possible in this environment, and counsel needs to know exactly why.

  1. No CourtListener MCP server was available. It is not connected to this session.
  2. The network egress proxy blocked every legal-research domain. Verified directly: leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, courtlistener.com, storage.courtlistener.com, courts.ca.gov, cite.case.law, justia.com, casetext.com, scholar.google.com, findlaw.com, leagle.com, casemine.com, law.resource.org, public.law, archive.org — all returned HTTP 403 / EGRESS_BLOCKED at the gateway.

Consequence: not a single judicial opinion was read in its native source. Case names, years, reporter citations and holdings in R1–R4 come from web-search result summaries.

What this means, stated plainly

Status
Statutory text Partially verified. R2 located the California Legislative Counsel's own PUBINFO database export (a July 9, 2026 snapshot, mirrored publicly) and read verbatim text for 22 code sections. R1, R3 and R4 obtained statutory text through search extraction only.
Case law NONE VERIFIED. No opinion was retrieved. No holding was read in the original.
Pin cites NONE CONFIRMED, ANYWHERE, IN ANY MEMO.

Treat R1–R4 as a research roadmap, not as research. They are useful for issue-spotting, for the statutory framework, and as a list of authorities to look up. They are not a basis for advising a client, drafting a brief, or making a representation to the court.

Mandatory before any use

  1. Re-run every issue in Westlaw or CoCounsel. Confirm each case exists, says what the memo says, and remains good law. Shepardize / KeyCite everything.
  2. Confirm every statutory quotation against leginfo, including the verbatim-sourced sections — the PUBINFO snapshot's completeness could not be independently confirmed.
  3. Do not cite anything from these memos in any filing without doing 1 and 2 first.

Specific traps flagged by the researchers — check these first

  • R1 — M. Lowenstein & Sons, Inc. v. Superior Court (1978) 80 Cal.App.3d 762: DO NOT CITE. Name, citation and holding all unconfirmed; a differently-named case surfaced instead. This was the intended support for the fact-of-service vs. proof-of-service distinction — our best non-prejudice argument on the § 998 POS defect. That argument currently rests on no verified citation.
  • R1 — Gorobets, reported as a California Supreme Court decision of August 6, 2026 (twelve days before this memo). A very recent decision found only through search summaries is exactly the kind of item most likely to be misdescribed. Verify its existence, holding and citation before relying on it for anything. Same for Madrigal — reporter cites unconfirmed for both.
  • R1 — Poster v. So. Cal. RTD (1990) 52 Cal.3d 266: the search record contains directly contradictory statements about whether CCP § 1013 extends the § 998 acceptance window to 35 days. The memo adopts 35 days but flags it. Counsel must read the opinion. This drives the expiration-date computation in the chronology.

  • R2 — Estate of Silveira is unpublished and not citable (CRC 8.1115), though the trigger question it raises is worth counsel's attention.
  • R2 — no published California case was found holding a partnership/LLC interest "unique" for specific-performance purposes, or applying appraisal-as-arbitration outside first-party insurance. Both gaps are material to our theory.

  • R3 — no case is cited for the surcharge elements or burden allocation; laches was not researched at all.
  • R4 — no California authority was located on the effect of a general release on the temporal scope of discovery. That analysis is first-principles inference only.
  • R4 — a search summary directly contradicted the statutory text it purported to quote (CCP § 2031.280(e)). Documented in that memo as evidence the summaries are unreliable unaided.

⚠️ A premise in R4 has since been disproved by the documents

R4's proportionality analysis leans on the December 7, 2017 Settlement Agreement and Mutual Release operating as a cutoff for pre-2017 claims and therefore limiting discovery.

The Settlement Agreement has now been read (see ../01-verified-facts/governing-instruments-extract.md). The release is narrow. ¶13 releases only claims relating to "the division of the real property," and ¶15 states that "the only issues resolved by this Settlement Agreement is [sic] the division of identified real property and the valuation of the improvements identified in the Agreement."

Accounting, draw, distribution and fiduciary claims appear to fall outside it. Counsel should read R4's release-based arguments with that correction in mind.

One finding worth counsel's early attention (still unverified)

R2 flags Civ. Code § 3390(b) — barring specific enforcement of "an obligation to employ another in personal service" — and § 3390(d) — barring an order compelling a party "to procure the act or consent of… any other third person."

Our § 998 offer and the Complaint's prayer both ask the court to order defendants to employ Stanley Xavier and Moss Adams, neither of whom is before the court. R2 reads § 3390 as aimed squarely at that form of relief, and suggests an alternative framing: judicial valuation, or appointment under CCP § 1281.6 (court "shall appoint the arbitrator" where the agreed method "fails or for any reason cannot be followed") or Evid. Code § 730.

This is potentially a structural problem with the relief we have pleaded, and it deserves counsel's attention early — but § 3390's text and its case-law gloss must be confirmed before anyone acts on it.

R1: CCP § 998 Offer Validity and Proof-of-Service Defects

ATTORNEY WORK-PRODUCT — PREPARED FOR COUNSEL — NOT LEGAL ADVICE

Prepared: August 18, 2026 | Matter: Leal Trust Management (Tulare County Superior Court)

READ THIS FIRST — RESEARCH-ENVIRONMENT LIMITATION. A CourtListener MCP server was not available in this environment. In addition, every direct document-fetch attempt in this environment was refused by the network egress proxy — including leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, law.justia.com, www.courtlistener.com, codes.findlaw.com, caselaw.findlaw.com, casetext.com, scholar.google.com, california.public.law, law.onecle.com, and courts.ca.gov / www4.courts.ca.gov. No statute and no opinion was opened and read in primary form for this memo. Everything below was assembled from a web search tool that returns indexed excerpts and summaries. Verification tags in the Authority section reflect that reduced standard and are defined there. Nothing in this memo is filing-ready. See Confidence and Gaps.

Issue

  1. What must a written offer contain, and how must it be served, to be a valid offer to compromise under Code of Civil Procedure § 998?
  2. What is the effect of defects in the proof of service — specifically a POS reciting service and execution "On January 3, 2018," more than eight years before the offer was actually served — on (a) the offer's enforceability and (b) § 998 cost-shifting?
  3. Do California courts apply strict compliance or substantial compliance to § 998? What are the leading authorities on each side?
  4. Does an undated offer affect validity, or the running of the acceptance period?
  5. When does the 30-day acceptance window under § 998(b)(2) begin, and does CCP § 1013's mail extension enlarge it?
  6. Can an offer containing no monetary term — here, specific performance requiring defendants to employ two named appraisers — trigger § 998 cost-shifting at all? How is "more favorable judgment" measured against a non-monetary offer?
  7. Who bears the burden of showing the offer was valid, and separately, that it was reasonable and made in good faith?

Short Answer

Threshold correction counsel should note at the outset. The tasking framed the exposure under § 998(c)(1). Subdivision (c)(1) governs an offer made by a defendant. Because our client is the plaintiff and made this offer, the operative cost-shifting provision is § 998(d), which gives the court discretion ("may require") to award the plaintiff post-offer expert-witness fees if the defendant fails to obtain a more favorable judgment. The upside is therefore narrower and wholly discretionary. Counsel should also note that Civil Code § 3291 prejudgment interest — the other classic reward for a plaintiff's rejected 998 offer — is by its terms confined to actions "to recover damages for personal injury," and so appears unavailable in a trust/real-property dispute.

On the merits. § 998(b)(1) requires that the offer be (i) in writing, (ii) served on the other party, (iii) not less than 10 days before trial or arbitration, (iv) containing a statement of the offer with the terms and conditions of the judgment, and (v) containing an acceptance provision. Service is a statutory element of the offer, not a formality collateral to it. California appellate authority on § 998 form requirements is predominantly strict-compliance and bright-line (Puerta, Mostafavi, Sanford), and the offer is construed against its proponent with validity reviewed de novo (Prince). A meaningful counter-current exists — courts have upheld offers against hyper-technical attacks and have allowed contemporaneous writings to resolve ambiguity (Prince, Berg, Goodstein) — but no located authority extends "substantial compliance" to excuse a missing statutory element.

The acceptance window runs 30 days from when the offer is "made," which practitioner authority uniformly treats as the date of service, not the date printed on the document; and secondary sources uniformly report that Poster v. Southern Cal. Rapid Transit Dist. (1990) 52 Cal.3d 266 holds § 1013's five-day mail extension does apply, giving a mailed offer a 35-day window. Counsel should be aware that this point is not as clean as it looks in the secondary literature — search results also surfaced a description of the Court of Appeal in Poster holding the opposite before review. That conflict is unresolved on this record and must be settled by reading the opinion.

The non-monetary term is the largest single vulnerability. Non-monetary terms do not automatically invalidate a 998 offer, but they must be "sufficiently certain and capable of valuation" so a court can decide whether the judgment beat the offer (Barella). The California Supreme Court reaffirmed a certainty-and-accurate-valuation requirement weeks ago in Gorobets v. Jaguar Land Rover N. Am., LLC (Aug. 6, 2026). An offer whose economic content is "value as determined by two appraisers, with discounts as determined by those appraisers" supplies no number ascertainable at the time the offer was made; counsel should treat this as the defect most likely to defeat cost-shifting outright.

The POS defects cut two ways. Because the offer itself is undated, the POS is the only intrinsic evidence of when the offer was "made" — and it says January 3, 2018, which on its face would place the offer's deemed-withdrawal date in early 2018. Against that, the fact of service and the proof of service are analytically distinct, and an obviously impossible date is a strong candidate for scrivener's error curable by extrinsic proof of actual service on 7/9/2026. The missing street address in the envelope address block is a separate, independent defect under CCP § 1013a(3) and § 1013(a).

Burden. Licudine allocates it in two parts: the offeror bears the burden of showing the offer was valid; the offeree bears the burden of showing an otherwise valid offer was not made in good faith. As offeror, our side carries the burden on every validity defect catalogued below.

Authority

How to read the verification tags

Because no source could be fetched directly (see banner), the requester's binary VERIFIED/UNVERIFIED scheme cannot be honestly applied. Three tags are used instead:

  • [TEXT-RETRIEVED-VIA-INDEX] — the search tool returned what it represented as verbatim statutory or opinion language, attributed to a named URL, and the citation was corroborated by two or more independent results. Still not read in primary form.
  • [CITE CORROBORATED / HOLDING SUMMARIZED] — case name, year, court and reporter citation corroborated across independent results; the holding is known to me only from secondary summaries, not the opinion.
  • [UNVERIFIED — COUNSEL MUST CONFIRM] — could not be adequately corroborated. Do not rely on or cite without independent retrieval.

No entry below carries a pin cite unless expressly marked "pin cite confirmed." None is so marked.

A. Statutes

Code of Civil Procedure § 998 — the governing statute.

  • (a): "The costs allowed under Sections 1031 and 1032 shall be withheld or augmented as provided in this section."
  • (b)(1): "Not less than 10 days prior to commencement of trial or arbitration … any party may serve an offer in writing upon any other party to the action to allow judgment to be taken or an award to be entered in accordance with the terms and conditions stated at that time. The written offer shall include a statement of the offer, containing the terms and conditions of the judgment or award, and a provision that allows the accepting party to indicate acceptance of the offer by signing a statement that the offer is accepted." Acceptance must be in writing and signed by counsel for the accepting party (or the party if unrepresented).
  • (b)(2): "If the offer is not accepted prior to trial or arbitration or within 30 days after it is made, whichever occurs first, it shall be deemed withdrawn, and cannot be given in evidence upon the trial or arbitration."
  • (b)(3): defines when trial/arbitration is "actually commenced" (opening statement, or oath to first witness, or introduction of evidence).
  • (c)(1): "If an offer made by a defendant is not accepted and the plaintiff fails to obtain a more favorable judgment or award, the plaintiff shall not recover his or her postoffer costs and shall pay the defendant's costs from the time of the offer."
  • (c)(2)(A): "In determining whether the plaintiff obtains a more favorable judgment, the court or arbitrator shall exclude the postoffer costs."
  • (d): "If an offer made by a plaintiff is not accepted and the defendant fails to obtain a more favorable judgment or award … the court or arbitrator, in its discretion, may require the defendant to pay a reasonable sum to cover postoffer costs of the services of expert witnesses, who are not regular employees of any party, actually incurred and reasonably necessary in either, or both, preparation for trial or arbitration, or during trial or arbitration, of the case by the plaintiff, in addition to plaintiff's costs."
  • (e): where a defendant's offer is not accepted and plaintiff fails to obtain a more favorable judgment, § 998 costs from the time of the offer are deducted from damages; if costs exceed damages, the net is awarded to defendant.
  • Tag: [TEXT-RETRIEVED-VIA-INDEX]. URLs indexed: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-ccp/part-2/title-14/chapter-3/section-998/; https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/code-of-civil-procedure/ccp-sect-998/; https://law.onecle.com/california/civil-procedure/998.html. leginfo.legislature.ca.gov was blocked and could not be used. Subdivisions (f) through (i) were not retrieved and are not summarized here.

Code of Civil Procedure § 1013(a) — service by mail; extension of time.

  • Requires deposit in a USPS facility, "in a sealed envelope, with postage paid, addressed to the person on whom it is to be served, at the office address as last given by that person on any document filed in the cause and served on the party making service by mail; otherwise at that party's place of residence."
  • "Service is complete at the time of the deposit, but any period of notice and any right or duty to do any act or make any response within any period or on a date certain after service of the document, which time period or date is prescribed by statute or rule of court, shall be extended five calendar days upon service by mail, if the place of address and the place of mailing is within the State of California, 10 calendar days if either is outside the State."

Code of Civil Procedure § 1013a — contents of the proof of service by mail. This is the provision the POS defects implicate directly.

  • The standard affidavit must show the exact title of the document served, the name and residence or business address of the person making service, that the person is a resident of or employed in the county where the mailing occurs, is over 18 and not a party, "the date and place of deposit in the mail, the name and address of the person served as shown on the envelope," and that the envelope was sealed and deposited with postage prepaid.
  • The business-practice alternative (the box checked on our POS) requires, among other elements: "(D) that he or she is readily familiar with the business practice for collection and processing of correspondence for mailing with the United States Postal Service, (E) that the correspondence would be deposited with the United States Postal Service that same day in the ordinary course of business, (F) the name and address of the person served as shown on the envelope, and the date and place of business where the correspondence was placed for deposit in the United States Postal Service, and (G) that the envelope was sealed and placed for collection and mailing on that date following ordinary business practices."

Code of Civil Procedure § 1015 — where a party has an attorney in the action, service of papers "must be upon the attorney instead of the party," except subpoenas, writs, other process, and papers to bring a party into contempt.

Civil Code § 3291 — prejudgment interest at 10% from the date of a plaintiff's first § 998 offer where the defendant does not accept and the plaintiff obtains a more favorable judgment. B. Strict compliance / bright-line authority

Puerta v. Torres (2011) 195 Cal.App.4th 1267. Reported to hold that § 998(b) requires the written offer to contain an acceptance provision; an offer lacking one is invalid, and the offeree's failure to accept does not trigger cost-shifting. Reported reasoning: § 998's language and structure set out mandatory requirements; a bright-line rule adds "consistency and predictability to section 998's operation"; where an offer fails to satisfy all statutorily required elements, "there is nothing for the receiving party to accept" in the first place; general contract principles do not override the statutory requirements.

Mostafavi Law Group, APC v. Larry Rabineau, APC (2021) 61 Cal.App.5th 614. Reported to hold that a § 998 offer lacking an acceptance provision is invalid, and a judgment entered on the purported acceptance of such an offer is void and subject to being set aside under CCP § 473(d) — even where the offeree hand-wrote an acceptance on the offer itself and filed a notice of acceptance.

  • Significance here: this is the strongest available demonstration that a § 998 form defect is not excused by the parties' evident intent or by actual performance of the acceptance ritual.

Sanford v. Rasnick (2016) 246 Cal.App.4th 1121. Reported to hold a joint § 998 offer invalid where it conditioned acceptance on "notarized execution and transmittal of a written settlement agreement and general release" whose terms were never set forth in the offer or communicated while the offer was open. Reported reasoning: the condition made the offer too indefinite; a "release" is not the same as a "settlement agreement," whose terms "can require considerable negotiation." Order awarding costs reversed.

C. Valuation / non-monetary and specific-performance offers

Barella v. Exchange Bank (2000) 84 Cal.App.4th 793. The central authority for Issue 6. Reported holdings:

  • "The inclusion of nonmonetary terms and conditions does not render a Section 998 offer invalid; but those terms or conditions must be sufficiently certain and capable of valuation to allow the court to determine whether judgment is more favorable than the offer."
  • Where an offer includes a non-monetary component, the offer must be evaluated "in light of all the terms and conditions attached to that offer and not simply the monetary amount."
  • On the facts, a confidentiality condition failed: its "value … is so highly subjective and elusive that no court can determine its monetary worth."
  • Also reported for: "the offering party has the burden of demonstrating that the offer is valid under section 998," and that a § 998 offer "must be strictly construed in favor of the party sought to be subjected to its operation."
  • Pin cite not confirmed. (Secondary sources cite the valuation holding to roughly pp. 799–801; that range is reported, not confirmed, and should not be used as a pin cite without reading the opinion.)

Gorobets v. Jaguar Land Rover North America, LLC, Cal. Supreme Court No. S287946, filed August 6, 2026. Official reporter citation not yet confirmed. Reported holding: a § 998 offer may present a choice between alternative sets of terms, so long as the offer clearly presents the alternatives and at least one alternative is sufficiently certain to permit an accurate valuation at the time the offer is made; if the judgment does not exceed the highest-valued valid alternative, cost-shifting is permitted. Facts: Land Rover offered either (1) a lump sum of $85,000 or (2) reimbursement of specified cost categories; jury awarded approximately $76,000.

Goodstein v. Bank of San Pedro (1994) 27 Cal.App.4th 899. Reported: § 998 offer of $150,000 in exchange for dismissal and a general release; the majority upheld the offer by construing the "general release" as reaching only the litigation in which it was offered, reasoning that a release of unknown claims arising from the underlying claim does not necessarily invalidate the offer.

D. Evaluability, ambiguity, and the flexibility counter-current

Berg v. Darden (2004) 120 Cal.App.4th 721. Reported for the offeree-side standard: a § 998 offer's terms must be sufficiently specific to permit the offeree "to evaluate it and make a reasoned decision whether to accept it, or reject it and bear the risk he may have to shoulder his opponent's litigation costs and expenses." Reported on the flexible side: the offer satisfied § 998's specificity requirement notwithstanding that it did not identify the method by which the litigation would finally be resolved.

  • Service caveat. Search results confirm that the appellant's opponent in Berg also argued the offer "was not properly served," and that the trial court found the offer ineffective. I could not determine from search results how the Court of Appeal resolved the service question, or the ultimate disposition. Because Berg is the one located California case where a § 998 service challenge was squarely raised, counsel should pull and read Berg in full before relying on it in either direction.

On the "substantial compliance" framing generally. I searched specifically for California authority applying a substantial-compliance doctrine to § 998 and did not locate a case so holding. The consistent report across practitioner sources is that § 998's form requirements are enforced strictly, while interpretive questions (ambiguity, scope of a release, whether the offer specified enough to be evaluated) are resolved with ordinary construction tools that can favor validity. Counsel should treat "strict vs. substantial compliance" as a false binary on this record, and should independently search for substantial-compliance authority in Westlaw before assuming none exists — my inability to locate it through a public search index is weak evidence.

E. Timing, the acceptance window, and § 1013

Poster v. Southern Cal. Rapid Transit Dist. (1990) 52 Cal.3d 266; 276 Cal.Rptr. 321; 801 P.2d 1072 (decided Dec. 24, 1990). Two reported holdings:

  1. A § 998 offer is not revoked by a counteroffer and may be accepted until expressly withdrawn by the offeror or deemed withdrawn under § 998 — contrary to the general contract rule.
  2. When a § 998 offer is served by mail, CCP § 1013 applies and extends the 30-day acceptance period by five days, i.e., the offeree has at least 35 days to accept. The reported reasoning: § 998 is not part of a specific procedural scheme conflicting with § 1013; both sit among the Code's miscellaneous provisions and apply generally to civil cases.
  • Pin cite not confirmed. Secondary sources repeatedly cite the § 1013 holding to p. 275; that page number is reported by secondary sources only and must not be used as a pin cite without reading the opinion.
  • ⚠ MATERIAL CONFLICT IN THE SEARCH RECORD — COUNSEL MUST RESOLVE. Some search results describe the Court of Appeal in Poster as having held that "section 1013, subdivision (a) … does not apply to section 998 offers, and therefore did not serve to extend the time for acceptance," and as having found the acceptance untimely and reversed on that basis. The most coherent reading of the whole search record is that the Court of Appeal so held and the Supreme Court reversed, adopting the +5-day rule that every practitioner source now states as settled law. But I could not read the opinion or its disposition line, and I cannot confirm which court held what. This is precisely the kind of point that must be verified before it appears in a brief.

When the offer is "made." Practitioner sources uniformly state that the § 998(b)(2) 30-day clock runs from the date the offer is served, and that each offer creates its own cost-shifting period from its service date. No case was located squarely holding that the service date rather than a date printed on the offer controls, and no authority whatsoever was located addressing an undated § 998 offer. § 998 as retrieved contains no express requirement that the offer bear a date.

F. Burden of proof

Licudine v. Cedars-Sinai Medical Center (2019) 30 Cal.App.5th 918. The cleanest located statement of the two-part allocation. Reported: "although the party making a 998 offer generally has the burden of showing that her offer is valid, it is the 998 offeree who bears the burden of showing that an otherwise valid 998 offer was not made in good faith." Reported three-factor good-faith framework: (1) how far into the litigation the offer was made; (2) the information available to the offeree before the offer expired; and (3) whether the offeree told the offeror it lacked sufficient information to evaluate the offer, and how the offeror responded. On the facts, an offer made 19 days after service of the complaint and 5 days after the answer was reasonably rejected as premature.

Application to Our Facts

Every statement in this section is framed as something counsel may consider or should evaluate. Nothing here predicts what any court will do, and nothing here should be read as a prediction that any argument will succeed or fail.

1. Counsel should first re-anchor the analysis on the correct subdivision

Counsel may consider that, because our client is the plaintiff/offeror, the tasking's focus on § 998(c)(1) is misdirected: (c)(1) by its terms addresses "an offer made by a defendant." Counsel should evaluate the exposure and the upside under § 998(d) instead, which is discretionary ("may require") and limited to post-offer expert-witness fees — meaning that even a flawlessly drafted offer would have purchased a discretionary remedy, not an automatic one. Counsel may consider that this materially changes the cost-benefit of litigating the offer's validity at all. Counsel should further evaluate whether Civil Code § 3291 interest is available; on the retrieved text it is confined to actions "to recover damages for personal injury," and counsel may consider that a trust and real-property dispute is unlikely to qualify — which would remove the largest potential payoff from a plaintiff-side 998 offer.

2. Counsel should audit the offer against each statutory element before anything else

Counsel should evaluate the offer document against § 998(b)(1)'s elements one at a time: (i) writing; (ii) service on each offeree; (iii) service not less than 10 days before commencement of trial or arbitration; (iv) a statement of the offer containing the terms and conditions of the judgment; and (v) a provision allowing the accepting party to indicate acceptance by signing a statement that the offer is accepted. Counsel may consider that element (v) deserves immediate confirmation from the document itself: the facts as reported describe a "request to enter judgment" with a blank date line, which is not necessarily the same thing as a statutory acceptance provision. Counsel should evaluate that, under Puerta and Mostafavi as summarized above, the absence of a conforming acceptance provision is reported to be fatal to validity — and under Mostafavi, reported to render even a judgment entered on an acceptance void. Counsel may consider that this is a defect no argument about prejudice would reach, because on the reported reasoning there would have been "nothing to accept."

3. Counsel should treat the appraiser-valuation structure as the primary exposure

Counsel should evaluate the offer's operative content: a judgment requiring defendants to employ Stanley Xavier of Correia-Xavier for real property appraisal and Moss Adams for partnership appraisal within 30 days, valuing defendants' interests as of Hazel Leal's date of death, "with discounts as determined by those appraisers," for purposes of sale to plaintiff. Counsel may consider that under Barella as summarized, non-monetary terms do not invalidate an offer per se, but must be "sufficiently certain and capable of valuation to allow the court to determine whether judgment is more favorable than the offer." Counsel should evaluate the argument that this offer supplies no ascertainable value at the time the offer was made, because the entire economic content — the valuations and the discounts — is expressly delegated to third parties who had not yet been engaged and had not yet performed. Counsel may consider that Gorobets, decided August 6, 2026, is reported to require that at least one set of terms be "sufficiently certain to permit an accurate valuation at the time the offer is made," and should evaluate whether an offer whose number would exist only after acceptance and after a future appraisal process can satisfy that formulation. Counsel should also evaluate the structural parallel to Sanford: an offer whose real terms are deferred to a future process not set out in the offer.

Counsel may consider the countervailing argument that appraisal is a routine, objective valuation method, that the subject matter (real property and a partnership interest) is exactly the kind of asset appraisers value as a matter of course, and that this distinguishes the offer from Barella's confidentiality condition, whose value was "highly subjective and elusive." Counsel should evaluate the practitioner commentary framing equity in real property as capable of valuation for § 998 purposes. Counsel may also consider that this argument is in tension with Gorobets's reported temporal framing — capable of valuation when made — and should evaluate whether the presence of an undetermined "discount" element (marketability, minority interest, or otherwise) is what pushes the offer from "valuable by an objective method" into "speculative."

4. Counsel should evaluate whether the $5,705,257.43 figure is part of the offer at all

Counsel may consider that the monetary sum appears only in the cover letter and not in the § 998 offer, and should evaluate whether that sum can be treated as an alternative term of the offer. Counsel should evaluate Gorobets on both sides of this: it is reported to permit alternative-terms offers, which helps, but it is reported to condition validity on the offer "clearly present[ing] the alternatives" — and counsel should evaluate whether a figure stated in a transmittal letter, absent from the offer document, clearly presents an alternative within the offer. Counsel may consider Prince as the best available support for reaching outside the four corners: it is reported to permit contemporaneous written clarification between sophisticated represented parties. Counsel should evaluate the limit of that argument — that Prince is reported to have resolved an ambiguity in an existing offer rather than to have imported a term that the offer omitted — and should evaluate whether importing a dollar figure is characterization or addition. Counsel may consider that if the letter's figure is treated as part of the offer, it could supply the certain, valuable alternative that Gorobets requires; and that if it is not, the offer is left with only the appraiser structure discussed above.

Counsel should also evaluate the interaction with Prince's reported de novo standard of review and its reported rule that ambiguity is construed against the proponent — which here is our client.

5. Counsel should evaluate the proof-of-service defects as three distinct problems

(a) The January 3, 2018 dates. Counsel should evaluate that the POS recites both service and execution on a date more than eight years before the reported actual service date of 7/9/2026. Counsel may consider that this fails CCP § 1013a's business-practice requirement of "the date and place of business where the correspondence was placed for deposit," because the date stated is not the date of deposit. Counsel should evaluate the compounding effect: because the offer itself is undated, the POS is the only intrinsic evidence of when the offer was "made" for § 998(b)(2) purposes — and on the face of the papers, an offer "made" January 3, 2018 would have been deemed withdrawn roughly 30 to 35 days later, in early 2018. Counsel should evaluate the risk that opposing counsel frames the offer as facially expired on its own documents.

(b) The missing street address. Counsel should evaluate that the envelope address block names the attorneys and firm but contains no street address, which appears to fail § 1013a's requirement of "the name and address of the person served as shown on the envelope," and is in tension with § 1013(a)'s requirement that the item be "addressed to the person on whom it is to be served, at the office address as last given by that person on any document filed in the cause."

(c) Whether these are validity defects or evidentiary defects. Counsel should evaluate the two available characterizations. On the adverse framing, counsel may consider that service is a statutory element of § 998(b)(1) ("any party may serve an offer in writing"), and that under the bright-line approach of Puerta and Mostafavi a failure to establish statutory service is not excused by intent or by the offeree's actual knowledge. On the favorable framing, counsel may consider the general principle — surfaced in search results but, importantly, without a confirmable California citation (see Authority § G) — that the fact of service and the proof of service are distinct, that a defective affidavit does not by itself undo a service that actually occurred, and that a proof of service creates a rebuttable presumption that may be impeached or supplemented by other evidence. Counsel should evaluate whether that principle can be located and cited in verified form before it is relied on, and should treat it as unsupported until it is.

(d) Curative proof. Counsel should evaluate what independent, admissible evidence exists that service actually occurred on 7/9/2026 — the mailing clerk's or paralegal's percipient declaration, calendar and mailroom records, postage-meter or docketing entries, the transmittal email if any, and any acknowledgment, response, or reference to the offer by opposing counsel. Counsel may consider that under Licudine our side bears the burden of showing validity, so this evidence would need to be assembled proactively rather than in reply. Counsel should evaluate whether an amended or corrected proof of service is available and appropriate, and what disclosure obligations attach to filing one.

6. Counsel should evaluate the undated offer separately from the POS

Counsel may consider that § 998 as retrieved contains no express requirement that the offer bear a date, and that no authority was located holding an undated § 998 offer invalid for that reason alone. Counsel should therefore evaluate the argument that the blank "Dated: ______" lines on both the offer and the request to enter judgment are not independently fatal. Counsel should simultaneously evaluate that the absence of a date removes the one internal cross-check that would have exposed the 2018 POS date as a clerical error, and that the two defects are more damaging together than either is alone. Counsel may consider that this is the point at which the "non-prejudicial scrivener's error" argument is strongest in substance — a January 3, 2018 execution date on a 2026 offer is facially impossible and would have been understood as such by any reader — and weakest in form, because our side must still carry the burden of proving when the offer was made.

7. Counsel should evaluate the 30-day versus 35-day mismatch

Counsel should evaluate that the offer was served by mail and that, if Poster holds what secondary sources uniformly report, § 1013 extended the acceptance period to 35 days, while our cover letter states the offer "shall remain open for a period of thirty (30) days." Counsel may consider two competing readings: that the letter merely restates the statutory default and is harmless surplusage; or that it purports to close the offer five days before the statute would, which opposing counsel may characterize as a non-conforming offer or as having misstated the offeree's rights. Counsel should evaluate whether any located authority permits an offeror to set a shorter acceptance period than § 998 provides — none was located either way — and should treat this as genuinely open. Counsel may consider that this point may matter little in practice if no acceptance was tendered at any point, and should evaluate whether it is worth briefing at all.

Counsel must independently verify the Poster holding before relying on the 35-day figure. As set out in Authority § E, the search record contains an unresolved conflict about whether the +5-day rule is the Supreme Court's holding or the Court of Appeal's rejected position.

8. Counsel should evaluate the burden allocation as it actually falls on our side

Counsel may consider that Licudine places the burden of establishing the offer's validity on the offeror — our client — meaning our side must affirmatively establish service, timing, form, and (given the non-monetary structure) valuability. Counsel should evaluate that this is the least favorable posture in which to litigate a defect-laden offer. Counsel may consider that the good-faith burden runs the other way under Licudine, and that under Elrod and Nelson, if our client ultimately obtains a judgment more favorable than the offer, the offer would be presumptively reasonable with the burden on defendants to show otherwise — but counsel should evaluate that this presumption is only reached after validity is established, and never rescues an invalid offer.

Counsel should also evaluate the Licudine good-faith factors prospectively: how far into the litigation this offer was made, what information defendants had when it expired, and whether defendants communicated that they lacked information to evaluate an appraisal-based offer and how our side responded. Counsel may consider preserving any correspondence bearing on that third factor.

9. Counsel should evaluate cure by re-service

Counsel may consider that the most direct response to nearly every defect above is to serve a new, clean § 998 offer: dated; containing an express statutory acceptance provision; stating a sum certain or, if alternatives are used, clearly presenting them within the offer document itself in the manner Gorobets is reported to require; and accompanied by a correct proof of service reciting the true mailing date and a complete address. Counsel should evaluate the § 998(b)(1) ten-day-before-trial cutoff and the current trial setting before doing so. Counsel may consider that a new offer does not retroactively repair the first one, and should evaluate what, if anything, is preserved by continuing to assert the July 2026 offer. Counsel should evaluate the reported effect of successive offers on when cost-shifting benefits vest — noting that this point was not researched or verified for this memo.

10. Counsel should evaluate the adverse brief before it is filed

Counsel may consider that opposing counsel (Nikole/Niki Cunningham, Whitney Thompson & Jeffcoach) has an unusually clean set of attacks available and should evaluate each in advance: (i) no ascertainable value at the time of the offer, under Barella and Gorobets; (ii) facial expiration in 2018 on our own proof of service; (iii) non-compliance with § 1013a as to both date and address; (iv) the monetary alternative living outside the offer document; (v) if applicable, absence of a conforming acceptance provision under Puerta and Mostafavi; and (vi) de novo review with ambiguity construed against our client under Prince. Counsel should evaluate which of these our side can neutralize with evidence, which require legal argument, and whether the aggregate risk justifies pressing the offer at all given that the only realistic recovery is discretionary expert fees under § 998(d).

Open Questions

  1. Does § 998 apply to this proceeding at all? This appears to be a trust matter. Search results indicate § 998 has been used in probate-context proceedings, but I located no authority resolving whether § 998 applies to a Probate Code petition as opposed to a civil action, and one practitioner source and one apparently-unpublished decision suggest the question has been litigated. Counsel should resolve this first — it is potentially dispositive of the entire memo.
  2. Does the offer contain a conforming acceptance provision? This cannot be answered without the document. It is the single highest-value fact to confirm.
  3. When was trial or arbitration set, and was the offer served at least 10 days before commencement?
  4. Was the offer also served electronically? If so, CCP § 1010.6's court-day extension may apply and may interact with Poster in ways not researched here. It could also supply independent, timestamped proof of the true service date.
  5. Is this a joint offer to multiple defendants? If so, allocation and apportionment issues arise that were not researched for this memo.
  6. Could the relief offered actually be entered as a judgment? An offer under § 998(b)(1) is an offer "to allow judgment to be taken." Counsel should evaluate whether a judgment compelling defendants to employ two named appraisers, on terms to be filled in later, is a judgment a court could enter and enforce.
  7. What is the correct reading of Poster? See the flagged conflict in Authority § E.
  8. Is there California authority applying substantial compliance to § 998? I could not locate any. Absence of evidence here is weak evidence of absence, given the search-only constraint.
  9. What is the verified source of the "strictly construed in favor of the party sought to be subjected to its operation" rule?
  10. Does the cover letter's "thirty (30) days" language have any legal effect if the statute plus § 1013 would give 35?
  11. What is the official reporter citation for Gorobets, and has it been modified or is rehearing pending? It is twelve days old.
  12. What did the Court of Appeal actually hold on the service challenge in Berg v. Darden?

Confidence and Gaps

State this plainly to anyone who relies on this memo.

Blocked hosts included leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, law.justia.com, www.courtlistener.com, codes.findlaw.com, caselaw.findlaw.com, casetext.com, scholar.google.com, california.public.law, law.onecle.com, courts.ca.gov, and www4.courts.ca.gov. Direct curl was equally blocked for all hosts. The tasking's instruction to "verify EVERY citation by fetching it" could not be carried out.

  3. Consequently: I did not read the text of a single statute or a single opinion cited in this memo. Everything above came from a web search tool returning indexed excerpts and machine summaries attributed to public URLs. Statutory language shown in quotation marks was returned by that tool as verbatim and was corroborated across multiple independent results, but was not read at its source. Case holdings are secondary-source characterizations.

  4. No pin cite in this memo is confirmed. Where secondary sources reported a page number (Poster at 275; Barella at 799–801; Berg at 727; Bias at 820), that number is identified as reported and is expressly not offered as a pin cite. Do not put any of these page numbers in a filing without opening the opinion.

  5. Citations I could NOT verify, restated for emphasis:

    • "M. Lowenstein & Sons, Inc. v. Superior Court" (1978) 80 Cal.App.3d 762 — case name, citation, and holding all unconfirmed; search returned a differently-named case. Do not cite.
    • Bias v. Wright (2002) 103 Cal.App.4th 811 — exists and is associated with § 998 in a CLE handout; holding unconfirmed.

The 35-day figure is used in this memo because that is what every secondary source states, but counsel must read the opinion before relying on it.

  7. This memo is research support, not a legal opinion, and it is not filing-ready. ALL authority cited here — every statute, every case, every quotation, every characterization of a holding — requires independent verification by counsel in Westlaw, Lexis, or CoCounsel before it is used in any brief, declaration, meet-and-confer letter, or oral argument. Given that nothing was read in primary form, counsel should treat this memo as a research map identifying what to pull and what to check, not as a verified record of the law.
