ADDENDUM 2 (8/18/2026) — SUCCESSIVE OFFERS: MARTINEZ v. BROWNCO NOW VERIFIED; A POSSIBLE EARLIER $5.75M OFFER SURFACED

Trigger. The drafts-folder sweep surfaced four cover letters dated 5/18/2026 for a $5,750,000 flat lump-sum § 998 offer, the final version fully addressed to opposing counsel and signed by Mr. Ormonde (verified_facts_memo §6.14). Whether it was served is NOT established (OI-41). If it was, this case has two successive § 998 offers by the same offeror, the second (7/2/2026, $5,705,257.43 structure) $44,742.57 lower than the first.

What is now VERIFIED (read in full via CourtListener, 8/18/2026):

Martinez v. Brownco Construction Co. (2013) 56 Cal.4th 1014 [157 Cal.Rptr.3d 558, 301 P.3d 1167] (Baxter, J.) — CourtListener cluster 899532. Verbatim from the opinion:

"The terms of section 998 do not prohibit a party from making more than one settlement offer, but they are silent as to the effect of a party's multiple offers. In this action, we consider whether a later offer extinguishes a previous offer for purposes of section 998's cost-shifting provisions. We conclude that where, as here, a plaintiff makes two successive statutory offers, and the defendant fails to obtain a judgment more favorable than either offer, allowing recovery of expert fees incurred from the date of the first offer is consistent with section 998's language and best promotes the statutory purpose to encourage settlements."

The opinion identifies (and engages, rather than mechanically applying) the two prior appellate approaches: Wilson v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. (1999) 72 Cal.App.4th 382 — the trial court below had relied on it for "[t]he most recently rejected offer is the only pertinent offer. All prior offers are extinguished by the subsequent offer" — and Distefano v. Hall (1968) 263 Cal.App.2d 380 (two defense offers under former § 997). It also restates T. M. Cobb Co. v. Superior Court (1984) 36 Cal.3d 273: general contract principles (e.g., Civ. Code § 1586 revocability) govern § 998 offers only when applying them "best promote[s]" the settlement policy — under T. M. Cobb, a § 998 offer is revocable prior to acceptance or statutory expiration.

UNVERIFIED / for counsel: subsequent history and citing treatment of all four cases (CourtListener cannot KeyCite); whether Martinez's first-offer rule extends beyond its facts (plaintiff's two offers, judgment worse than both, expert fees) to an offeror whose SECOND offer is LOWER, and to our posture (buyout plaintiff paying money). Martinez involved escalating offers; ours would be de-escalating — the equities the Court stressed (offeree can never be worse off for rejecting a later, more favorable offer) run differently here. This is a briefing question, not an assumption, in BOTH directions:

  1. If the 5/18 offer was served and expired, the cost-shifting baseline analysis must address Martinez/Wilson — and note the July offer's validity problems (§§ A–D above) would then coexist with a facially cleaner (if also unlocated) May offer.
  2. Revocation angle (T. M. Cobb): a served-then-superseded May offer was likely extinguished as an offer capable of acceptance by the later July offer or by its own 30-day lapse — but Martinez holds extinction for acceptance purposes does not automatically erase it for cost-shifting purposes.
  3. Optics/good-faith: a second offer $44,742.57 below the first invites a "token/ negotiated" attack on both. The fresh-corrected-998 recommendation in Addendum 1 remains the cleaner path — one new offer, correct in form, with a current interest figure (see adverse analysis A-35: the $677,830.41 interest component is stale as of 5/1/2026).

Action for counsel: resolve OI-41 (service status) first; then decide whether the baseline argument is built on the May offer, the July offer, or a fresh corrected offer. Everything in this addendum informs; none of it predicts.

ADDENDUM 3 (8/18/2026) — THE AS-SERVED PACKAGE: TWO-TRACK STRUCTURE, DUAL-METHOD SERVICE, NEW CAPTION DEFECT

Trigger: client produced counsel-file copies (S-14; transcription in ../01-verified-facts/998-as-served-extract.md): a 7/9/2026 transmittal letter ("U.S. MAIL and VIA EMAIL"), a previously unknown 7/8/2026 letter with an Evid. Code § 1152 header, and the first two pages of the 998 as served. Three consequences for this memo:

1. The Mostafavi/Gorobets analysis must be re-aimed. The 7/8 letter states the architecture: the 998 carries ONLY the specific-performance terms (employ Correia-Xavier and Moss Adams), and the $5,705,257.43 is "an alternative … monetary settlement offer" outside the 998, under § 1152. So the Mostafavi "terms must be in the offer" problem is NOT that a monetary term was left out of the offer that contains it — the monetary offer was never a 998. The live questions become: (a) is an employ-two-appraisers-and-sell offer sufficiently certain and valuable to function as a 998 baseline at all (how does a court later determine whether the judgment obtained is "more favorable" than an offer with no sum)? (b) does the offer's incorporation of external instruments ("pursuant to the terms of the Settlement Agreement and Tenants-in Common Agreement… with discounts applied as determined by [the appraiser]") satisfy the certainty requirement, or does it delegate the price to a third party in a way Bewick/§ 730 contemplate for the COURT, not for a 998? (c) Gorobets (alternatives must be clearly structured IN the offer): the monetary alternative lives in a separate § 1152 letter — arguably cleaner (it is not part of the 998 at all), arguably worse (an offeree could say the package as a whole was ambiguous about what acceptance meant). All three are briefing questions; none is resolved here.

2. Dual-method service adds a § 1010.6 branch to the expiration analysis. The transmittal says U.S. Mail AND email. Poster's 35-day figure is a § 1013 (mail) analysis. If electronic service governs, CCP § 1010.6's 2-court-day extension (whether it applies to 998 acceptance periods was flagged UNRESEARCHED in the base memo) gives: 30 days from 7/9 → 8/8 (Sat) → 8/10 (Mon) + 2 court days → 8/12; the mail branch gives 8/13. Every branch expired before 8/18/2026. Which branch governs — and whether simultaneous dual-method service picks the longer or the shorter — is for counsel with the statutes in hand (§§ 1010.6, 1013, 998(b)(2); none read in primary form here).

3. Defect inventory, as-served version. Corrected from the Drive draft: plaintiff's body name; Thompson/firm spellings. Persisting: "For the purpose of Under Code of Civil Procedure Section 998"; ¶2's "sale of the Partnership real Property." New: the caption case number reads "VCU3627028" (extra digit) on the document the acceptance clause instructs the offerees to file with the Court Clerk. Unknown (pages not produced): whether the as-served offer is DATED, and what the as-served POS recites — the 1/3/2018 POS finding (base memo §A) attaches so far only to the Drive version. The fresh-corrected-998 recommendation stands, and the correction list now includes the case number. Also note the offer defines "Real Property" as "the 652.02 acres" — the valuations sweep reports NO located document that produces 652.02 acres; derive or source that figure before it is repeated (OI-52).

ADDENDUM 3 (9/26/2026) — THE NO-MONETARY-TERM STRUCTURE WAS DELIBERATE; THE CRITIQUE IS RE-AIMED

New fact (privileged; counsel's own email, 6/16/2026, thread 19ed33e5a03baa31): prior counsel wrote that he "revisited the complaint in order to ensure that the offer is within the bounds of the request sought in the complaint… Our complaint seeks specific performance… we are not requiring a specific purchase price. I researched the 998 as it pertains to the specific performance and our offer would need to stay within those bounds… we would likely need to simply send a settlement offer identifying our numeric offer and then within that same offer send the 998…" The client agreed.

Consequence for this memo. The served package is two instruments by design: (1) a § 998 offer whose terms — judgment requiring the parties to employ Correia-Xavier and Moss Adams — ARE stated in the offer itself; (2) a separate monetary settlement proposal ($5,705,257.43) that was never intended as a § 998 offer. Addendum 1's reliance on Mostafavi fn. 6 and Gorobets ("terms must be in the offer") therefore aims at the wrong target: the monetary figure's absence from the 998 is not a defect of the 998, because the money was never a 998 term. The live § 998 questions become: (a) whether a non-monetary, specific-performance-only offer can support cost-shifting at all — i.e., whether a court can determine that a later judgment is "not more favorable" than an offer to employ named appraisers (UNVERIFIED — research target; the comparison problem for non-monetary offers is the crux); (b) the independent service/form defects (POS executed "January 3, 2018"; undated offer; case-number variant; misspellings) — service DATE now documented as 7/9/2026 by counsel's office; (c) the offer's validity given the § 3390 personal-services problem with an order to "employ" named non-parties (Woolley) — a judgment the court arguably could not enter cannot anchor cost-shifting (UNVERIFIED). The "fresh corrected 998" recommendation survives, re-grounded: a new offer should either be a monetary 998 aligned with an amended prayer (Bewick/§ 730 price-fixing relief) or a specific-performance 998 whose judgment is one the court can actually enter. Also: the 5/18/2026 $5.75M "offer" was a client draft and very likely never served — the Martinez two-offer discussion in Addendum 2 is probably moot (confirm with prior counsel).

R2: Specific Performance of Buyout and Appraisal Provisions

ATTORNEY WORK-PRODUCT — PREPARED FOR COUNSEL — NOT LEGAL ADVICE

Matter: Manuel Stephen Leal v. Ashley Garabedian and Hazel Susan Leal, successor co-trustees of the Hazel J. Leal Revocable Trust dated November 3, 2008 (Tulare County Superior Court) Prepared: August 18, 2026

RESEARCH-METHOD DISCLOSURE (read before relying on anything below)

A CourtListener MCP server was not available for this research. Public web sources were used instead. In this session the network egress policy blocked every dedicated legal-research host, including leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, courtlistener.com, law.justia.com, casetext.com, scholar.google.com, codes.findlaw.com, caselaw.findlaw.com, law.onecle.com, california.public.law, leagle.com, casemine.com, scocal.stanford.edu, courts.ca.gov, and case.law. Full opinion text could not be fetched for any case cited below.

Two different verification levels are therefore used, and each authority is tagged:

  • VERIFIED (STATUTE) — full verbatim statutory text was actually retrieved and read. Source: the California Legislative Counsel Bureau's own PUBINFO database export (the LAW_SECTION_TBL table and its CAML .lob section files — the same data that drives leginfo), mirrored at a public GitHub repository reachable from this session. Each entry gives the .lob file and the Legislative Counsel history note as retrieved. Counsel should still confirm each section against leginfo or Westlaw, because the mirror is a third-party copy of the official export (export date stated in the repository: July 9, 2026) and currency cannot be independently confirmed here.
  • SEARCH-VERIFIED ONLY (CASE) — the case exists and was located through web search returning multiple independent reporter-citation sources; case name, year, court, and reporter citation are corroborated, and the described holding comes from search-result content. The opinion text itself was NOT read. No pin cites are confirmed. Every case below must be pulled and read in full on Westlaw/Lexis/CoCounsel before it is cited to the Court.

Nothing in this memo predicts an outcome. All application is framed as considerations for counsel.

Issue

  1. What must a plaintiff establish to obtain specific performance in California under Civil Code sections 3384, 3390, and 3391 — inadequacy of the legal remedy, definite and certain terms, adequate consideration, mutuality of remedy, and ability to perform?
  2. May a contractual buyout provision in a partnership agreement or a settlement agreement be specifically enforced, and is a partnership or LLC interest treated as sufficiently "unique" that damages are inadequate?
  3. Where a contract requires the parties to employ an appraiser or to submit to an appraisal/valuation formula, is that term sufficiently certain to be specifically enforceable, or is it an unenforceable agreement to agree? Will a California court supply a valuation method — or fix value itself — when the designated appraiser is unavailable or a party refuses to cooperate?
  4. Are appraisal provisions treated as arbitration under Code of Civil Procedure section 1280 et seq., such that the enforcement vehicle becomes a petition to compel rather than a specific-performance decree?
  5. In the trust context, may a buy-sell or option be specifically enforced against a trustee, and can a co-trustee be compelled to perform?
  6. How does the Civil Code section 3387 presumption that land is unique apply to a tenancy-in-common interest?
  7. What defenses — unclean hands, laches, uncertainty, lack of mutuality, impossibility — bear on the claim?

Short Answer

On the elements. California has a codified specific-performance scheme. Civil Code section 3384 authorizes the remedy generally; section 3390 lists what cannot be specifically enforced (including, at subdivision (e), an agreement whose terms "are not sufficiently certain to make the precise act which is to be done clearly ascertainable"); section 3391 bars enforcement against a party who received inadequate consideration or as to whom the contract is not just and reasonable; and section 3392 bars enforcement in favor of a party who has not performed his own conditions precedent. Statutory text for each was retrieved verbatim and appears below.

On mutuality. The classical mutuality-of-remedy requirement has been displaced by statute. Civil Code section 3386, as amended in 1969, permits specific performance "[n]otwithstanding that the agreed counterperformance is not or would not have been specifically enforceable," provided the remedy is otherwise appropriate and the counterperformance has been substantially performed or is assured or securable. Search-verified case law (Ellis v. Mihelis (1963) 60 Cal.2d 206) reflects the related principle that a plaintiff suing for specific performance of a real-property sale satisfies mutuality by submitting himself to the court's jurisdiction.

On agreements to appraise — the central issue. The research located directly on-point California authority, and the answer is favorable to enforceability in principle. Civil Code section 1613 provides that where a contract prescribes an exclusive method of ascertaining consideration that is possible on its face but in fact becomes impossible, only that provision is void — the contract survives. In Bewick v. Mecham (1945) 26 Cal.2d 92, a lease option priced "at a price and terms then to be agreed on ... and if not agreed on then to be fixed by arbitration" was enforced after the lessor refused to appoint an arbitrator; the trial court fixed the price and decreed specific performance, and the judgment was affirmed. Petrolink, Inc. v. Lantel Enterprises (2018) 21 Cal.App.5th 375 and (2022) 81 Cal.App.5th 156 reflect the same modern practice: on a lease option to purchase at "fair market value" by appraisal, where the parties' competing appraisals diverged sharply, the trial court appointed an independent appraiser, found value, and ordered specific performance. Civil Code section 1611 supplies a default measure — reasonable worth — where a contract does not determine consideration or leaves it to an interested party's discretion. Together these indicate that a valuation mechanism is materially different from an agreement to agree (contrast Bustamante v. Intuit, Inc. (2006) 141 Cal.App.4th 199), because the price is ascertainable by an objective process without any further assent from the parties.

But there is a real countercurrent specific to this complaint's prayer. The relief sought is an order that defendants employ two named third parties — Stanley Xavier of Correia-Xavier and Moss Adams. Civil Code section 3390(b) bars specific enforcement of "[a]n obligation to employ another in personal service," and section 3390(d) bars specific enforcement of "[a]n agreement to procure the act or consent of ... any other third person." Neither named appraiser can be compelled by this decree to accept the engagement. Counsel should expect that framing, and should note that Bewick, Civil Code section 1613, and Evidence Code section 730 all point toward a fallback in which the court determines value (or appoints its own appraiser) rather than commanding defendants to hire particular professionals.

On appraisal-as-arbitration. Code of Civil Procedure section 1280(a) expressly defines "Agreement" for purposes of the California Arbitration Act to "include[], but [not be] limited to, agreements providing for valuations, appraisals, and similar proceedings." Search-verified case law confirms courts treat appraisals as arbitrations (Kacha v. Allstate Ins. Co. (2006) 140 Cal.App.4th 1023; Lambert v. Carneghi (2008) 158 Cal.App.4th 1120; Louise Gardens of Encino Homeowners' Assn., Inc. v. Truck Ins. Exchange, Inc. (2000) 82 Cal.App.4th 648) — though all located cases arise in the insurance context, and no published non-insurance California decision was located in this session. This cuts both ways: it may expose the specific-performance claim to a motion to compel arbitration, and it simultaneously supplies a powerful cure for non-cooperation, because section 1281.6 directs that "if the agreed method fails or for any reason cannot be followed," the court "shall appoint the arbitrator" on petition.

On the trust context. Probate Code section 15620 makes a power vested in two or more trustees exercisable only by unanimous action unless the instrument provides otherwise — so relief likely must run against both co-trustees. Section 16013 imposes on each co-trustee a duty to participate in administration. Sections 850 and 856 authorize a petition and an order directing a fiduciary to execute a conveyance where a decedent was bound by a written contract to convey and the contract "is one which can be specifically enforced," and sections 17200 and 17206 give the probate court broad power over the internal affairs of a trust and to "make any orders and take any other action necessary or proper."

On real property. Civil Code section 3387's presumption that a breach of an agreement to transfer real property cannot be adequately relieved by money is conclusive only for a single-family dwelling the plaintiff intends to occupy; in all other cases — including 652.02 acres of agricultural land — it is only "a presumption affecting the burden of proof." No California authority applying section 3387 specifically to an undivided tenancy-in-common interest was located.

On the discount question. Genuinely two-sided; analyzed in the Application section below. In short: leaving discounts to appraiser discretion helps certainty by supplying a mechanism that requires no further party assent (sections 1611, 1613; Bewick; Petrolink), and hurts certainty to the extent section 3390(e) requires "the precise act which is to be done" to be "clearly ascertainable" and the aggregate discount is large enough to put Civil Code section 3391's "adequate consideration" and "just and reasonable" limits in play.

Authority

A. Specific performance — the Civil Code framework

Cal. Civ. Code § 3384 — "Section Thirty-three Hundred and Eighty-four. Except as otherwise provided in this Article, the specific performance of an obligation may be compelled." Holding/effect: General authorization for the remedy, subject to the Article's exceptions. Note the section is codified with brackets — "[3384.]" — in the Legislative Counsel database. VERIFIED (STATUTE) — retrieved verbatim. History as retrieved: "Amended by Code Amendments 1873-74, Ch. 612." Source file LAW_SECTION_TBL_39593.lob. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aaronjuar-ez/PUBINFO-2025/main/LAW_SECTION_TBL_39593.lob (canonical, blocked in session: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3384.)

Cal. Civ. Code § 3386 — "Notwithstanding that the agreed counterperformance is not or would not have been specifically enforceable, specific performance may be compelled if: (a) Specific performance would otherwise be an appropriate remedy; and (b) The agreed counterperformance has been substantially performed or its concurrent or future performance is assured or, if the court deems necessary, can be secured to the satisfaction of the court." Holding/effect: Statutorily displaces the classical mutuality-of-remedy bar; substitutes an assurance-of-counterperformance test. VERIFIED (STATUTE) — retrieved verbatim. History: "Amended by Stats. 1969, Ch. 156." LAW_SECTION_TBL_39594.lob. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aaronjuar-ez/PUBINFO-2025/main/LAW_SECTION_TBL_39594.lob

Cal. Civ. Code § 3387 — "It is to be presumed that the breach of an agreement to transfer real property cannot be adequately relieved by pecuniary compensation. In the case of a single-family dwelling which the party seeking performance intends to occupy, this presumption is conclusive. In all other cases, this presumption is a presumption affecting the burden of proof." Holding/effect: Land-is-unique presumption; conclusive only for owner-occupied single-family dwellings, otherwise rebuttable and burden-shifting. VERIFIED (STATUTE) — retrieved verbatim. History: "Amended by Stats. 1984, Ch. 937, Sec. 1." LAW_SECTION_TBL_39595.lob. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aaronjuar-ez/PUBINFO-2025/main/LAW_SECTION_TBL_39595.lob

Cal. Civ. Code § 3388 — "A party who has signed a written contract may be compelled specifically to perform it, though the other party has not signed it, if the latter has performed, or offers to perform it on his part, and the case is otherwise proper for enforcing specific performance." VERIFIED (STATUTE) — retrieved verbatim. History: "Enacted 1872." LAW_SECTION_TBL_11621.lob.

Cal. Civ. Code § 3389 — "A contract otherwise proper to be specifically enforced, may be thus enforced, though a penalty is imposed, or the damages are liquidated for its breach, and the party in default is willing to pay the same." Holding/effect: A liquidated-damages or penalty clause does not by itself convert the contract into one enforceable only in damages. VERIFIED (STATUTE) — retrieved verbatim. History: "Enacted 1872." LAW_SECTION_TBL_39596.lob.

Cal. Civ. Code § 3390 — "The following obligations cannot be specifically enforced: (a) An obligation to render personal service. (b) An obligation to employ another in personal service. (c) An agreement to perform an act which the party has not power lawfully to perform when required to do so. (d) An agreement to procure the act or consent of the spouse of the contracting party, or of any other third person. (e) An agreement, the terms of which are not sufficiently certain to make the precise act which is to be done clearly ascertainable." Holding/effect: The statutory certainty requirement (subd. (b)) and on compelling a party to procure a third person's act or consent (subd. (d)). VERIFIED (STATUTE) — retrieved verbatim. History: "Amended by Stats. 2016, Ch. 50, Sec. 12. Cal. Civ. Code § 3391 — "Specific performance cannot be enforced against a party to a contract in any of the following cases: 1. If he has not received an adequate consideration for the contract; 2. If it is not, as to him, just and reasonable; 3. Bewick v. Mecham (1945) 26 Cal.2d 92 (Cal. Supreme Court) Holding as described by search sources: A lease contained an option to purchase "at a price and terms then to be agreed on between the parties hereto, and if not agreed on then to be fixed by arbitration, each of the parties hereto selecting one arbitrator, and the two selected a third." After the option was exercised the lessor refused to sell and refused to appoint an arbitrator. Plaintiff sued to have the court fix the purchase price and decree specific performance. Applying Civil Code section 1613, the court reasoned that where a contract provides an exclusive method of ascertaining consideration that appears possible but in fact becomes impossible of execution, only that provision is void, and the impossibility of ascertaining price by the contractual method does not preclude a court from giving effect to the contract by ascertaining the consideration in place of the arbitrators or appraisers. The trial court fixed a purchase price and ordered specific performance; affirmed. Pin cite not confirmed. The opinion was not retrieved and the reporter citation was not independently corroborated in this session. Do not cite without pulling it.

Blackburn v. Charnley (2004) 117 Cal.App.4th 758 Holding as described by search sources: Properly admitted extrinsic evidence rendered the description of lots conveyed by purchase agreements sufficiently definite for enforcement, and the trial court did not err in ordering specific performance. Search sources also attribute to this case the principle that in an action for specific performance — where the court must direct a party to perform certain acts — the contract's provisions must be more specific than would be required in an action for damages. Pin cite not confirmed. SEARCH-VERIFIED ONLY (CASE) — https://caselaw.findlaw.com/ca-court-of-appeal/1239849.html (blocked in session). Note this case is two-sided: it supports use of extrinsic evidence to cure indefiniteness, but it also states the heightened-specificity principle defendants will rely on.

Tamarind Lithography Workshop, Inc. v. Sanders (1983) 143 Cal.App.3d 571 Holding as described by search sources: Arising from a written settlement agreement between the parties, in which Sanders performed but Tamarind failed to provide a contractually stipulated screen credit. A jury found breach and awarded $25,000, and the trial court denied injunctive relief. The appeal concerned "whether an award of damages is an adequate remedy at law in lieu of specific performance for the breach of an agreement to give screen credits." Pin cite not confirmed. The precise disposition on appeal was not confirmed from search sources. SEARCH-VERIFIED ONLY (CASE) — https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/3d/143/571.html (blocked in session). Relevant here chiefly for the proposition that specific performance is available to enforce a settlement agreement where damages are inadequate. Counsel must read it before citing; the described facts (creative/artistic credit) limit its transferability.

C. Mutuality and adequacy of consideration

Ellis v. Mihelis (1963) 60 Cal.2d 206, 32 Cal.Rptr. 415, 384 P.2d 7 (Cal. Supreme Court) Holding as described by search sources: Action to compel specific performance of a contract for the sale of real property. The court stated that it has been established from an early date in California that where a party commences an action to compel specific enforcement of an agreement for the sale of real property, the requirement of mutuality is satisfied, on the theory that by bringing the action the plaintiff has submitted himself to the jurisdiction of equity and thereby enabled the court to assure performance by him. The court also addressed adequacy of consideration, construing a $5,000 buyer deposit securing performance on penalty of forfeiture as consideration making the offer irrevocable for 30 days. Pin cite not confirmed. SEARCH-VERIFIED ONLY (CASE) — https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2d/60/206.html (blocked in session).

Secondary corroboration for the statutory abolition of mutuality of remedy: California Law Revision Commission, "Mutuality of Remedies in Suits for Specific Performance," Printed Reports Pub. 080, https://clrc.ca.gov/pub/Printed-Reports/Pub080.pdf — UNVERIFIED (host blocked; document not retrieved). This report appears to be the study underlying the 1969 amendment to Civil Code section 3386. Counsel may find it useful legislative history; it was not read here.

D. Appraisal as arbitration

Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1280(a) — "As used in this title: (a) 'Agreement' includes, but is not limited to, agreements providing for valuations, appraisals, and similar proceedings and agreements between employers and employees or between their respective representatives." Holding/effect: The California Arbitration Act's definition of "agreement" expressly reaches valuation and appraisal agreements. This is the single most important provision on Issue 4. Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1281 — "A written agreement to submit to arbitration an existing controversy or a controversy thereafter arising is valid, enforceable and irrevocable, save upon such grounds as exist for the revocation of any contract." VERIFIED (STATUTE) — retrieved verbatim. History: "Repealed and added by Stats. 1961, Ch. 461." LAW_SECTION_TBL_7427.lob.

Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1281.2 — "On petition of a party to an arbitration agreement alleging the existence of a written agreement to arbitrate a controversy and that a party to the agreement refuses to arbitrate that controversy, the court shall order the petitioner and the respondent to arbitrate the controversy if it determines that an agreement to arbitrate the controversy exists, unless it determines that: (a) The right to compel arbitration has been waived by the petitioner; or (b) Grounds exist for rescission of the agreement. (c) A party to the arbitration agreement is also a party to a pending court action or special proceeding with a third party, arising out of the same transaction or series of related transactions and there is a possibility of conflicting rulings on a common issue of law or fact. ..." (Full text retrieved, including the court's options under subdivision (c) to refuse enforcement, order joinder, stay the action, or stay the arbitration.) Holding/effect: The petition-to-compel vehicle, including the waiver defense and the third-party/conflicting-rulings discretion. VERIFIED (STATUTE) — retrieved verbatim. History: "Amended by Stats. 2018, Ch. 106, Sec. 1. (AB 3247) Effective January 1, 2019." LAW_SECTION_TBL_7416.lob.

Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1281.6 — "If the arbitration agreement provides a method of appointing an arbitrator, that method shall be followed. If the arbitration agreement does not provide a method for appointing an arbitrator, the parties ... may agree on a method ... In the absence of an agreed method, or if the agreed method fails or for any reason cannot be followed, or when an arbitrator appointed fails to act and his or her successor has not been appointed, the court, on petition of a party to the arbitration agreement, shall appoint the arbitrator. When a petition is made to the court to appoint a neutral arbitrator, the court shall nominate five persons from lists of persons supplied jointly by the parties ... or obtained from a governmental agency concerned with arbitration or private disinterested association concerned with arbitration. The parties ... may within five days of receipt of notice of the nominees from the court jointly select the arbitrator whether or not the arbitrator is among the nominees. If the parties fail to select an arbitrator within the five-day period, the court shall appoint the arbitrator from the nominees." Holding/effect: The statutory cure for a failed or obstructed appraisal mechanism. If the appraisal clause is an "agreement" under section 1280(a), a designated appraiser's unavailability or a party's refusal to cooperate triggers a mandatory judicial appointment on petition. VERIFIED (STATUTE) — retrieved verbatim. History: "Amended by Stats. 2001, Ch. 362, Sec. 3. Effective January 1, 2002." Kacha v. Allstate Ins. Co. (2006) 140 Cal.App.4th 1023 Holding as described by search sources: Fire loss to a home and personal property. "Appraisal hearings are a form of arbitration and are generally subject to the rules governing arbitration"; the court held the appraisal proceedings constitute "arbitration." The court also held the appraisal panel exceeded its authority by making coverage/causation determinations and ordered the award vacated, observing that unlike arbitrators, who can decide issues of law, appraisers have much more limited authority and may determine only the actual cash value of the property in question. Pin cite not confirmed. SEARCH-VERIFIED ONLY (CASE) — https://caselaw.findlaw.com/ca-court-of-appeal/1063960.html (blocked in session). Two-sided: the scope-of-authority holding is a live constraint on what an appraiser may decide.

Lambert v. Carneghi (2008) 158 Cal.App.4th 1120, 70 Cal.Rptr.3d 626 (1st Dist.) Holding as described by search sources: Negligence claims against appraisers arising from a fire-insurance appraisal under Insurance Code section 2071. The court concluded that an appraisal proceeding under section 2071 is an arbitration and that the appraiser was immune from suit (arbitral immunity); appraisers determining the amount payable under such a policy "are arbitrators within the meaning of Code of Civil Procedure section 1280." Pin cite not confirmed. SEARCH-VERIFIED ONLY (CASE) — https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2244928/lambert-v-carneghi/ (blocked in session).

Louise Gardens of Encino Homeowners' Assn., Inc. v. Truck Ins. Exchange, Inc. (2000) 82 Cal.App.4th 648, 98 Cal.Rptr.2d 378 Holding as described by search sources: An agreement to conduct an appraisal contained in a policy of insurance is an arbitration agreement subject to the statutory contractual arbitration law; appraisals are generally subject to contractual arbitration law and its related statutory scheme. The opinion also recognizes distinctions between appraisal and arbitration (search sources report that, at least as to government-declared disasters, appraisal procedures could not be compelled in the same way arbitration is mandatory on demand), and addresses when challenges to an award must be raised. Pin cite not confirmed. The disaster-related qualification is reported only in secondary summary and must be checked against the opinion. SEARCH-VERIFIED ONLY (CASE) — https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/4th/82/648.html (blocked in session).

Gap flag: every located California case treating appraisal as arbitration arises in the first-party insurance context. No published California decision applying that characterization to a partnership, trust, or settlement-agreement valuation clause was located in this session. The textual reach of section 1280(a) is not limited to insurance, but counsel should not represent to the Court that non-insurance authority exists until it is found.

E. Trust context

Cal. Prob. Code § 850(a) — Retrieved in full. Materially: "(a) The following persons may file a petition requesting that the court make an order under this part: ... (2) The personal representative or any interested person in any of the following cases: (A) Where the decedent while living is bound by a contract in writing to convey real property or to transfer personal property and dies before making the conveyance or transfer and the decedent, if living, could have been compelled to make the conveyance or transfer. (B) Where the decedent while living binds himself or herself or his or her personal representative by a contract in writing to convey real property or to transfer personal property upon or after his or her death and the contract is one which can be specifically enforced. (C) Where the decedent died in possession of, or holding title to, real or personal property, and the property or some interest therein is claimed to belong to another. (D) Where the decedent died having a claim to real or personal property, title to or possession of which is held by another. (3) The trustee or any interested person in any of the following cases: (A) Where the trustee is in possession of, or holds title to, real or personal property, and the property, or some interest, is claimed to belong to another. (B) Where the trustee has a claim to real or personal property, title to or possession of which is held by another. (C) Where the property of the trust is claimed to be subject to a creditor of the settlor of the trust. (b) The petition shall set forth facts upon which the claim is based." Holding/effect: Express statutory vehicle keyed to a written contract to convey that "can be specifically enforced." VERIFIED (STATUTE) — retrieved verbatim. F. Partnership buyout

Cal. Corp. Code § 16701 — Retrieved in full. Materially: "(a) If a partner is dissociated from a partnership, the partnership shall cause the dissociated partner's interest in the partnership to be purchased for a buyout price determined pursuant to subdivision (b). (b) The buyout price of a dissociated partner's interest is the amount that would have been distributable to the dissociating partner under subdivision (b) of Section 16807 if, on the date of dissociation, the assets of the partnership were sold at a price equal to the greater of the liquidation value or the value based on a sale of the entire business as a going concern without the dissociated partner and the partnership was wound up as of that date. ... (i) A dissociated partner may maintain an action against the partnership ... to determine the buyout price of that partner's interest, any offsets under subdivision (c), or other terms of the obligation to purchase. ... The court shall determine the buyout price of the dissociated partner's interest, any offset due under subdivision (c), and accrued interest, and enter judgment for any additional payment or refund. ... The court may assess reasonable attorney's fees and the fees and expenses of appraisers or other experts for a party to the action, in amounts the court finds equitable, against a party that the court finds acted arbitrarily, vexatiously, or not in good faith." Holding/effect: The Legislature expressly contemplates a court determining a partnership buyout price with appraiser assistance and fee-shifting for bad-faith conduct — a strong structural analogy against an argument that valuing a partnership interest is beyond judicial competence. Note this is the statutory default for dissociation, which a partnership agreement may displace. VERIFIED (STATUTE) — retrieved verbatim. History: "Amended by Stats. 2007, Ch. 263, Sec. 15. Effective January 1, 2008." LAW_SECTION_TBL_4258.lob. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aaronjuar-ez/PUBINFO-2025/main/LAW_SECTION_TBL_4258.lob

Drever and Kajima/Ray Wilson v. G. Enforcement mechanics

Cal. Evid. Code § 730 — "When it appears to the court, at any time before or during the trial of an action, that expert evidence is or may be required by the court or by any party to the action, the court on its own motion or on motion of any party may appoint one or more experts to investigate, to render a report as may be ordered by the court, and to testify as an expert at the trial of the action relative to the fact or matter as to which the expert evidence is or may be required. The court may fix the compensation for these services ... Nothing in this section shall be construed to permit a person to perform any act for which a license is required unless the person holds the appropriate license to lawfully perform that act." Holding/effect: Vehicle for a court-appointed neutral appraiser (the mechanism reportedly used in Petrolink). Note the final sentence — appraisal licensure. VERIFIED (STATUTE) — retrieved verbatim. History: "Amended by Stats. 1990, Ch. 295, Sec. 1." LAW_SECTION_TBL_3244.lob.

Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 664.6 — Retrieved in full. Materially: "(a) If parties to pending litigation stipulate, in a writing signed by the parties outside of the presence of the court or orally before the court, for settlement of the case, or part thereof, the court, upon motion, may enter judgment pursuant to the terms of the settlement. If the parties to the settlement agreement or their counsel stipulate in writing or orally before the court, the court may dismiss the case as to the settling parties without prejudice and retain jurisdiction over the parties to enforce the settlement until performance in full of the terms of the settlement. ... (c) Paragraphs (2) and (3) of subdivision (b) do not apply in a civil harassment action, an action brought pursuant to the Family Code, an action brought pursuant to the Probate Code, or a matter that is being adjudicated in a juvenile court or a dependency court. ... (i) This section shall become operative on January 1, 2025." Holding/effect: Summary enforcement of settlements requires a pending action and (ordinarily) retained jurisdiction; it is not a freestanding vehicle for enforcing a settlement agreement years later in a new action. Note also the current version was repealed and re-added by Stats. 2023, Ch. 478, Sec. 13 (AB 1756), operative January 1, 2025 — counsel must apply the version in effect at the relevant time. Application to Our Facts

(Framed throughout as considerations. No outcome is predicted.)

1. Framing the elements

Counsel may consider organizing the specific-performance showing around the statutory scheme rather than a common-law element list, because Civil Code sections 3384, 3386, 3387, 3390, 3391, and 3392 supply the operative rules and each has been verified verbatim above. Counsel should evaluate whether the operative pleading affirmatively alleges each statutory predicate — an enforceable written obligation, inadequacy of the legal remedy, certainty of terms under section 3390(e), adequacy of consideration and substantive fairness as to the defendant co-trustees under section 3391, and plaintiff's own performance or excuse under section 3392. Counsel should evaluate whether plaintiff's ability and willingness to pay the eventual appraised, discounted price is pleaded with the specificity section 3392 contemplates, and whether a tender allegation (or an allegation excusing tender because the price is not yet ascertained) is present. Counsel may consider that section 3386 removes the classical mutuality objection as a freestanding bar, and that Ellis v. Mihelis (if it reads as the search sources describe) supplies the complementary proposition that a plaintiff seeking specific performance of a real-property sale submits himself to the court's jurisdiction.

2. The three instruments and which one supplies the obligation

Counsel should evaluate, instrument by instrument, whether the December 7, 2017 Settlement Agreement and Mutual Release, the Tenants-in-Common Agreement, or the Manuel C. Leal & Son Dairy Partnership Agreement is the source of the buyout right, because the certainty analysis, the arbitration analysis, and the trust-vehicle analysis may each come out differently depending on which document controls. Counsel may consider that a claim resting on the 2017 Settlement Agreement invites reliance on the principle (reflected in Tamarind, subject to counsel reading it) that a settlement agreement may be specifically enforced where damages are inadequate. Counsel should evaluate whether the 2017 Settlement Agreement was made in a then-pending action and, if so, whether the court retained jurisdiction under Code of Civil Procedure section 664.6 — noting the verified text limits that vehicle to pending litigation and expressly carves out actions brought under the Probate Code at subdivision (c), and noting the section was repealed and re-added operative January 1, 2025, so the correct version must be identified. Counsel should evaluate whether the instruments contain their own arbitration, mediation, or dispute-resolution clauses, since none of the instruments were reviewed for this memo and such a clause would materially change the enforcement vehicle.

3. The certainty question and the "discounts as determined by the appraisers" problem — both sides

Counsel may consider that the strongest framing of plaintiff's position is that the instruments do not contain an agreement to agree but a completed agreement with a valuation mechanism, because the price is ascertainable by an objective process — appraisal by identified professionals as of a fixed date — without any further assent from either party. Counsel may consider that Civil Code section 1611 supports this framing directly, since it supplies "so much money as the object of the contract is reasonably worth" where a contract does not determine consideration, does not supply a method, or leaves the amount to the discretion of an interested party — and counsel should evaluate the argument that an independent appraiser is precisely not an interested party, so the clause is better than the situation section 1611 was written to rescue. Counsel may consider that Civil Code section 1613 and Bewick v. Mecham together supply the answer to non-cooperation: where an exclusive valuation method appears possible but becomes impossible in execution, only that provision fails and the court may ascertain the consideration in place of the appraisers. Counsel may consider that Petrolink illustrates the modern application of that principle on facts structurally similar to ours — an option priced at appraised fair market value, irreconcilable competing appraisals, a court-appointed independent appraiser, a judicial value finding, and a specific-performance decree.

Counsel should evaluate the opposing side of this issue honestly, because it is genuinely two-sided. Counsel should evaluate that Civil Code section 3390(e) requires terms "sufficiently certain to make the precise act which is to be done clearly ascertainable," and that a defendant will argue the precise act is not ascertainable where the ultimate price depends on discounts committed to appraiser discretion rather than fixed in the instruments. Counsel should evaluate the argument, drawn from Blackburn v. Charnley as described in search sources, that a contract must be more specific to support specific performance than to support damages — a proposition that, if the opinion bears it out, is the defense's best certainty authority and should be confronted rather than ignored. Counsel should evaluate whether Bustamante v. Intuit is distinguishable on the ground that the Bustamante parties had never settled the identity of the controlling owner, funding, or compensation — i.e., open deal terms requiring further negotiation — whereas the present instruments arguably leave open only an application of an agreed mechanism.

Counsel should evaluate the specific tension created by the 2017 Xavier valuation, in which a 90% contractual buyout discount and a 25% minority interest discount were reportedly applied per our counsel's correspondence. Counsel should evaluate whether the 90% figure is a contractual discount fixed by the instruments (in which case it supports certainty, because it is not discretionary at all) or an appraiser-selected figure (in which case it is the defense's central indefiniteness exhibit). Counsel should evaluate whether the 25% minority-interest discount is the kind of professional judgment ordinarily committed to a qualified appraiser under recognized valuation standards, which may support the argument that the mechanism supplies an ascertainable answer even though it does not supply a number. Counsel should evaluate that the mixed provenance of the two discounts — one apparently contractual, one apparently appraiser-determined — may itself generate an ambiguity argument about which discounts the phrase "as determined by" the appraisers is meant to reach.

Counsel should evaluate the fairness consequence of the discount stack independently of certainty, because Civil Code section 3391 bars specific enforcement against a party who "has not received an adequate consideration" or as to whom the contract "is not ... just and reasonable." Counsel should evaluate that a 90% discount compounded with a 25% minority discount produces a price that is a small fraction of undiscounted value, and should anticipate a section 3391 defense framed as substantive unfairness to the co-trustees and, derivatively, to the trust beneficiaries. Counsel should evaluate that section 3391's inquiry is expressly directed at the position of the resisting party, so evidence about what Hazel J. Leal or the trust received in exchange in 2017 — including any mutual releases — may be central. Counsel may consider that Civil Code section 3389 forecloses one adjacent argument, since the presence of a liquidated-damages or penalty provision would not by itself defeat specific enforcement.

4. The "employ an appraiser" prayer specifically

Counsel should evaluate the risk that the prayer as framed — an order that defendants employ Stanley Xavier of Correia-Xavier and employ Moss Adams — runs into Civil Code section 3390(b), which bars specific enforcement of "[a]n obligation to employ another in personal service." Counsel should evaluate the parallel risk under Civil Code section 3390(d), which bars specific enforcement of "[a]n agreement to procure the act or consent of ... any other third person," because neither Mr. Xavier nor Moss Adams is before the Court and neither can be compelled by this decree to accept the engagement, to be available, or to perform on any timetable. Counsel should evaluate whether either named appraiser has confirmed availability and willingness to perform a date-of-death valuation, and whether either has a conflict, since Mr. Xavier's prior 2017 engagement may be argued either as continuity (favorable) or as prior alignment with one side (unfavorable).

Counsel may consider pleading and briefing an alternative framing that does not depend on compelling an employment relationship: an order declaring the buyout right, directing the parties to cooperate in a valuation, and — if the designated mechanism fails — asking the Court to determine value itself under Civil Code section 1613 and Bewick, or to appoint a neutral appraiser under Evidence Code section 730 as reportedly occurred in Petrolink. Counsel should evaluate that Evidence Code section 730's closing sentence preserves licensure requirements, so any court-appointed valuer of the real property should hold the appropriate California appraisal license. Counsel may consider that framing the relief as a judicial valuation rather than a compelled hiring also blunts the section 3390(b) and (d) objections without giving up the substance of the remedy.

5. Appraisal-as-arbitration — vehicle risk and vehicle opportunity

Counsel should evaluate whether the appraisal provisions in the Settlement Agreement, Tenants-in-Common Agreement, or Partnership Agreement fall within Code of Civil Procedure section 1280(a)'s definition of "Agreement," which by its verified terms "includes, but is not limited to, agreements providing for valuations, appraisals, and similar proceedings." Counsel should evaluate the downside: if the provision is an arbitration agreement, defendants may petition to compel under section 1281.2 and argue the specific-performance cause of action must be stayed or that the valuation dispute belongs before the appraisers, not the Court. Counsel should evaluate the waiver exposure that runs in both directions under section 1281.2(a), including whether plaintiff's filing of a civil complaint seeking specific performance could later be characterized as inconsistent with a right to compel, and whether defendants' litigation conduct could waive theirs.

Counsel may consider the corresponding upside, which is substantial: section 1281.6 provides that "if the agreed method fails or for any reason cannot be followed, or when an arbitrator appointed fails to act and his or her successor has not been appointed, the court, on petition of a party to the arbitration agreement, shall appoint the arbitrator," and prescribes the five-nominee procedure. Counsel should evaluate that this statutory route may be a cleaner and faster answer to a refusal to cooperate or to an appraiser's unavailability than a contested specific-performance trial, and may consider whether a petition to compel plus a section 1281.6 appointment request should be pleaded in the alternative. Counsel should evaluate Kacha's reported scope limitation — that appraisers, unlike arbitrators, may have materially narrower authority and may not resolve legal or coverage-type questions — and should consider whether the contested issues here (which instrument governs, whether a triggering event occurred, what the correct valuation date is, whether the 90% discount is contractual) are legal questions reserved to the Court even if pure valuation goes to appraisers. Counsel should evaluate that no located California case applies appraisal-as-arbitration outside the insurance context, so any brief on this point should rest primarily on the text of section 1280(a) and should candidly acknowledge the insurance provenance of Kacha, Lambert, and Louise Gardens.

6. Trust-specific considerations

Counsel should evaluate whether relief must be directed at both successor co-trustees, because Probate Code section 15620 makes a power vested in two or more trustees exercisable only by unanimous action unless the trust instrument provides otherwise — meaning an order binding only one co-trustee may be ineffective to convey. Counsel should evaluate whether the Hazel J. Leal Revocable Trust dated November 3, 2008 contains a contrary provision permitting majority or several action, since that would change the analysis. Counsel may consider Probate Code section 16013(a), which imposes on each co-trustee an affirmative duty to participate in administration, as support for the proposition that a co-trustee cannot defeat a trust obligation by simply declining to act, and section 16000, which requires administration according to the trust instrument.

Counsel should evaluate whether a Probate Code section 850 petition is a better or additional vehicle than a civil specific-performance complaint. Counsel should evaluate that section 850(a)(2)(A) and (B) are keyed to a decedent who while living was bound by a written contract to convey real property or transfer personal property and who died before conveying — which may map onto Hazel J. Leal's execution of the 2017 Settlement Agreement before her death — and that subdivision (a)(2)(B) expressly conditions relief on the contract being "one which can be specifically enforced," so the specific-performance analysis is imported wholesale. Counsel should evaluate the fit problem: subdivision (a)(2) speaks of the decedent and is available to "the personal representative or any interested person," while subdivision (a)(3), the trustee-facing provision, is drafted around claims by the trustee or creditor-of-settlor claims, and its subdivision (a)(3)(A) reaches property held by the trustee that "is claimed to belong to another" — a phrase counsel should evaluate for whether a contractual buyout right qualifies. Counsel may consider that Probate Code section 856 supplies the operative order — directing "the personal representative or other fiduciary" to execute a conveyance "or granting other appropriate relief" — which is a close statutory analogue to a specific-performance decree against a trustee. Counsel should evaluate Probate Code sections 17200 and 17206 as an alternative or supplemental route, while noting that section 17200(a) by its verified terms confers petition standing on "a trustee or beneficiary," so counsel should evaluate whether plaintiff qualifies as a beneficiary of this trust or must rely on section 850's broader "any interested person" language. Counsel should evaluate whether the matter belongs in, or should be coordinated with, the probate department of the Tulare County Superior Court, and whether any consolidation or related-case notice is appropriate.

7. The real property and the tenancy-in-common interest

Counsel may consider that Civil Code section 3387 supplies a presumption that breach of an agreement to transfer real property cannot be adequately relieved by money, and should evaluate that on these facts the presumption is the rebuttable kind — a presumption affecting the burden of proof — because 652.02 acres of agricultural land is not "a single-family dwelling which the party seeking performance intends to occupy." Counsel should evaluate that the practical effect is burden-shifting rather than conclusive, so defendants may attempt to prove that money would in fact make plaintiff whole. Counsel may consider marshalling the ordinary uniqueness proof anyway — the specific acreage, water rights, soil and irrigation characteristics, the dairy operation's dependence on the parcels, and the absence of a substitute — rather than resting on the presumption alone. Counsel should evaluate that no California authority applying section 3387 to an undivided tenancy-in-common interest was located in this session, and should therefore anticipate an argument that a fractional undivided interest is a financial rather than a possessory asset and is more readily monetized than a fee. Counsel may consider that Real Estate Analytics, LLC v. Vallas (if it reads as search sources describe) supports the proposition that refusing specific performance for a breached land sale can be an abuse of discretion, while also noting the search-reported wrinkle that Code of Civil Procedure section 405.33 makes section 3387's presumption inapplicable in a discrete lis pendens undertaking context — a limitation counsel should confirm before relying on the case.

8. The partnership interest

Counsel should evaluate that no published California authority holding a partnership or LLC interest to be "unique" for specific-performance purposes was located, and should not assert such a rule to the Court without independent verification. Counsel may consider building the inadequacy showing for the partnership interest on facts rather than a presumption — that the Manuel C. Leal & Son Dairy Partnership is a closely held family enterprise with no market for its interests, that the interest carries governance and control rights that money cannot replicate, and that the interest is functionally intertwined with the 652.02 acres. Counsel may consider Corporations Code section 16701 as a structural analogy rather than as direct authority: subdivision (i) expressly directs that "[t]he court shall determine the buyout price" of a dissociated partner's interest and authorizes the court to shift "the fees and expenses of appraisers or other experts" against a party who "acted arbitrarily, vexatiously, or not in good faith." Counsel should evaluate that this analogy answers a competence objection (courts do value partnership interests) but does not by itself supply the buyout right here, since section 16701 is a dissociation default that a partnership agreement may displace and this claim rests on the parties' own instruments. Counsel should evaluate whether any dissociation or dissolution event has occurred that would make section 16701 directly applicable in the alternative, and should evaluate the good-faith fee-shifting provision as potential leverage if defendants' non-cooperation is established.

Counsel should evaluate — because it is the most dangerous unaddressed issue surfaced by this research — whether the buyout was triggered at all, given that the unpublished Estate of Silveira decision reportedly held that the death of an original partner did not trigger a buy-sell where the partnership interest had already been transferred to a trust. Counsel should evaluate whether the Manuel C. Leal & Son Dairy partnership interest was transferred into the Hazel J. Leal Revocable Trust before Hazel Leal's death, and whether the governing buy-sell language keys to the death of a partner, of a person, or to a transfer event. Counsel should evaluate that Estate of Silveira is unpublished and cannot be cited by either side under California Rules of Court, rule 8.1115, but that the underlying interpretive question is one opposing counsel may raise on its own reasoning.

9. Defenses

Counsel should evaluate uncertainty under Civil Code section 3390(e) as the defense most likely to be pressed, and should prepare the section 1611 / section 1613 / Bewick answer in the moving papers rather than in reply. Counsel should evaluate impossibility in its precise statutory form: Civil Code section 1612 provides that where an exclusive valuation method is impossible on its face, the entire contract is void, while section 1613 saves the contract where the method was possible on its face but becomes impossible in fact. Counsel should evaluate which side of that line a clause naming two specific appraisers falls on if one or both are now unavailable, since naming particular individuals invites an argument that the method was always dependent on third-party willingness — and counsel should evaluate that the answer likely turns on whether the clause is read as requiring these appraisers exclusively or as designating them subject to substitution. Counsel should evaluate lack of mutuality as largely foreclosed by Civil Code section 3386 and by Ellis v. Mihelis, but should evaluate whether section 3386(b) is satisfied — i.e., whether plaintiff's counterperformance (payment of the discounted price) is "substantially performed or its concurrent or future performance is assured or ... can be secured to the satisfaction of the court" — and may consider offering to deposit funds or post security to remove the issue. Counsel should evaluate unclean hands and laches as fact-driven equitable defenses, and should specifically evaluate the elapsed time between the December 7, 2017 Settlement Agreement, Hazel Leal's death, and the filing of this action, together with any prejudice defendants may claim from valuation drift, changed agricultural conditions, or the death or unavailability of witnesses. Counsel should evaluate that a date-of-death valuation date partially neutralizes a laches-prejudice argument as to price, while potentially sharpening it as to evidence availability. Counsel should evaluate Civil Code section 3392 as an affirmative hurdle rather than a defense — plaintiff must have "fully and fairly performed all the conditions precedent" — and should identify every condition precedent in each instrument. Counsel should evaluate Civil Code section 3391(3) and (4) exposure if defendants contend Hazel Leal's 2017 assent was procured by misrepresentation or given under mistake, particularly given the 90% discount figure.

10. Enforcement of any decree

Counsel may consider that even a favorable decree requires an execution mechanism against a fiduciary who declines to sign, and should evaluate the elisor practice reflected in Blueberry Properties, LLC v. Chow, in which the court appointed the clerk of the court to sign escrow documents for a refusing seller. Counsel should evaluate the statutory basis for elisor appointment independently, because the search sources conflicted on the citation and it was not verified here. Counsel may consider that Civil Code section 3395 may matter if any interest in the subject property has been transferred since the obligation arose, since it extends enforceability to persons claiming under the obligor by a subsequently created title, excepting good-faith purchasers and encumbrancers for value.

Open Questions

  1. Which instrument controls? None of the three instruments was reviewed for this memo. The buyout trigger, the appraisal mechanism, the discount language, the identity of "as determined by" discounts, and any dispute-resolution clause all need to be read against the analysis above.
  2. Is the 90% discount contractual or appraiser-determined? This single fact materially changes the certainty analysis in section 3 of the Application and should be resolved from the instruments, not from correspondence.
  3. Do the instruments contain an arbitration or ADR clause independent of the appraisal provision? If so, the vehicle question is not merely whether appraisal is arbitration.
  4. Was the partnership interest transferred into the Trust before Hazel Leal's death, and does the buy-sell key to the death of a "partner"? See the Estate of Silveira flag; this may be a threshold trigger issue rather than a remedy issue.
  5. Are Stanley Xavier and Moss Adams available, willing, conflict-free, and appropriately licensed? Sections 3390(b) and (d) make this a live enforceability question, not merely a logistics question.
  6. Is plaintiff a beneficiary of the Hazel J. Leal Revocable Trust? This determines standing under Probate Code section 17200(a) and may affect which Probate Code vehicle is available.
  7. Was the 2017 Settlement Agreement entered in a then-pending action with retained jurisdiction? Determines whether Code of Civil Procedure section 664.6 is available at all, and which version applies.
  8. What is the correct valuation date, and is it disputed? The prayer specifies Hazel Leal's date of death; whether the instruments so provide was not verified.
  9. Statute of limitations. Not researched. The limitations period for an action on a written contract and for specific performance, and any Probate Code limitations or claim-presentation requirements, were not examined and must be analyzed independently.
  10. Is there published California authority treating a non-insurance valuation clause as arbitration, or holding a partnership interest unique? Both gaps should be closed on Westlaw or CoCounsel before briefing.
  11. Standard of review and burden allocation for the section 3387 rebuttable presumption as applied to an undivided interest — not researched.
  12. Beneficiary notice and consent. Whether other trust beneficiaries must be joined or noticed to any order compelling a sale of trust assets at a discounted price was not researched.

Confidence and Gaps

What is solid. The statutory framework is the strongest part of this memo. Verbatim text was actually retrieved and read for Civil Code sections 3384, 3386, 3387, 3388, 3389, 3390, 3391, 3392, 3395, 1611, 1612, and 1613; Code of Civil Procedure sections 1280, 1281, 1281.2, 1281.6, and 664.6; Probate Code sections 850, 856, 15620, 16000, 16013, 17200, and 17206; Corporations Code section 16701; and Evidence Code section 730. Each was pulled from the California Legislative Counsel Bureau's own PUBINFO LAW_SECTION_TBL export, with the Legislative Counsel history note carried through. The two provisions doing the most analytical work — Code of Civil Procedure section 1280(a)'s inclusion of "valuations, appraisals, and similar proceedings," and Civil Code section 1613's rule that a failed exclusive valuation method voids only that provision — were read directly and are quoted exactly.

What is not solid. No case text was read. Every case in this memo is tagged SEARCH-VERIFIED ONLY, meaning the case name, year, and reporter citation were corroborated across multiple search sources and the described holding comes from search-result content — not from the opinion. No pin cite in this memo is confirmed; none is given. Several specific uncertainties should be carried forward: the Bewick citation must be checked against a 1944 Court of Appeal decision bearing the same case name; the Petrolink line spans at least three appellate decisions and counsel must confirm which one supports which proposition (and the reported value figure differs by $9 between sources); Tamarind's disposition on appeal was not confirmed; Louise Gardens' reported disaster-related qualification was not confirmed; and the statutory basis for the Blueberry Properties elisor appointment was reported inconsistently and was not verified.

Authorities expressly not usable. King v. Stanley, Stephenson v. Drever, Kajima/Ray Wilson, the Law Revision Commission report, Figi, and Klubnikin are listed above as UNVERIFIED and must not be cited on the strength of this memo. Estate of Silveira is unpublished and not citable under rule 8.1115.

Research gaps that matter. No published California authority was located holding a partnership or LLC interest "unique" for specific-performance purposes; no published California authority was located applying appraisal-as-arbitration outside the first-party insurance context; and no authority was located applying Civil Code section 3387 to an undivided tenancy-in-common interest. Statute of limitations, Probate Code claim procedures, beneficiary joinder, and the standard of review on the section 3387 presumption were not researched at all.

Tooling limitation. A CourtListener MCP server was not available for this research. Public web sources were used instead, and in this session the network egress policy blocked every dedicated legal-research host — leginfo, CourtListener, Justia, Casetext, Google Scholar, FindLaw, Leagle, Casemine, onecle, california.public.law, scocal.stanford.edu, courts.ca.gov, and case.law. Statutes were recovered only because the Legislative Counsel's own database export was reachable through a public code-hosting mirror; case law could be reached only through search. Counsel should assume this memo has the reliability of a well-sourced starting outline, not of a verified brief.

Required next step before any filing. Every authority in this memo — statutes included — must be independently pulled, read in full, cite-checked, and validated (KeyCite/Shepard's) on Westlaw, Lexis, or CoCounsel before it is cited to the Tulare County Superior Court. The statutory text should additionally be confirmed against leginfo.legislature.ca.gov for currency, since the mirror used here reflects an export dated July 9, 2026 and its completeness could not be independently confirmed.

ADDENDUM (8/18/2026) — THE CONTRACT'S OWN PRICE-FIXING MACHINERY IS NOW VERIFIED (executed TIC §11; 1983 Agreement Art. XIX)

The valuations/instruments sweep read the EXECUTED TIC and the 1983 Partnership Agreement in full (../01-verified-facts/drive-sweep/valuations-instruments-sweep.md §§10-11). Both contain appraiser mechanisms that answer this memo's Bewick/Evid. Code § 730 concern (court cannot write the price; someone must fix it):

  • TIC §11 (verbatim in the sweep): FMV "shall be that value determined in good faith by a qualified, professional appraiser… jointly appointed by all the parties, and his or her decision shall be in writing and binding and conclusive"; failing joint appointment within 30 days, each side appoints one within 15 days, and if the two cannot agree in 30 days they appoint a third — "the decision in writing of any two of the three appraisers… binding and conclusive." Costs of joint appraisers split; unilateral appraisers at appointing party's cost.
  • 1983 Agreement Art. XIX: same 2-of-3 binding structure, with the 90%-of-FMV rule for the both-parents-deceased purchase and detailed net-price mechanics (capital-account credit added; note offsets; drawing-account debits deducted).

Why this matters to specific performance: the decree need not fix a price (Bewick problem) — it can compel PERFORMANCE OF THE CONTRACTUAL APPRAISAL MECHANISM, which is ministerial and complete on its face. § 730 remains the fallback if the mechanism deadlocks. Factual predicate worth building (counsel to weigh): if the Ex. E/G email record (Esraelian proposed Stanley Xavier; our side agreed; engagement followed) makes Correia-Xavier the "jointly appointed" appraiser under §11, then CX's written conclusion ($14,220,000, no discounts identified) is contractually binding and conclusive — and the later unilateral JHA engagement ($18,100,000) is priced by §11 at the appointing party's cost and without binding effect. The counter-facts (CX's client line names Esraelian alone; CX's intended use is estate-tax; the MA review calls CX "hired by the potential buyer") are laid out in the sweep — this is an argument to build or discard with the engagement letters in hand (OI-54), not to assume. UNVERIFIED as to law: enforceability of appraisal clauses under CCP § 1281 et seq. / case law on binding appraisals — Westlaw before use.
