R3: Trustee Duty to Account, Omitted Assets, and Surcharge

ATTORNEY WORK-PRODUCT — PREPARED FOR COUNSEL — NOT LEGAL ADVICE

Matter: Manuel Stephen Leal v. Ashley Garabedian and Hazel Susan Leal, successor co-trustees of the Hazel J. Leal Revocable Trust dated November 3, 2008 (Tulare County Superior Court) Prepared: August 18, 2026 Related instruments: Manuel C. Leal Living Trust; Manuel C. Leal Bypass Trust uta dtd 2.14.05 as amended; Settlement Agreement and Mutual Release dated December 7, 2017 Related entity: Manuel C. Leal & Son Dairy Partnership

RESEARCH METHOD AND A MATERIAL LIMITATION — READ FIRST

A CourtListener MCP server was NOT available for this memo. Research was conducted using public web sources only.

More seriously: in this session, direct retrieval (WebFetch) of every primary legal source was blocked at the network egress gateway (HTTP 403 to CONNECT). The following domains were each attempted and each refused: leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, law.justia.com, codes.findlaw.com, caselaw.findlaw.com, casetext.com, scholar.google.com, california.public.law, casemine.com, case.law / static.case.law / cite.case.law, law.resource.org, leagle.com, openjurist.org, anylaw.com, courts.ca.gov, clrc.ca.gov, and courtlistener.com.

Consequently no authority in this memo was retrieved by opening the source document. Every quotation below was returned through a web search tool, which surfaces text extracted from those same sources but which I could not independently open and read end-to-end.

Tagging convention used throughout:

Tag Meaning
VERIFIED-BY-SEARCH Text below was returned as apparently verbatim statutory or judicial language by the search tool, from an identified primary-source URL. Direct fetch was blocked. Treat as reliable-but-unconfirmed.
PARAPHRASE-ONLY Only a summary/paraphrase was returned. The substance is likely right; the wording is not quotable.
UNVERIFIED — counsel must confirm Could not retrieve adequate text. Do not rely on it.

No pin cites are asserted anywhere in this memo except where expressly noted, and the one noted exception is itself flagged as secondary-sourced. Where a pin cite would normally appear, this memo says "pin cite not confirmed." That is deliberate, not an oversight.

Counsel must independently verify every citation in this memo on Westlaw, Lexis, or CoCounsel before any of it is filed, served, or relied upon. This memo is a research map, not a citation-ready product.

Issue

  1. What does Probate Code § 16060 et seq. require of a trustee by way of keeping beneficiaries informed and rendering accounts (§§ 16060, 16061, 16062, 16063, 16064)?
  2. Who is entitled to an account, and what must a compliant account contain?
  3. What does Probate Code § 17200 permit — who has standing to petition to compel an account, and what relief may the probate court grant?
  4. What limitations periods and equitable time bars apply to accounting and breach-of-trust claims (§§ 16460, 16461; laches)?
  5. What remedies exist for omitted estate assets — property that should have been, but was not, inventoried into or included in a trust estate (§ 850 et seq.; § 859 double damages)?
  6. What are the standards for surcharging a trustee (§§ 16400, 16401, 16402, 16403, 16420, 16440, 16441)? What must be proven, who bears the burden, is bad faith required, and how are damages measured?
  7. Does a trustee's failure to account shift any burden to the trustee, and is there authority construing gaps and ambiguities in trust records against the fiduciary who had the duty to keep them?
  8. What is a trustee's duty to account for a partnership interest held by the trust, and how do partnership-level books interact with trust-level accounting?

Cross-cutting: Because our client is both the plaintiff-beneficiary and the managing partner who kept the partnership books — and possibly a fiduciary of one or more of the related trusts — this memo analyzes the accounting-duty authority in both directions, including squarely against our own side.

Short Answer

  1. The duty is layered, and only the outer layer is waivable. § 16060 imposes a general, affirmative duty to keep beneficiaries reasonably informed. § 16061 adds a duty to furnish information on reasonable request. § 16062(a) requires an account at least annually, at termination, and on a change of trustee. § 16063 dictates minimum contents. § 16064 lists the exceptions — trust-instrument waiver, beneficiary waiver, and the revocable-trust period under § 15800 — but even a waiver yields where the court finds it "reasonably likely that a material breach of the trust has occurred."

  2. Entitlement runs to current income/principal beneficiaries under § 16062(a); remainder beneficiaries get information and can compel through § 17200. A compliant account must contain the five categories in § 16063(a), including a notice advising the recipient of the right to seek court review and — critically for limitations purposes — a notice of the three-year bar. A court-filed account additionally must satisfy §§ 1060–1064.

  3. § 17200 is the vehicle, and the court's remedial power under § 17206 is broad. § 17200(b)(5) reaches settling accounts and passing on trustee acts; § 17200(b)(7) reaches compelling information and accounts, subject to a 60-day-after-written-request predicate (and, for accounts, a no-account-within-six-months predicate).

  4. Three years is the governing period under § 16460, but the trigger differs. If a written account or report adequately disclosed the claim, three years runs from receipt. If it did not, or none was ever received, three years runs from actual or constructive discovery. Exculpatory clauses under § 16461 cannot reach intentional, grossly negligent, bad-faith, or recklessly indifferent breaches, or profits derived from a breach.

  5. Omitted assets are addressed by a § 850 petition, with § 856 relief and § 859 double damages. § 850(a)(3) expressly covers both directions — trustee holding property claimed by another, and trustee claiming property held by another. Heggstad supplies the substantive route for property never formally re-titled. § 859 requires bad faith; Levin v. Winston-Levin holds that even a finding of undue influence does not by itself supply it.

  6. Surcharge requires a breach plus causation plus loss — not bad faith. § 16400 makes any duty violation a breach; § 16440(a) supplies three alternative measures (loss with interest, trustee's profit with interest, lost profit); § 16441 fixes interest at the greater of the legal judgment rate or interest actually received. Bad faith is not an element — but its absence is what unlocks the § 16440(b) and § 16441(b) equitable excuse, and its presence is what defeats § 16461 exculpation and unlocks § 859. Uzyel v. Kadisha confirms lost-profit/appreciation damages and disgorgement without tracing.

  7. Yes — this is the strongest doctrinal lever in the memo, and it cuts both ways. Purdy v. Johnson and Estate of McCabe place the burden on the accounting fiduciary to prove every item by satisfactory evidence, and resolve every doubt arising from the fiduciary's own failure to keep proper records against the fiduciary. This is a rule about whoever kept the books.

  8. A partnership interest does not shrink the trust-level duty; it is simply one asset that must be reported. Corporations Code § 16403 gives partners and former partners a right of access to partnership books, which means a trustee holding a partnership interest generally cannot plead inability to obtain the underlying records. Probate Code § 1061 treats a trade or business as a net-reported item with a supporting schedule. No California case squarely addressing trust-level accounting for a partnership interest was located.

Bidirectional caution: The § 16060-series and Purdy/McCabe record-keeping authority is not plaintiff-friendly by nature. It is book-keeper-hostile. Our client kept the partnership books. To the extent he also served in a fiduciary capacity as to the Bypass Trust or the partnership interest, the same authority we would deploy is available in mirror image.

Authority

A. The duty to inform and to account

History returned as: Enacted by Stats. 1990, Ch. 79. Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prob/division-9/part-4/chapter-1/article-3/section-16060/ (fetch blocked; text via search)

Cal. Prob. Code § 16061 — VERIFIED-BY-SEARCH Text returned: "Except as provided in Section 16069, on reasonable request by a beneficiary, the trustee shall report to the beneficiary by providing requested information to the beneficiary relating to the administration of the trust relevant to the beneficiary's interest." History returned as: Amended by Stats. 2010, Ch. 621, Sec. 3, eff. Jan. 1, 2011. Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/2011/prob/division-9/16060-16069/16061

Note the § 16069 carve-out. Search results indicate § 16069 excuses the § 16061 information duty in certain circumstances (revocable trusts; beneficiary and trustee the same person). The full text of § 16069 was NOT retrieved — UNVERIFIED — counsel must confirm. This matters here: the Hazel J. Leal Revocable Trust was revocable for part of the relevant period.

Cal. Prob. Code § 16062 — VERIFIED-BY-SEARCH (all five subdivisions returned)

  • (a) "Except as otherwise provided in this section and in Section 16064, the trustee shall account at least annually, at the termination of the trust, and upon a change of trustee, to each beneficiary to whom income or principal is required or authorized in the trustee's discretion to be currently distributed."
  • (b) Trustee of a living trust created by an instrument executed before July 1, 1987 is not subject to the (a) duty.
  • (c) Trustee of a trust created by a will executed before July 1, 1987 is not subject to the (a) duty, except on removal from continuing court jurisdiction under Art. 2 (§ 17350 et seq.).
  • (d) Continuation of the former § 1120.1a duty for pre-July 1, 1977 testamentary trusts removed from court jurisdiction.
  • (e) "Any limitation or waiver in a trust instrument of the obligation to account is against public policy and shall be void as to any sole trustee who is either of the following: (1) A disqualified person as defined in former Section 21350.5 … (2) Described in subdivision (a) of Section 21380, but not described in Section 21382."

Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prob/division-9/part-4/chapter-1/article-3/section-16062/

The 1987 dates in (b) are not a problem here. Both trusts at issue post-date 1987 (2008 and 2005). Note also that § 16062(e) applies only to a sole trustee — the Hazel Trust has co-trustees, so the (e) public-policy override likely does not apply to them by its terms. Counsel should confirm.

Cal. Prob. Code § 16063 — VERIFIED-BY-SEARCH as to (a)(1)–(a)(5); (a)(6) and (b) VERIFIED-BY-SEARCH but with a caution noted below

  • (a)(1) A statement of receipts and disbursements of principal and income during the last complete fiscal year or since the last account.
  • (a)(2) A statement of the assets and liabilities of the trust as of the end of the last complete fiscal year or the end of the period covered.
  • (a)(3) The trustee's compensation for that period.
  • (a)(4) The agents hired by the trustee, their relationship to the trustee (if any), and their compensation, for that period.
  • (a)(5) A statement that the recipient may petition the court pursuant to Section 17200 to obtain court review of the account and of the acts of the trustee.
  • (a)(6) A statement that claims against the trustee for breach of trust may not be made after the expiration of three years from the date the beneficiary receives an account or report disclosing facts giving rise to the claim.
  • (b) All accounts filed to be approved by a court shall be presented in the manner provided in Chapter 4 (commencing with § 1060) of Part 1 of Division 3.

Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prob/division-9/part-4/chapter-1/article-3/section-16063/

Caution on (a)(6)/(b): the search response for these two items mixed in commentary from a 1995 California Law Revision Commission staff memorandum referring to a then-draft "subdivision (f)." The substance of (a)(6) and (b) as stated above appears correct and is consistent across sources, but the exact subdivision lettering should be confirmed against the current code before any pleading cites it. Pin cite not confirmed.

Cal. Prob. Code § 16064 — VERIFIED-BY-SEARCH (subdivision lettering partially garbled in retrieval — see caution) Substance returned: "The trustee is not required to account to a beneficiary as described in subdivision (a) of Section 16062, in any of the following circumstances:"

  • (a) "To the extent the trust instrument waives the account, except that no waiver described in subdivision (e) of Section 16062 shall be valid or enforceable. Regardless of a waiver of accounting in the trust instrument, upon a showing that it is reasonably likely that a material breach of the trust has occurred, the court may compel the trustee to account."
  • (b) As to a beneficiary who has waived in writing the right to an account. A waiver may be withdrawn in writing at any time as to accounts for transactions occurring after the date of the written withdrawal.
  • (c) In the case of a beneficiary of a revocable trust, as provided in Section 15800, for the period when the trust may be revoked.

Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prob/division-9/part-4/chapter-1/article-3/section-16064/

This is the single most useful sentence in Article 3 for a petitioner: even where accounting is waived, "upon a showing that it is reasonably likely that a material breach of the trust has occurred, the court may compel the trustee to account." Note the standard is "reasonably likely," not proof of breach. Pin cite/subdivision lettering not confirmed — the retrieval returned (b) and (c) without their letters.

Cal. Prob. Code § 15800 — VERIFIED-BY-SEARCH Text returned: "During the time that a trust is revocable and at least one person holding the power to revoke the trust is competent, the person holding the power to revoke, and not the beneficiary, has the rights afforded beneficiaries under this division, and the duties of the trustee are owed to the person holding the power to revoke." Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prob/division-9/part-3/chapter-2/section-15800/

§ 15800 was materially amended effective 2022 to expand revocable-trust beneficiary rights where the holder of the power to revoke is incompetent. The amended text was NOT retrieved — UNVERIFIED — counsel must confirm the version in force during each relevant period. For pre-2022 conduct the pre-amendment version governs.

Cal. Prob. Code §§ 16061.7, 16061.8 — PARAPHRASE-ONLY § 16061.7: notification by trustee required within 60 days of the triggering event (or of the trustee learning of a person entitled to notice). Triggering events include a revocable trust becoming irrevocable by reason of a settlor's death, and a change of trustee of an irrevocable trust. § 16061.8: where a revocable trust becomes irrevocable by reason of a settlor's death, the notice must warn that no action to contest the trust may be brought more than 120 days from service of the notification, or 60 days from delivery of a copy of the trust terms within that 120-day window, whichever is later. Sources: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prob/division-9/part-4/chapter-1/article-3/section-16061.7/; https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/probate-code/prob-sect-16061-7/

Do not conflate the § 16061.8 period with the accounting/breach limitations period. § 16061.8 bars trust contests. Breach-of-trust and accounting claims are governed by § 16460's three-year scheme. Counsel should keep these separate in any demurrer/anti-SLAPP or limitations briefing.

Cal. Prob. Code §§ 1060–1064 (court-filed accounts) — PARAPHRASE-ONLY An account filed with the court must state the period covered and contain a Summary of Account supported by detailed schedules, with CHARGES (property on hand at beginning; additional property received; receipts; gains on sale; net income from trade or business) and CREDITS (disbursements; losses on sale; net loss from trade or business; distributions; property on hand at close), such that total charges equal total credits. A schedule showing estimated current market value of assets on hand at period end is required in all cases. Sources: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prob/division-3/part-1/chapter-4/; https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/california/codes/california_probate_code_1061

The "net income from trade or business" line is the doctrinal hinge for Issue 8. See § G below. Full verbatim text of §§ 1061–1062 NOT retrieved — counsel must confirm the exact schedule requirements.

B. Who is entitled to an account; standing to compel

Cal. Prob. Code § 17200 — VERIFIED-BY-SEARCH as to (a), (b)(5), (b)(7)(B); PARAPHRASE-ONLY as to the balance

  • (a) "Except as provided in Section 15800, a trustee or beneficiary of a trust may petition the court under this chapter concerning the internal affairs of the trust or to determine the existence of the trust."
  • (b) "Proceedings concerning the internal affairs of a trust include, but are not limited to, proceedings for any of the following purposes …"
  • (b)(5) "Settling the accounts and passing upon the acts of the trustee, including the exercise of discretionary powers."
  • (b)(7)(B) Compelling the trustee to "[p]rovide information about the trust under Section 16061 if the trustee has failed to provide the requested information within 60 days after the beneficiary's reasonable written request …"
  • (b)(7) [account subpart] Compelling the trustee to account, "if (A) the trustee has failed to submit a requested report or account within 60 days after written request of the beneficiary and (B) no report or account has been made within six months preceding the request."

Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prob/division-9/part-5/chapter-3/section-17200/

The 60-day / 6-month predicate is a real gating requirement. Counsel should confirm a written request was made and that 60 days elapsed before any petition to compel an account is filed. The precise subparagraph lettering within § 17200(b)(7) was returned inconsistently across searches — pin cite not confirmed.

Cal. Prob. Code § 17206 — VERIFIED-BY-SEARCH Text returned: "The court in its discretion may make any orders and take any other action necessary or proper to dispose of the matters presented by the petition, including appointment of a temporary trustee to administer the trust in whole or in part." Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prob/division-9/part-5/chapter-3/section-17206/

Esslinger v. Cummins (2006) 144 Cal.App.4th 517 — PARAPHRASE-ONLY Reported holding: a remainder beneficiary has standing under Prob. Code § 17200(b)(7) to petition to compel a trustee to account; § 16061 gives a remainder beneficiary the right to request information and to petition under § 17200(b)(7) if the trustee unreasonably fails to comply. Sources: https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/ca-court-of-appeal/1219015.html; https://case-law.vlex.com/vid/esslinger-v-cummins-no-885558637 Pin cite not confirmed. Caution: do not confuse with Smith v. Esslinger (1994) 26 Cal.App.4th 579, a different case surfaced in the same search.

Estate of Giraldin (2012) 55 Cal.4th 1058 — PARAPHRASE-ONLY Reported holding: where the trustee of a revocable trust is someone other than the settlor, the trustee owes fiduciary duties to the settlor, not the beneficiaries, while the settlor lives, and accounts to the settlor only. After the settlor dies, the beneficiaries have standing to sue the trustee for breach of the duty owed to the settlor, to the extent that breach harmed the beneficiaries. Sources: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2012/s197694.html; https://scocal.stanford.edu/opinion/estate-giraldin-34171 Pin cite not confirmed.

Giraldin is likely the most important standing case in this memo. It is the bridge that lets a post-death beneficiary reach lifetime conduct in a revocable trust. It is also the case that will be cited against our side if our client acted as a fiduciary during Hazel's lifetime.

Salter v. Lerner (2009) 176 Cal.App.4th 1184 — PARAPHRASE-ONLY Reported: dispute over administration of the Glenn and Elsa Lerner Trust; the narrow appellate issue was whether a proposed petition sought more than enforcement of the trustee's nonwaivable duty under § 16060 to provide reasonable information about trust administration, such that it would violate the trust's no-contest clause; the court held it did not. Secondary sources report the court explained that § 16060 creates an affirmative duty to keep beneficiaries reasonably informed that is separate from the more specific duties under §§ 16061 and 16062. Sources: https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/ca-court-of-appeal/1422359.html; https://www.leagle.com/decision/incaco20090728002 Pin cite not confirmed. The characterization of § 16060 as "nonwaivable" is drawn from secondary reporting and should be treated with care — § 16064 expressly permits waiver of the § 16062 account, which is a different duty. Counsel should read the opinion before asserting nonwaivability.

Barefoot v. Jennings (2020) 8 Cal.5th 822 — PARAPHRASE-ONLY Reported: addressed standing under § 17200(a); the court observed that because the settlor had died, § 15800 was no longer relevant. Source: https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/ca-supreme-court/2043430.html Pin cite not confirmed. Full holding NOT retrieved. Cited here only for the § 15800/§ 17200 interaction, not for its principal holding on trust-contest standing.

C. Limitations, exculpation, consent, and release

Cal. Prob. Code § 16460 — VERIFIED-BY-SEARCH

  • If a beneficiary has received an interim or final account in writing, or other written report, that adequately discloses the existence of a claim against the trustee for breach of trust, the claim is barred as to that beneficiary unless a proceeding to assert it is commenced within three years after receipt of the account or report.
  • "An account or report adequately discloses existence of a claim if it provides sufficient information so that the beneficiary knows of the claim or reasonably should have inquired into the existence of the claim."
  • If the account or report does not adequately disclose the claim, or if the beneficiary received no written account or report at all, the claim is barred unless a proceeding is commenced within three years after the beneficiary discovered, or reasonably should have discovered, the subject of the claim.

Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prob/division-9/part-4/chapter-4/article-4/section-16460/ Subdivision lettering not confirmed — the retrieval returned the substance without reliable (a)/(b) designations.

Cal. Prob. Code § 16461 — VERIFIED-BY-SEARCH as to (b); PARAPHRASE-ONLY as to (a), (c), (d)

  • (a) Except as provided in (b), (c), or (d), the trustee can be relieved of liability for breach of trust by provisions in the trust instrument.
  • (b) A trust provision is not effective to relieve the trustee of liability for a breach committed intentionally, with gross negligence, in bad faith, or with reckless indifference to the interest of the beneficiary, or for any profit that the trustee derives from a breach of trust.
  • (c) Subject to (b), a provision releasing the trustee if a beneficiary fails to object to an item in an interim or final account or other written report within a specified time is effective only if stated conditions are met, including that the objection period is not less than 180 days, or the trustee elects the (d) procedure.

Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prob/division-9/part-4/chapter-4/article-4/section-16461/ Subdivision (d) NOT retrieved — UNVERIFIED — counsel must confirm.

Cal. Prob. Code § 16463 (consent) — PARAPHRASE-ONLY A beneficiary may not hold the trustee liable for an act or omission as a breach of trust if the beneficiary consented before or at the time of the act or omission. Consent does not preclude liability where: the beneficiary was under an incapacity; the beneficiary did not know of the beneficiary's rights and of material facts the trustee knew or should have known; the consent was induced by improper conduct of the trustee; or, where the trustee had an interest in the transaction adverse to the beneficiary, the transaction was not fair and reasonable to the beneficiary. Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prob/division-9/part-4/chapter-4/article-4/ (fetch blocked)

Cal. Prob. Code § 16464 (release) — PARAPHRASE-ONLY A beneficiary may be precluded from holding the trustee liable by the beneficiary's release or contract effective to discharge the trustee's liability for that breach. A release or contract is not effective where the beneficiary was under an incapacity; did not know of the beneficiary's rights and material facts the trustee knew or should have known; the release was induced by improper conduct of the trustee; or the transaction involved a bargain that was not fair and reasonable. Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prob/division-9/part-4/chapter-4/article-4/section-16464/

§ 16464 is directly implicated by the December 7, 2017 Settlement Agreement and Mutual Release. See Application, § 5 below. Exact statutory text NOT retrieved — counsel must confirm before briefing scope-of-release.

Cal. Prob. Code § 16465 — UNVERIFIED — counsel must confirm. Appears within the same Article 4 (Limitations and Exculpation) but no text was retrieved.

Laches as applied to trust accounting claims — UNVERIFIED — counsel must confirm. No California case applying laches specifically to a petition to compel a trust account was retrieved. Searches for Estate of Bonaccorsi and for laches in the probate-accounting context returned only general statements of the doctrine (inexcusable delay in the exercise of a known right, plus resulting prejudice) from secondary sources. This memo does not cite any laches authority. Counsel should research this independently — it is a foreseeable defense given the 2015 and 2017 dates, and its absence from this memo is a gap, not a conclusion that the defense is unavailable.

D. Omitted estate assets — §§ 850 et seq., 856, 859

Cal. Prob. Code § 850 — VERIFIED-BY-SEARCH as to the § 850(a)(3) trust subparts The section identifies categories of persons who may petition for an order under Part 19. As to trusts, § 850(a)(3) reaches:

  • (A) "Where the trustee is in possession of, or holds title to, real or personal property, and the property, or some interest, is claimed to belong to another."
  • (B) "Where the trustee has a claim to real or personal property, title to or possession of which is held by another."
  • (C) Where the property of the trust is claimed to be subject to a creditor of the settlor of the trust.

The petition "shall set forth facts upon which the claim is based." Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prob/division-2/part-19/section-850/ Subparagraph lettering within (a)(3) is as returned by search; pin cite not confirmed.

§ 850(a)(3)(B) is the omitted-asset provision. It is expressly bidirectional — a trustee may use it offensively to pull property in, and a claimant may use it to pull property out. Note that § 850 requires "the trustee" as the petitioner for (a)(3) in the text returned; whether a beneficiary may petition under (a)(3) or must proceed under a different subdivision was not resolved by the retrieval — UNVERIFIED — counsel must confirm. This is a live standing question for our client, who is a beneficiary, not (as to the Hazel Trust) the trustee.

Cal. Prob. Code § 856 — VERIFIED-BY-SEARCH Text returned: "Except as provided in Sections 853 and 854, if the court is satisfied that a conveyance, transfer, or other order should be made, the court shall make an order authorizing and directing the personal representative or other fiduciary, or the person having title to or possession of the property, to execute a conveyance or transfer to the person entitled thereto, or granting other appropriate relief." History returned as: Added by Stats. 2001, Ch. 49, Sec. 1, eff. Jan. 1, 2002. Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prob/division-2/part-19/section-856/

Note "or granting other appropriate relief" — the remedial hook is broader than a bare conveyance order.

Cal. Prob. Code §§ 851, 853, 854 — UNVERIFIED — counsel must confirm. § 851 (notice and hearing) and the §§ 853/854 carve-outs referenced in § 856 were not retrieved.

Cal. Prob. Code § 859 — VERIFIED-BY-SEARCH Text returned: "If a court finds that a person has in bad faith wrongfully taken, concealed, or disposed of property belonging to a conservatee, a minor, an elder, a dependent adult, a trust, or the estate of a decedent, or has taken, concealed, or disposed of the property by the use of undue influence in bad faith or through the commission of elder or dependent adult financial abuse, as defined in Section 15610.30 of the Welfare and Institutions Code, the person shall be liable for twice the value of the property recovered by an action under this part. In addition, except as otherwise required by law, including Section 15657.5 of the Welfare and Institutions Code, the person may, in the court's discretion, be liable for reasonable attorney's fees and costs." Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prob/division-2/part-19/section-859/

Estate of Heggstad (1993) 16 Cal.App.4th 943 — PARAPHRASE-ONLY Reported holding: the settlor's written declaration that property was held in trust was sufficient to create a trust in the subject real property without a formal conveyance of title to the settlor as trustee during the settlor's lifetime. Facts: property listed on a Schedule A attached to the trust instrument but never separately deeded; other Schedule A properties had been formally deeded. Sources: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/4th/16/943.html; https://www.quimbee.com/cases/estate-of-heggstad Pin cite not confirmed.

Heggstad is the doctrinal route for an omitted partnership interest. If the partnership interest appears on a trust schedule or in a written declaration but was never formally assigned, Heggstad + § 850 is the mechanism. Counsel must obtain and examine the actual trust schedules before relying on this.

Estate of Kraus (2010) 184 Cal.App.4th 103 — PARAPHRASE-ONLY, WITH A FLAGGED INTERNAL CONFLICT Reported facts: probate court ordered return of $197,402 to a court-appointed estate representative plus statutory double damages of $394,804; the underlying conduct was use of an invalid power of attorney to withdraw funds from a dying sister's accounts the day before her death. Reported reasoning: "the statutory emphasis is not on to whom the property belongs, but whether the person in possession in bad faith wrongfully acquired it"; once title is established, the court may consider double damages upon proof that the taking was wrongful and made in bad faith. Sources: https://case-law.vlex.com/vid/in-re-estate-of-885121907; https://www.adrservices.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/Probate-Series-3-850-Actions-859-Double-Damages-Handout-Materials.pdf Pin cite not confirmed.

FLAG: the search response returned both "section 859 is punitive in nature" and "section 859 double damages are not punitive damages." These are not necessarily inconsistent (penal in character ≠ punitive damages under Civ. Code § 3294), but the retrieval blended Kraus with later authority. Counsel must read Kraus directly before attributing either proposition to it.

Hill v. Superior Court (2016) 244 Cal.App.4th 1281 — PARAPHRASE-ONLY Reported: co-executors sued their stepfather to recover estate property plus § 859 double damages; after the stepfather died mid-action his successor argued the double damages were "punitive" and not recoverable against him. Reported holding: "double damages under section 859 are not punitive 'damages recoverable under section 3294 of the Civil Code.'" Sources: https://case-law.vlex.com/vid/hill-v-superior-court-886304128; https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/ca-court-of-appeal/1726562.html Pin cite not confirmed. Caution: several unrelated "Hill v. Superior Court" cases exist, including a California Supreme Court decision at 10 Cal.3d 812. Confirm the correct case.

Levin v. Winston-Levin (2019) 39 Cal.App.5th 1025 — PARAPHRASE-ONLY Reported holding: a finding of bad faith is a prerequisite to a § 859 double-damages award premised on a theory of undue influence. Although undue influence may give rise to financial elder abuse liability with its own enhanced remedies, § 859 requires an additional showing of bad faith; "[n]ot all instances of undue influence entail bad faith." On the facts, the amendment was invalidated and return of property ordered, but the double-damages award was not sustained for want of a separate bad-faith finding. Sources: https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/ca-court-of-appeal/2019597.html; https://calawyers.org/trusts-and-estates/elizabeth-levin-v-debra-winston-levin/ Pin cite not confirmed.

Levin is the case that disciplines § 859 expectations. A § 850 recovery does not automatically carry double damages. Counsel should plead bad faith as a discrete, separately-supported element with its own evidentiary basis, not as a rhetorical add-on.

E. Surcharge — breach, measure of liability, burden

Cal. Prob. Code § 16400 — VERIFIED-BY-SEARCH Text returned: "A violation by the trustee of any duty that the trustee owes the beneficiary is a breach of trust." History returned as: Enacted by Stats. 1990, Ch. 79. Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prob/division-9/part-4/chapter-4/article-1/section-16400/

Cal. Prob. Code § 16401 (agents) — PARAPHRASE-ONLY "Except as provided in subdivision (b), the trustee is not liable to the beneficiary for the acts or omissions of an agent." The trustee is liable for an agent's act or omission that would be a breach if committed by the trustee where the trustee: directs the act; delegates authority the trustee had a duty not to delegate; fails to use reasonable prudence in selecting or retaining the agent; fails to periodically review the agent's overall performance and compliance; conceals the agent's act; or neglects to take reasonable steps to compel the agent to redress the wrong. Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prob/division-9/part-4/chapter-4/article-1/section-16401/

Cal. Prob. Code § 16402 (cotrustees) — PARAPHRASE-ONLY A trustee is liable to the beneficiary for a breach committed by a cotrustee where the trustee: participates in the cotrustee's breach; improperly delegates administration to the cotrustee; approves, knowingly acquiesces in, or conceals the cotrustee's breach; negligently enables the cotrustee to commit the breach; or neglects to take reasonable steps to compel the cotrustee to redress the breach. Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prob/division-9/part-4/chapter-4/article-1/section-16402/

§ 16402 matters directly here — the Hazel Trust has successor co-trustees (Ashley Garabedian and Hazel Susan Leal). Neither can insulate herself by pointing at the other where any § 16402 predicate is met.

Cal. Prob. Code § 16403 (successor trustees) — PARAPHRASE-ONLY "Except as provided in subdivision (b), a successor trustee is not liable to the beneficiary for a breach of trust committed by a predecessor trustee." A successor is liable where the successor knows or has information from which the successor reasonably should have known of a situation constituting a predecessor's breach and improperly permits it to continue, or neglects to take reasonable steps to compel the predecessor to deliver the trust property or to redress a breach. Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prob/division-9/part-4/chapter-4/article-1/section-16403/

⚠ CITATION TRAP — READ THIS. There are two different § 16403s in play in this matter: Probate Code § 16403 (successor-trustee liability, above) and Corporations Code § 16403 (partnership books and records, § G below). They are unrelated. Any brief in this case must state the code name every time.

Probate Code § 16403 is a live theory as to the Hazel Trust co-trustees, who are successor trustees. Whether they took reasonable steps to compel delivery of trust property — including any omitted partnership interest — is squarely within (b).

Cal. Prob. Code § 16420 (remedies) — VERIFIED-BY-SEARCH If a trustee commits or threatens a breach of trust, a beneficiary or cotrustee may commence a proceeding for any of the following that is appropriate: (1) to compel the trustee to perform the trustee's duties; (2) to enjoin a breach; (3) to compel the trustee to redress a breach by payment of money or otherwise; (4) to appoint a receiver or temporary trustee; (5) to remove the trustee; (6) subject to § 18100, to set aside acts of the trustee; (7) to reduce or deny compensation of the trustee; (8) subject to § 18100, to impose an equitable lien or constructive trust; (9) subject to § 18100, to trace trust property wrongfully disposed of and recover the property or its proceeds. Provision of these remedies does not prevent resort to any other appropriate statutory or common-law remedy. Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prob/division-9/part-4/chapter-4/article-2/section-16420/

Cal. Prob. Code § 16421 — PARAPHRASE-ONLY "The remedies of a beneficiary against the trustee are exclusively in equity." Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/2005/prob/16420-16421.html

Cal. Prob. Code § 16440 (measure of liability) — VERIFIED-BY-SEARCH

  • (a) If the trustee commits a breach of trust, the trustee is chargeable with any of the following that is appropriate under the circumstances:
    • (1) "Any loss or depreciation in value of the trust estate resulting from the breach of trust, with interest."

Code § 16441 (interest) — PARAPHRASE-ONLY If the trustee is liable for interest pursuant to § 16440, the trustee is liable for the greater of: (1) the amount of interest that accrues at the legal rate on judgments in effect during the period when the interest accrued; or (2) the amount of interest actually received. Subdivision (b) contains the same reasonable-and-good-faith equitable excuse as § 16440(b). Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prob/division-9/part-4/chapter-4/article-3/section-16441/ Exact text NOT retrieved verbatim — counsel must confirm, particularly the (b) excuse.

Cal. Prob. Code § 16040 (standard of care) — PARAPHRASE-ONLY

  • (a) The trustee shall administer the trust with reasonable care, skill, and caution under the circumstances then prevailing that a prudent person acting in a like capacity would use in the conduct of an enterprise of like character and with like aims to accomplish the purposes of the trust as determined from the trust instrument.

Cal. Prob. Code §§ 16006, 16009 — PARAPHRASE-ONLY § 16006: "The trustee has a duty to take reasonable steps under the circumstances to take and keep control of and to preserve the trust property." § 16009: duty to keep trust property separate from other property and to see that it is designated as property of the trust. § 16006 is the omitted-asset duty. A trustee who never took control of a trust asset — e.g., a partnership interest — has a § 16006 problem independent of any accounting failure. § 16009 is the commingling duty, and commingling is what triggers the McCabe presumptions (below).

Cal. Prob. Code § 16004(c) (burden-shifting presumption) — VERIFIED-BY-SEARCH Text returned: "A transaction between the trustee and a beneficiary which occurs during the existence of the trust or while the trustee's influence with the beneficiary remains and by which the trustee obtains an advantage from the beneficiary is presumed to be a violation of the trustee's fiduciary duties. This presumption is a presumption affecting the burden of proof." The subdivision does not apply to provisions of an agreement between trustee and beneficiary relating to the hiring or compensation of the trustee. Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prob/division-9/part-4/chapter-1/article-1/section-16004/

§ 16004(c) is a statutory burden-shifter and should be pleaded expressly where the facts support it. It is not a general accounting burden-shifter — it applies to trustee/beneficiary transactions conferring an advantage on the trustee. Note the 2017 Settlement Agreement may itself be such a transaction — see Application § 5 and Open Questions.

Uzyel v. Kadisha (2010) 188 Cal.App.4th 866 — PARAPHRASE-ONLY Reported facts: trustee sold trust Qualcomm stock to raise cash for his own use and transferred it to himself via a fictitious loan; the stock subsequently appreciated dramatically. After a nonjury trial the trial court awarded over $59 million in compensatory damages and disgorgement, plus $5 million punitive damages. Reported holdings: (1) tracing is not required for disgorgement of profits made by the trustee "through the breach of trust" under § 16440(a)(2); (2) the fact that an act is consistent with — or even compelled by — the duty of prudent investing does not excuse a trustee from liability for breach of the duty of loyalty, including liability for appreciation damages as lost profits under § 16440(a)(3). Sources: https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2278013/uzyel-v-kadisha/; https://www.leagle.com/decision/incaco20100922045; https://case-law.vlex.com/vid/uzyel-v-kadisha-b196045-888884316 Pin cite not confirmed.

Uzyel is the leading modern California surcharge-measure case. It is the authority for (i) appreciation/lost-profit damages and (ii) disgorgement without tracing. It is worth counsel's time to read in full.

Burden of proof on the elements of surcharge (breach / causation / damages) — UNVERIFIED — counsel must confirm. Searches returned only law-firm secondary content stating the conventional four-element formulation (fiduciary relationship; breach; causation; damages) with the burden initially on the petitioner, subject to shifting on self-dealing. No California case was retrieved for this proposition and none is cited here. Counsel should locate primary authority (and consider Evid. Code § 500 and § 16004(c)) before briefing burden allocation.

F. Failure to account; construing gaps against the record-keeping fiduciary

This is the doctrinal core of Issue 7, and the two cases below are old, durable, and frequently cited.

Purdy v. Johnson (1917) 174 Cal. 521 — VERIFIED-BY-SEARCH (language returned as apparently verbatim) Reported language: "whatever doubts arise from a trustee's failure to keep proper records or inability to establish the items of their accounts must be resolved against them"; this result "follows from the failure and neglect of the trustees to perform their duty of keeping full and accurate accounts of their transactions." Further: "it is the duty of the trustees to support every item of their account, and wherever they fail to support the correctness of a charge or credit by satisfactory evidence, the item must be disallowed." Sources: https://www.casemine.com/judgement/us/5914a8fdadd7b04934707f6b; also surfaced in Estate of Bissinger, https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2d/60/756.html Pin cite not confirmed (commonly cited around 174 Cal. at 527–528, but this memo does not assert that).

Estate of McCabe (1950) 98 Cal.App.2d 503 — VERIFIED-BY-SEARCH (language returned as apparently verbatim) Reported language: trustees are under an obligation to render to beneficiaries a full account of all their dealings with the trust property, and "where there has been a negligent failure to keep true accounts all presumptions are against them upon a settlement." Trustees are under a duty to prove every item of their account by "satisfactory evidence"; "the burden of proof is on them and not on the beneficiary"; and "any doubt arising from their failure to keep proper records, or from the nature of the proof they produce, must be resolved against them." Reported application: the trustee had mingled trust funds with her own, omitted to invest them so as to provide an income, and negligently failed to keep any records enabling a true account — all bearing on whether charges were established by satisfactory evidence "in the absence of any vouchers or records of any kind, and when all presumptions are against the trustee." Sources: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2d/98/503.html; https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/ca-court-of-appeal/1798125.html Pin cite not confirmed.

Caution: there is a related but distinct Estate of McCabe at 87 Cal.App.2d 430. Confirm the correct citation.

Lynch v. John M. Redfield Foundation (1970) 9 Cal.App.3d 293 — UNVERIFIED — counsel must confirm. Frequently cited for trustee liability for interest on funds left unproductive. No text was retrieved in this session. Not relied upon in this memo; noted only as a research lead for counsel on the § 16441 interest question.

THIS SECTION CUTS BOTH WAYS AND COUNSEL SHOULD SAY SO INTERNALLY BEFORE OPPOSING COUNSEL DOES. Purdy and McCabe are not "beneficiary wins" cases. They are "the person who had the duty to keep the books bears the consequences of not keeping them" cases. Our client kept the partnership books. See Application § 8 and § 9.

G. Partnership interest held by a trust; partnership books vs. trust accounting

No California case addressing trust-level accounting for a partnership interest was located. This is a genuine gap in this memo. — UNVERIFIED. The analysis below is assembled from statutes, each individually sourced.

Cal. Corp. Code § 16403 (partnership books and records) — VERIFIED-BY-SEARCH

  • "A partnership shall keep its books and records, if any, in writing or in any other form capable of being converted into clearly legible tangible form, at its chief executive office."
  • The partnership "shall provide partners and their agents and attorneys access to its books and records, and shall provide former partners and their agents and attorneys access to books and records pertaining to the period during which they were partners." The right of access includes the opportunity to inspect and copy during ordinary business hours; a reasonable copying charge may be imposed.
  • "Each partner and the partnership shall furnish to a partner … any information concerning the partnership's business and affairs reasonably required for the proper exercise of the partner's rights and duties under the partnership agreement or this chapter, and on demand, any other information concerning the partnership's business and affairs, except to the extent the demand or the information demanded is unreasonable or otherwise improper under the circumstances."

Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-corp/title-2/chapter-5/article-4/section-16403/ Subdivision lettering not confirmed.

This is the pivot for Issue 8. A trustee holding a partnership interest is (or holds the interest of) a partner, and § 16403 gives partners and former partners a statutory right of access to the books. That right substantially undercuts a trustee's defense that it "could not obtain" partnership-level information. It equally means that the partner who holds the books owes production — including to a trustee-partner and, derivatively, to that trust's beneficiaries.

Cal. Corp. Code § 16404 (partner fiduciary duties) — VERIFIED-BY-SEARCH

  • The fiduciary duties a partner owes to the partnership and the other partners are the duty of loyalty and the duty of care set forth in subdivisions (b) and (c).
  • Duty of loyalty includes "[t]o account to the partnership and hold as trustee for it any property, profit, or benefit derived by the partner in the conduct and winding up of the partnership business or derived from a use by the partner of partnership property or information, including the appropriation of a partnership opportunity"; refraining from dealing with the partnership as or on behalf of a party having an adverse interest; and refraining from competing with the partnership before dissolution.
  • Duty of care is "limited to refraining from engaging in grossly negligent or reckless conduct, intentional misconduct, or a knowing violation of law."

Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-corp/title-2/chapter-5/article-4/section-16404/

Note the asymmetry that matters for our client. The partnership duty of care is a gross negligence standard (Corp. Code § 16404(c)) — materially more forgiving than the trustee standard of "reasonable care, skill, and caution" (Prob. Code § 16040). But the partnership duty of loyalty expressly includes a duty to account and to hold as trustee any benefit derived from partnership property or information. A managing partner therefore gets a friendlier negligence standard but not a friendlier accounting standard.

Cal. Corp. Code § 16405 — VERIFIED-BY-SEARCH

  • (a) "A partnership may maintain an action against a partner for a breach of the partnership agreement, or for the violation of a duty to the partnership, causing harm to the partnership."
  • (b) "A partner may maintain an action against the partnership or another partner for legal or equitable relief, with or without an accounting as to partnership business."

Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-corp/title-2/chapter-5/article-4/section-16405/

§ 16405(b) is the direct partner-vs-partner accounting hook, and it does not require dissolution — relief may be had "with or without an accounting." This provision is available against our client as managing partner, by any partner, including a trustee-partner.

Leff v. Gunter (1983) 33 Cal.3d 508 — PARAPHRASE-ONLY, with one secondary-sourced pin cite Reported language: "Partners are trustees for each other, and in all proceedings connected with the conduct of the partnership every partner is bound to act in the highest good faith to his copartner and may not obtain any advantage over him in the partnership affairs by the slightest misrepresentation, concealment, threat or adverse pressure of any kind." Sources: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/3d/33/508.html; https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/ca-supreme-court/1838610.html A secondary source (https://www.berliner.com/articles/fiduciary-duties-between-partners-and-joint-venturers-101) attributes this passage to 33 Cal.3d at 514. That pin cite is reported by a secondary source only and was NOT independently confirmed. Do not use it without checking.

Cal. Prob. Code § 1061 — "net income from trade or business" — PARAPHRASE-ONLY (see § A above) A court-filed account reports a trade or business on a net basis as a summary line, supported by a schedule — it does not fold gross partnership receipts and disbursements into the trust's own receipt and disbursement schedules.

Synthesis for Issue 8 (this is analysis, not authority): the statutory materials point toward a two-tier structure. At the trust level, the trustee must report the partnership interest as an asset (§ 16063(a)(2)), report distributions actually received as receipts (§ 16063(a)(1)), report net trade-or-business results on a schedule (§ 1061), and furnish partnership information "relevant to the beneficiary's interest" on request (§ 16061). At the partnership level, the books belong to the partnership, and access is governed by Corp. Code § 16403 with enforcement under § 16405(b). The trustee cannot use the entity as a shield, because § 16403 gives the trustee-partner the access needed to satisfy § 16061 and § 16063. But the beneficiary also cannot simply demand partnership books through a trust accounting petition — the partnership is a separate legal person with its own records regime. No case confirming this two-tier synthesis was retrieved. Counsel must verify it before advancing it.

Application to Our Facts

Framing note: everything in this section is offered as considerations for counsel. Nothing here predicts any outcome, and no statement below should be read as a forecast of how the Tulare County Superior Court would rule.

1. Counsel may consider establishing the accounting timeline before anything else

The accounting duty is date-driven, and two of the three governing dates are unresolved.

  • Manuel C. Leal appears to have died 3/25/2015, based on a partnership capital transfer recorded as "to Steve/Bypass Trust 3/25/15." Counsel may consider that this is a bookkeeping inference, not a proved date of death, and that a certified death certificate should be obtained before any date-dependent argument is made.
  • Hazel J. Leal's date of death is not established in the records reviewed. Counsel may consider that this is the single most consequential open fact in the matter. Under § 16062(a) the accounting obligation attaches on a change of trustee; under § 15800 the successor co-trustees' duties to beneficiaries (as opposed to the settlor) as to the Hazel Revocable Trust did not arise until the power to revoke ended; under § 16061.7 the 60-day notification clock ran from that date; and the $327,427.02 figure in our counsel's letter is expressly measured "through Hazel's date of death." Counsel may consider that a valuation pegged to an unestablished date is vulnerable on that ground alone.
  • The December 7, 2017 Settlement Agreement and Mutual Release sits between these events and may operate as a temporal boundary on claims. See § 5.

Counsel may consider building a single dated matrix — trust, capacity, trustee identity, accounting period, and limitations trigger — before drafting any petition.

2. Counsel may consider which trust is being accounted for, and by whom

Three instruments are in play with different accounting regimes:

  • Hazel J. Leal Revocable Trust (11/3/2008). Revocable during Hazel's competent lifetime. Under § 15800 and Giraldin, the trustee's duties during that period ran to Hazel, not to remainder beneficiaries. Under § 16064(c) no account to beneficiaries was owed for the revocable period. After Hazel's death, § 16062(a) attaches (annually, at termination, on change of trustee), and Giraldin may permit reaching pre-death conduct to the extent it harmed the beneficiaries. Counsel may consider that the § 15800 2022 amendment does not govern conduct predating its effective date, and that the correct statutory version must be matched to each period.
  • Manuel C. Leal Bypass Trust (uta dtd 2/14/05, as amended). A bypass trust is ordinarily irrevocable on the first settlor's death. If Manuel died 3/25/2015, counsel may consider that the § 16062(a) annual accounting duty attached to the Bypass Trust from that date forward, running to each beneficiary to whom income or principal is required or authorized to be currently distributed — which, in the typical bypass structure, would include Hazel as lifetime income beneficiary.
  • Manuel C. Leal Living Trust. Role and current status not established in the records reviewed.

Counsel may consider that the identity of the Bypass Trust's trustee from 3/25/2015 forward is a threshold question that has not been answered — and that the answer may be adverse. See § 9.

3. Counsel may consider § 17200 as the procedural vehicle, and the 60-day predicate as a gating item

Counsel may consider that § 17200(b)(5) (settling accounts and passing on trustee acts) and § 17200(b)(7) (compelling information and accounts) supply the petition framework, and that § 17206 gives the court discretion to "make any orders and take any other action necessary or proper," including appointment of a temporary trustee.

Counsel may consider two practical gates:

  • § 17200(b)(7) requires a written request and a 60-day lapse, and as to accounts additionally requires that no report or account was made within the preceding six months. Counsel may consider confirming, in writing and on a datable record, that these predicates are satisfied before filing.
  • If the Hazel Trust instrument waives accounting, § 16064(a) still permits the court to compel an account "upon a showing that it is reasonably likely that a material breach of the trust has occurred." Counsel may consider that this is a lower threshold than proving breach, and that an omitted partnership interest — if one exists — is the kind of fact that could be marshalled to meet it.

Counsel may consider that under Esslinger v. Cummins, remainder-beneficiary status is not an obstacle to standing to compel an account, though that case must be read before it is cited.

4. Counsel may consider the limitations exposure in both directions under § 16460

Under § 16460 the three-year period runs from receipt of an adequately disclosing account or report, and otherwise from discovery or constructive discovery.

Counsel may consider:

  • If the co-trustees never rendered an account, the three-year clock is a discovery clock, not a receipt clock — which generally favors our side on the accounting and omitted-asset claims.
  • But discovery is constructive as well as actual. Counsel may consider that our client's position as managing partner who kept the partnership books is precisely the kind of fact a court could treat as bearing on when he "reasonably should have discovered" a discrepancy between partnership capital accounts and trust asset schedules. This is a real risk and should be assessed candidly, not minimized.
  • § 16063(a)(6) requires an account to carry the three-year warning. Counsel may consider whether any document the co-trustees characterize as an "account or report" carried that notice, and whether its absence bears on the "adequately discloses" question under § 16460.
  • Counsel may consider that § 16061.8's 120-day period is a trust-contest bar and does not govern breach-of-trust or accounting claims — a distinction worth preserving in writing before it is blurred in briefing.
  • Laches has not been researched. Counsel may consider that a laches defense is foreseeable given the 2015 and 2017 dates and that this memo supplies no authority on it.

5. Counsel may consider that the 2017 Settlement Agreement and Mutual Release is a two-edged instrument

Counsel may consider that § 16464 governs the effect of a beneficiary's release on trustee liability, and that a release is not effective where the beneficiary was under an incapacity, did not know of the beneficiary's rights and of material facts the trustee knew or should have known, the release was induced by improper conduct of the trustee, or the bargain was not fair and reasonable.

Counsel may consider the following, in both directions:

  • Offensively: if the release was signed without disclosure of an omitted partnership interest or of undistributed Bypass Trust income, the "did not know of material facts the trustee knew or should have known" prong of § 16464 may be worth developing. § 16004(c) may also be worth examining — if the 2017 agreement was a transaction between a trustee and a beneficiary by which the trustee obtained an advantage, the statutory presumption affecting the burden of proof may apply.
  • Defensively: the same analysis is available to the co-trustees against our client, and the release may on its face bar claims arising before 12/7/2017. Counsel may consider that a mutual release cuts symmetrically and that the scope, defined terms, carve-outs, and effective date of the actual agreement must be read before any of this is asserted. This memo has not seen the agreement.

6. Counsel may consider a § 850 petition for any omitted partnership interest

If a partnership interest (or a capital account balance) belonged to a trust but was never formally assigned or scheduled, counsel may consider that:

  • § 850(a)(3)(B) reaches the case "[w]here the trustee has a claim to real or personal property, title to or possession of which is held by another," and § 856 authorizes an order directing conveyance "or granting other appropriate relief."
  • Estate of Heggstad supplies the substantive theory where a written declaration or trust schedule evidences trust ownership without a recorded transfer. Counsel may consider that this requires the actual trust schedules, which should be obtained and examined.
  • Standing is a live question. The § 850(a)(3) text returned names the trustee as petitioner. Counsel may consider confirming whether a beneficiary may petition under (a)(3), or whether the petition must be brought by or in the name of a trustee — a question this memo could not resolve.

On § 859 double damages, counsel may consider proceeding with discipline:

  • Bad faith is a separate, required element. Under Levin v. Winston-Levin, even a successful undue-influence showing does not supply it. Counsel may consider that pleading § 859 without an independent, evidence-backed bad-faith theory invites the Levin result — recovery of the property without the multiplier.
  • Counsel may consider that a failure to inventory an asset, standing alone, is a long distance from "in bad faith wrongfully taken, concealed, or disposed of." A record of concealment — e.g., affirmative misstatements about what the trust held — would be doing the work, not the omission itself.
  • Counsel may consider that § 859 also permits reasonable attorney's fees and costs in the court's discretion, which may be the more attainable component.

7. Counsel may consider the surcharge theory as breach-plus-causation, not bad faith

Counsel may consider the following structure:

  • § 16400 — any duty violation is a breach. Candidate duties: § 16060 (keep informed), § 16062 (account), § 16006 (take and keep control of trust property — the omitted-asset duty), § 16009 (keep property separate and designated), § 16040 (reasonable care, skill, and caution).
  • § 16440(a) — three alternative measures, and counsel may consider pleading them in the alternative rather than electing early: (1) loss or depreciation with interest; (2) trustee's profit through the breach, with interest; (3) profit that would have accrued. Under Uzyel v. Kadisha, tracing is not required for (a)(2) disgorgement, and lost-profit/appreciation damages are available under (a)(3).
  • § 16441 — interest at the greater of the legal judgment rate or interest actually received.
  • § 16420 — the remedial menu, including redress by payment of money, removal, and reduction or denial of trustee compensation. Counsel may consider that compensation reduction under § 16420(a)(7) is a remedy that does not depend on proving a dollar loss.
  • § 16402 and Prob. Code § 16403 — because the Hazel Trust has successor co-trustees, counsel may consider whether either co-trustee approved, knowingly acquiesced in, concealed, or negligently enabled a breach by the other (§ 16402), and whether either failed to take reasonable steps to compel a predecessor trustee to deliver trust property or redress a breach (Prob. Code § 16403(b)) — a theory that maps directly onto an omitted asset.

Counsel may consider that bad faith is not an element of surcharge, but that it is decisive at three other points: it defeats § 16461 exculpation, it forecloses the § 16440(b)/§ 16441(b) equitable excuse, and it is required for § 859. Conversely, counsel may consider that the co-trustees' most likely defensive move is § 16440(b) — "acted reasonably and in good faith" — and that anticipating it is more useful than pleading around it.

Counsel may consider that under § 16421 the beneficiary's remedies against the trustee are exclusively in equity, with the jury-trial consequences that follow. This should be verified before any trial-setting decision.

8. Counsel may consider the partnership-interest accounting as a two-tier problem

Counsel may consider that:

  • At the trust level, § 16063(a)(2) requires a statement of assets and liabilities, which would include a partnership interest; § 16063(a)(1) captures distributions actually received; and Prob. Code § 1061 reports a trade or business on a net basis with a supporting schedule.
  • At the partnership level, Corp. Code § 16403 gives partners and former partners a right to inspect and copy the books, and obliges each partner and the partnership to furnish information reasonably required for the exercise of a partner's rights, and on demand any other information about the partnership's business and affairs, subject to a reasonableness limit.
  • Corp. Code § 16405(b) permits a partner to sue another partner for legal or equitable relief "with or without an accounting as to partnership business" — no dissolution required.
  • Corp. Code § 16404(b)(1) imposes on every partner a duty to account to the partnership and to hold as trustee any property, profit, or benefit derived from the use of partnership property or information.

Counsel may consider that the practical consequence is that a trustee-partner cannot plead inability to obtain partnership records, because § 16403 supplies the access. Counsel may equally consider that this argument is fully available in reverse against the partner who holds the books.

Counsel may consider that no case authority for this two-tier synthesis was located, and that the synthesis is therefore argument, not authority.

9. THE DEFENSIVE POSTURE — what these same duties would require OF OUR SIDE

This section is written adversely on purpose. Counsel may consider that the following exposure is structural, not speculative, and that it should be assessed before a petition is filed rather than after it draws a cross-petition.

(a) Our client kept the books, and the record-keeping cases are neutral as to which side benefits. Purdy and McCabe do not say "resolve doubts in favor of beneficiaries." They say the accounting party must prove every item by satisfactory evidence, that the burden is on that party, and that doubts arising from that party's own failure to keep proper records are resolved against that party. Counsel may consider that as managing partner of Manuel C. Leal & Son Dairy Partnership, our client is the party who kept the books that any accounting will be built from. If those books have gaps — missing vouchers, unsupported capital-account entries, undocumented allocations, informal draws — McCabe's "all presumptions are against them" language is available to the co-trustees against our client with no modification.

(b) The 3/25/15 capital transfer entry is our own document, and it cuts both ways. Counsel may consider that the entry "to Steve/Bypass Trust 3/25/15" is a record our client created or controlled. It is useful to us as evidence that a partnership interest moved to the Bypass Trust. It is equally useful to the other side as evidence that our client knew, as of 3/25/2015, that the Bypass Trust held a partnership interest — which bears directly on constructive discovery under § 16460 and on any laches defense.

(c) If our client served as trustee of the Bypass Trust, he owes the § 16062 account for the very income he is claiming. Counsel may consider that the $327,427.02 is characterized in our counsel's letter as "earned but undistributed income from the Manuel C. Leal Bypass Trust through Hazel's date of death." Counsel may consider the following chain:

  1. If the Bypass Trust became irrevocable on Manuel's death (3/25/2015), § 16062(a) required annual accounts from that date to each beneficiary entitled to current income or principal.
  2. Hazel would ordinarily be that income beneficiary.
  3. Income "earned but undistributed" is, by its own description, income the trustee did not distribute.
  4. Under § 16000-series duties and § 16440(a), a trustee who failed to distribute required income, and who failed to account for it annually, has the exposure — and the person asserting the claim would ordinarily be Hazel's successor in interest, i.e., the Hazel Trust, of which the defendant co-trustees are the fiduciaries.

Counsel may consider that if our client was the Bypass Trust trustee during that period, the $327,427.02 is not obviously an asset of our claim — it may be a measure of our liability. Counsel may consider that establishing who served as Bypass Trust trustee from 3/25/2015 forward is urgent and should precede any demand letter that repeats the figure. If our client was not the trustee, this concern substantially dissolves, and the figure becomes a claim against whoever was.

(d) Corp. Code § 16405(b) is a ready-made cross-petition. Counsel may consider that any partner — including the Hazel Trust or Bypass Trust as a partner, acting through its trustees — may sue our client for legal or equitable relief with or without an accounting, without dissolution. Combined with § 16403's books-and-records access right and § 16404(b)(1)'s duty to account for benefits derived from partnership property or information, counsel may consider that a partnership accounting cross-claim is the most predictable responsive pleading in this matter.

(e) The partnership duty-of-care standard helps us; the loyalty and accounting duties do not. Counsel may consider that Corp. Code § 16404(c) limits a partner's duty of care to gross negligence, recklessness, intentional misconduct, or knowing violation of law — materially more protective than Prob. Code § 16040's reasonable-care standard. Counsel may consider that this asymmetry is worth preserving by resisting any characterization of our client's partnership conduct as trustee conduct. Counsel may equally consider that this protection does not extend to the § 16404(b)(1) duty to account, which is a loyalty duty, not a care duty.

(f) Dual-capacity risk. Counsel may consider that if our client acted both as managing partner (owing Corp. Code § 16404 duties to co-partners) and as a fiduciary of a trust holding a partnership interest (owing Probate Code duties to that trust's beneficiaries), the two roles create conflict exposure under Prob. Code § 16004, and any transaction between the partnership and the trust would be examined against that backdrop. Counsel may consider mapping every capacity our client held, by date, before taking any position on the co-trustees' capacities.

(g) Symmetry of the § 16464 release analysis. Counsel may consider that every argument for setting aside the 2017 release as to the co-trustees is available to the co-trustees as to our client, and that a mutual release is by construction bilateral.

Open Questions

  1. Hazel J. Leal's date of death. Unestablished in the records reviewed. Drives § 15800, § 16062(a), § 16061.7/.8, § 16460, and the valuation date for the $327,427.02 claim. Highest priority.
  2. Manuel C. Leal's date of death. Inferred from a bookkeeping entry (3/25/15), not from a death certificate.
  3. Who served as trustee of the Manuel C. Leal Bypass Trust from 3/25/2015 forward? Determines whether the $327,427.02 is our claim or our exposure. Second-highest priority.
  4. Was Hazel competent throughout the period the Hazel Trust remained revocable? Determines which version of § 15800 applies and whether beneficiary rights arose before death.
  5. Do the Hazel Trust and Bypass Trust instruments contain accounting waivers? If so, § 16064(a) and the "reasonably likely that a material breach has occurred" showing become central. Note § 16062(e) applies only to a sole trustee.
  6. Do the trust instruments contain exculpatory clauses, and do they include a § 16461(c)-type objection-period release requiring a minimum 180-day window?
  7. What are the precise scope, defined terms, carve-outs, and effective date of the December 7, 2017 Settlement Agreement and Mutual Release? Not reviewed for this memo.
  8. Was any document ever tendered as an "account or report" by the co-trustees, and did it carry the § 16063(a)(6) three-year notice? Drives which § 16460 trigger applies.
  9. Was a § 16061.7 notification ever served, on whom, and when?
  10. What are the trust schedules? Determines whether a Heggstad theory is available for any omitted partnership interest.
  11. Did our client make a written § 16061 request, and have 60 days elapsed (and no account within the preceding six months)? § 17200(b)(7) predicate.
  12. Was the partnership interest ever formally assigned to either trust, and what do the capital account records show for each period?
  13. Does a beneficiary have standing to petition under § 850(a)(3), or must the petition be brought by a trustee?
  14. Is there a written partnership agreement, and does it modify the Corp. Code § 16404 duties within the limits the statute permits?
  15. What is the state of the partnership books for 2015 forward — completeness, vouchers, allocation support? This is the Purdy/McCabe exposure question for our own side.
  16. Laches — entirely unresearched. See Confidence and Gaps.
