Verification Report — CourtListener Pass

ATTORNEY WORK-PRODUCT — VERIFICATION PASS VIA COURTLISTENER MCP, AUGUST 18, 2026

Leal v. Garabedian (Tulare County Superior Court). Prepared to verify or refute authorities cited in memos R1–R4, which were drafted without database access. Sources: CourtListener opinion database (full-text reads and targeted in-opinion searches). Every quotation below was copied from opinion text actually displayed in this session. CourtListener has no statute database, so statutory text is verified only as quoted inside opinions.

Tag key

  • VERIFIED (read full) — the entire opinion was read in this session.
  • VERIFIED (read operative passages) — the case was located and the passages containing the holding/language quoted here were read; the full opinion was not read end to end.
  • EXISTS–NOT-READ — existence and identity confirmed; text not read. Do not cite for a holding.
  • NOT-FOUND — could not be located in CourtListener.
  • CONTRADICTED — earlier description conflicts with what the opinion actually says.

Caution on CourtListener metadata: CL's court/district labels are unreliable (it labels both Licudine and Petrolink "5th District"; both are not — see below). Take court and division from the opinion text, never from CL metadata. CL also lacks official reporter cites for several recent cases noted below.

PRIORITY 1 — Dissociation / buyout (Corp. Code §§ 16601, 16603, 16701, 16103)

Rappaport v. Gelfand (2011) 197 Cal.App.4th 1213 — VERIFIED (read operative passages)

CL cluster 5810457, opinion 5665898 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810457/rappaport-v-gelfand/). 2d Dist., Croskey, J. Bench trial to determine the "buyout price" of a dissociating law-firm partner under § 16701(b); described in the opinion as "this apparent case of first impression in California."

Quotes § 16701(a)–(b) verbatim, including the interest sentence (at pp. 1217, 1225–1226):

"(a) If a partner is dissociated from a partnership, the partnership shall cause the dissociated partner's interest in the partnership to be purchased for a buyout price determined pursuant to subdivision (b). [¶] (b) The buyout price of a dissociated partner's interest is the amount that would have been distributable to the dissociating partner under subdivision (b) of Section 16807 if, on the date of dissociation, the assets of the partnership were sold at a price equal to the greater of the liquidation value or the value based on a sale of the entire business as a going concern without the dissociated partner and the partnership was wound up as of that date. Interest shall be paid from the date of dissociation to the date of payment."

Interest from dissociation date applied in the judgment (at p. 1223): "the trial court entered judgment in favor of Rappaport for his 31 percent share of the partnership in the sum of $230,758 plus interest from November 1, 2005 [the day after the agreed Oct. 31, 2005 dissociation date], to the date of judgment. (§ 16701, subd. (b).)" The Court of Appeal affirmed the trial court's interpretation and application of § 16701(b) (valuing individual assets as liquidated over time and bringing the value "back" to the dissociation date), reversed only the individual liability of the two partners, and corrected a small math error.

§ 16103 default-rule principle quoted (at p. 1225): "relations among the partners and between the partners and the partnership are governed by the partnership agreement. To the extent the partnership agreement does not otherwise provide, this chapter governs relations among the partners and between the partners and the partnership." Followed by: "Thus, parties are free to enter into their own agreements concerning the buyout of a dissociating partner's interest. However, in the absence of such an agreement, the buyout of a departing partner's interest in the partnership business is governed by section 16701."

Han v. Hallberg (2019) 35 Cal.App.5th 621 — VERIFIED (read operative passages) — ⚠️ REVIEW GRANTED

CL cluster 6240500, opinion 6107449 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/6240500/han-v-hallberg/). Dental partnership; partner transferred his interest to his trust; question whether the trust (or trustee-as-such) is the partner and what his death did.

Construing § 16601 — note the subdivision numbers as the opinion states them. Individual partner's death is § 16601, subd. (7)(A); the trust provision is subd. (8):

"Section 16601 of the UPA states that a partner is dissociated from a partnership 'upon the occurrence of any of the following events.' (Corp. Code, § 16601.) Those include, '[i]n the case of a partner who is an individual,' the partner's death. (Id., subd. (7)(A))."

"the statute contemplates no termination of partnership status when the trustee of a trust is replaced or dies." (at pp. 632–633.)

"Whether the partner is 'a trust' or 'is acting as a partner by virtue of being a trustee of a trust,' makes no discernable difference; in both cases, the partner is not dissociated from the partnership by the death of the trustee. On the contrary, that partner, whether trust or trustee, is dissociated only by 'distribution of the trust's entire transferable interest in the partnership,' and not by 'the substitution of a successor trustee.' (§ 16601, subd. (8).)" (at pp. 635–636.)

The opinion expressly disagrees with Presta v. Tepper (2009) 179 Cal.App.4th 909 on the trust-as-partner analysis.

⚠️ Subsequent history flag: The California Supreme Court granted review: Han v. Hallberg, No. S256659, Aug. 21, 2019 (CL cluster 8256537; reported at 250 Cal.Rptr.3d 720, 446 P.3d 234). The ultimate disposition of the review proceeding is not in CourtListener and was not verified in this pass. Do not cite Han for any purpose until its current status and citability under Cal. Rules of Court, rule 8.1115(e) are confirmed on Westlaw.

Corrales v. Corrales (2011) 198 Cal.App.4th 221 — VERIFIED (read operative passages)

CL cluster 5810484, opinion 5665925 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810484/corrales-v-corrales/). 4th Dist. Div. 3.

Quotes § 16601(1) ("Section 16601, subdivision (1) allows dissociation upon '[t]he partnership's having notice of the partner's express will to withdraw as a partner or on a later date specified by the partner.'") and § 16701(b) verbatim (fn. 5). Holding (at pp. 227–228):

"A person cannot dissociate from a dissolved partnership, and the buyout rule of section 16701 does not apply to a two-person partnership when one partner leaves. When that happens, the dissolution procedures take over. The partnership is wound up, its business is completed, and the partners make whatever adjustments are necessary to their own accounts after paying the creditors. (§ 16807.)"

"The use of the buyout remedy of section 16701 was error, and we must reverse the judgment and remand it to the trial court with instructions to enter a judicial dissolution of the partnership under sections 16801 and 16807."

Case-mapping note: if the Manuel C. Leal & Son Dairy partnership has (or is argued to have) only two partners, Corrales threatens the entire § 16701 buyout framework — the remedy would be dissolution/wind-up under §§ 16801/16807, not a § 16701 buyout with interest. Conversely, if the Trust remained a partner via successor trustees (Han), there may be no dissociation at all. Both branches must be mapped to our facts.

Jones v. Goodman (Cal. Ct. App., filed Nov. 17, 2020) — VERIFIED (read operative passages)

CL cluster 4806805, opinion 4587152 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4806805/jones-v-goodman/). CL carries no reporter citation (memo sources give 57 Cal.App.5th 620 — confirm on Westlaw).

Quotes § 16701(i) verbatim:

"[t]he court may assess reasonable attorney's fees and the fees and expenses of appraisers or other experts for a party to the action, in amounts the court finds equitable, against a party that the court finds acted arbitrarily, vexatiously, or not in good faith. The finding may be based on the partnership's failure to tender payment or an offer to pay or to comply with subdivision (g)." (§ 16701, subd. (i).)

Also quotes § 16701(b) in full (fn. 9), § 16701(g) (buyout offer must be accompanied by financial statements and "[a]n explanation of how the estimated amount of the payment was calculated"), and § 16405(b)(2)(B) (partner's action to have the interest purchased). Holding: affirms denial of § 16701(i) fees; the statutory terms "arbitrarily, vexatiously, or not in good faith" are disjunctive; fee award discretionary. (Note: the slip opinion refers once to "Section 16601, subdivision (a)" for the express-will provision that Corrales cites as § 16601(1) — use the numbered-paragraph form.)

Mar v. Perkins (Cal. Ct. App., filed May 22, 2024) — VERIFIED (read operative passages)

CL cluster 9506420, opinion 9973033 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/9506420/mar-v-perkins/). No reporter cite in CL (memo sources suggest 102 Cal.App.5th 201 — confirm). A partner-buyout action under "Corporations Code section 16701, subdivisions (a) and (e)" (120-day written demand recited); the appeal concerned a motion to compel arbitration via employee handbook. Holding: "where, as here, the employee promptly rejects the arbitration agreement and makes clear he or she refuses to be bound by the agreement, there is no mutual assent to arbitrate. We affirm." Useful as a recent published example of the § 16701(a)/(e) demand-then-suit mechanism (determination of buyout price; order to pay buyout price plus interest; appraiser/expert fees).

Corp. Code § 16603 — NOT-FOUND in case law

A search for "16603" in California appellate opinions returned only false positives (Elections Code and other statutes). No California appellate opinion quoting Corp. Code § 16603 (effect of dissociation) was located in CourtListener. The § 16603 text in memo R4 rests on an unofficial source (Justia) and still needs verification against the official code on Westlaw.

Corp. Code § 16103(b) (nonwaivable provisions) — NOT-FOUND in case law (this pass)

Rappaport supplies § 16103's default-rule principle (above), but no opinion quoting § 16103(b)'s list of provisions a partnership agreement may NOT waive was located. If the waiver question matters, verify § 16103(b) on Westlaw.

PRIORITY 2 — CCP § 998 (memo R1)

Poster v. Southern California Rapid Transit District (1990) 52 Cal.3d 266 — VERIFIED (read operative passages + full § 1013 discussion)

CL cluster/opinion 1442502 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1442502/poster-v-southern-california-rapid-transit-district/). Broussard, J. Issue as framed (at p. 269): "whether when a section 998 offer is served by mail, section 1013, subdivision (a) applies to extend the time to respond by five days."

Holding (at p. 275):

"Accordingly, we conclude that when a statutory settlement offer pursuant to section 998 is served by mail, the provisions of section 1013 apply and extend the 30-day period for acceptance of the offer by 5 days."

Supporting reasoning (at pp. 273–275): § 1013 is "a procedural statute of general application"; "By its terms, section 1013 appears clearly to apply to the time period prescribed by section 998 for accepting statutory offers of compromise"; the 30-day limit is not jurisdictional. Disposition: Court of Appeal reversed insofar as it held § 1013 inapplicable; affirmed insofar as it held a counteroffer does not revoke a § 998 offer. This resolves R1's flagged confusion: the "§ 1013 does not apply" description in search snippets was the Court of Appeal's holding, which the Supreme Court reversed. Post-2005 corroboration: Licudine (2019, below) applied the same rule ("§§ 998, subd. (b)(2) [offer expires 30 days after it is made], 1013, subd. (a) [five additional days added for mailed offers]" — Licudine at p. 922).

Gorobets v. Jaguar Land Rover North America, LLC (Cal. Aug. 6, 2026, S287946) — VERIFIED (read holding, background, summary, disposition — chunks 1–2 and 8–9 of 9)

CL cluster 10940921, opinion 11408504 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10940921/gorobets-v-jaguar-land-rover-north-america-llc/). The case exists exactly as memo R1 described it: Supreme Court of California, No. S287946, filed August 6, 2026, Corrigan, J., for a unanimous court (Guerrero, C.J., Liu, Kruger, Groban, Evans, JJ., and Feuer, J. [assigned]). Review of Gorobets v. Jaguar Land Rover North America, LLC (2024) 105 Cal.App.5th 913 (2d Dist. Div. 2, B327745; LA Super. Ct. 19STCV11540). No official Cal.5th cite assigned yet in CL.

General validity test restated (slip op. p. 1):

"Under a well-established test developed by our lower courts, a 998 offer is valid for cost-shifting purposes only if its terms are sufficiently certain or specific to permit the offeree and the trial court to assess its value as of the time the offer was made. (Valentino v. Elliott Sav-On Gas, Inc. (1988) 201 Cal.App.3d 692, 698 …; Fassberg Construction Co. v. Housing Authority of City of Los Angeles (2007) 152 Cal.App.4th 720, 764 …)"

Holding (slip op. p. 2):

"We hold that such a 998 offer can be valid so long as (1) the offer is structured so that it clearly presents the alternatives available to the offeree, and (2) at least one of the two independent sets of terms is sufficiently certain to permit an accurate valuation at the time the offer is made."

Operative summary (slip op. pp. 30–31):

"In this regard, the 998 offer must delineate the specific terms attributable to each choice presented and provide that the offeree must affirmatively choose one or the other set of terms by way of acceptance. … The rebuffed offeror seeking cost shifting bears the burden of showing its 998 offer was valid, meaning it was sufficiently certain."

Disposition: "We affirm that portion of the judgment affirming the trial court's award. We reject and overturn its holding that section 998 categorically prohibits alternative-choice offers." Facts match R1 (lump-sum $85,000 alternative vs. itemized-reimbursement alternative; net jury award $76,155.27; cost-shifting upheld because the $85,000 alternative was valid and unbeaten). The Court assumed without deciding that the second (reimbursement/dispute-resolution) alternative was independently invalid (fn. 9) — useful: a term structure requiring later itemization, proof, and court determination was treated below as not amenable to valuation, and the Supreme Court did not disturb that.

M. Lowenstein & Sons, Inc. v. Superior Court (1978) 80 Cal.App.3d 762 — VERIFIED (read full) — case is REAL; earlier "possibly nonexistent" flag is resolved

CL cluster/opinion 2144688 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2144688/m-lowenstein-sons-inc-v-superior-court/). Third District (Reynoso, J.; Puglia, P.J., and Paras, J., concurring), filed May 9, 1978; parallel cite 145 Cal.Rptr. 814. The real party in interest was plaintiff Grant Davidson — which explains the stray "Lowenstein Sons Inc v. Davidson" name R1's search returned.

It is a service-of-summons case, not a § 998 case: out-of-state service by mail on a foreign corporation under CCP § 415.40; constitutionality; and whether a defective return required dismissal under former § 581a. It supports exactly the proposition R1 wanted it for, via the Judicial Council comment it quotes and applies (at p. 770):

"'Jurisdiction depends on the fact of service, rather than the proof thereof. … Consequently, if the process is in correct form, properly issued and served, and the proof of service is timely filed with the clerk, a defective affidavit will not destroy jurisdiction; the court may permit an amendment of the affidavit to conform to the facts.'"

And its holding (at p. 771): "The trial court could accept the return receipt and the letter as satisfactory evidence of actual delivery to the petitioner. … The authority of a court to allow the filing of a proper affidavit nunc pro tunc to conform to proof is well-established. … We conclude that the return of service, as amended, operated to take the case at bench out of the provisions of section 581a." Directly useful for defending our misdated proof of service: the fact of service controls, and POS defects are amendable. (Whether the fact-vs-proof principle carries from summons service to § 998 service is an argument, not a holding — no § 998 case adopting it was located in this pass.)

Puerta v. Torres (2011) 195 Cal.App.4th 1267 — VERIFIED (read full)

CL cluster 5810288, opinion 5665721 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810288/puerta-v-torres/). 4th Dist. Div. 3 (Moore, J.). Quotes § 998(b) verbatim, including that the written offer "shall include a statement of the offer, containing the terms and conditions of the judgment or award, and a provision that allows the accepting party to indicate acceptance of the offer by signing a statement that the offer is accepted" (at pp. 1270–1271). Holding (at p. 1273):

"This case … deals with the provision that sets forth two mandatory requirements about what shall be included in a section 998 offer: the offer shall be written, and it shall contain a provision stating that the recipient can accept the offer 'by signing a statement that the offer is accepted.' The offer at issue here contained nothing regarding acceptance, only the terms of the offer itself and its expiration date. It was therefore invalid under the plain language of the statute, regardless of whether Puerta ever intended to accept the offer or not."

Also describes Berg v. Darden (2004) 120 Cal.App.4th 721 at length (see cover-letter question below).

Mostafavi Law Group, APC v. Larry Rabineau, APC (2021) — VERIFIED (read full)

CL cluster 4860916, opinion 4664695 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4860916/mostafavi-law-group-apc-v-larry-rabineau-apc/). 2d Dist. Div. 4 (Currey, J.), B302344, filed 3/3/21, certified for publication. CL lacks the reporter cite; memo cite 61 Cal.App.5th 614 is consistent with the date — confirm on Westlaw. Holding: purported acceptance of a § 998 offer lacking an acceptance provision produces a void judgment; trial court's vacatur under § 473(d) affirmed. Key language:

"where a section 998 offer is invalid based on its failure to satisfy all of the 'statutorily required elements[,] … there is nothing for the receiving party to accept' in the first place. (Perez, supra, 206 Cal.App.4th at p. 426.)"

Footnote 6 — terms must live in the offer itself:

"had Rabineau's section 998 offer contained an acceptance provision, and had it been accepted in accordance with that provision, Rabineau could not have later conditioned payment of the settlement funds on MLG's execution of a settlement agreement containing terms not specified in the offer … Rabineau's attempt to introduce additional terms outside of the offer is inconsistent with the plain language of section 998, subdivision (b), which requires the offer itself to 'contain[] the terms and conditions of the judgment or award.'"

Barella v. Exchange Bank (2000) 84 Cal.App.4th 793 — VERIFIED (read full)

CL cluster/opinion 2257340 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2257340/barella-v-exchange-bank/). 1st Dist. Div. 5. Review denied Jan. 24, 2001 (noted at end of opinion). Three verified holdings:

  1. Burden on offeror (at p. 799): "In interpreting section 998, this court has placed squarely on the offering party the burden of demonstrating that the offer is a valid one under section 998. (Taing v. Johnson Scaffolding Co. (1992) 9 Cal.App.4th 579, 585.)"
  2. Strict construction (at p. 799): "The corollary to this rule is that a section 998 offer must be strictly construed in favor of the party sought to be subjected to its operation. (Garcia v. Hyster Co. (1994) 28 Cal.App.4th 724, 732-733.)" Also: "while the statute contemplates that an offer … may properly include nonmonetary terms and conditions, the offer itself must, nonetheless, be unconditional. (Hutchins v. Waters (1975) 51 Cal.App.3d 69, 73.)"
  3. Non-monetary term incapable of valuation invalidates (at p. 803): "We conclude that the task of valuing a confidentiality clause attached to a settlement offer in a defamation action is too subjective and, therefore, cannot be done. Thus, a confidentiality condition in such a settlement offer will render the offer invalid for purposes of shifting costs to the plaintiff." The opinion adopts Valentino's framework, including that terms may "render it difficult to accurately value the monetary term of the offer so the court cannot fairly determine whether the damage award is 'more favorable'" (quoting Valentino, 201 Cal.App.3d at pp. 697–698, at Barella pp. 800–801).

Licudine v. Cedars-Sinai Medical Center (2019) 30 Cal.App.5th 918 — VERIFIED (read full)

CL cluster 6240159, opinion 6107092 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/6240159/licudine-v-cedars-sinai-med-ctr/). 2d Dist. Div. 2 (Hoffstadt, J.; Ashmann-Gerst, Acting P.J., Chavez, J.) — CL's "5th District" label is wrong. Plaintiff's $249,999.99 offer served 19 days after the complaint and 5 days after the answer; $2.3M prejudgment-interest request stricken; affirmed.

Three-factor test (at pp. 924–926): "(1) how far into the litigation the 998 offer was made; (2) the information available to the offeree prior to the 998 offer's expiration; and (3) whether the offeree let the offeror know it lacked sufficient information to evaluate the offer, and how the offeror responded."

Good-faith standard (at p. 924): "A 998 offer is made in good faith only if the offer is ''realistically reasonable under the circumstances of the particular case'' … that is, if the offer 'carr[ies] with it some reasonable prospect of acceptance' (Regency, at p. 531)."

Burden allocation (at p. 926):

"Although the party making a 998 offer generally has the burden of showing that her offer is valid (Timed Out, supra, 21 Cal.App.5th at p. 942; Barella, supra, 84 Cal.App.4th at p. 799), it is the 998 offeree who bears the burden of showing that an otherwise valid 998 offer was not made in good faith. (Elrod, supra, 195 Cal.App.3d at p. 700 …)"

The cover-letter question (terms in the offer document vs. transmittal letter)

No case squarely holding that a monetary term stated only in a cover letter can or cannot supply a § 998 term was located in this pass. What is verified:

  • § 998(b) as quoted in Puerta/Mostafavi: the written offer "shall include a statement of the offer, containing the terms and conditions of the judgment or award."
  • Mostafavi fn. 6 (quoted above): terms outside the offer are inconsistent with § 998(b).
  • Gorobets (slip op. p. 30): the offer "must delineate the specific terms attributable to each choice presented."
  • Berg v. Darden (2004) 120 Cal.App.4th 721 — EXISTS–NOT-READ (described in Puerta, which I read): a § 998 offer that was "the last paragraph of a letter addressed to other issues" was held valid; "[a]n otherwise clear section 998 offer is not rendered invalid simply because it does not track precisely the language of the statute" (Berg at p. 728, as quoted in Puerta at p. 1272). Berg cuts toward substance-over-form for the offer's format, but it involved an offer contained in the letter, not a term outside the offer document. Read Berg directly before using.

PRIORITY 3 — Civ. Code § 3390 / failed valuation mechanisms

Bewick v. Mecham (1945) 26 Cal.2d 92 — VERIFIED (read full)

CL cluster/opinion 1134157 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1134157/bewick-v-mecham/). Traynor, J. Lease option to purchase at a price "to be fixed by arbitration" (three appraisers); lessor refused to appoint; trial court fixed the price itself ($9,000) and decreed specific performance; affirmed.

  • Appraisal ≠ arbitration (at pp. 97–98): CCP §§ 1280/1283 (old law) inapplicable because "it is clear that the parties intended not a formal arbitration, but an evaluation by appraisers whom they regarded as experienced and familiar with the conditions in question."
  • Prevention doctrine (at p. 99): "Each party to a contract has a duty to do everything that the contract presupposes that he will do to accomplish its purpose … and a duty not to prevent or hinder performance by the other party. … A party who prevents fulfillment of a condition of his own obligation commits a breach of contract … and cannot rely on such condition to defeat his liability."
  • Court fixes the price under Civ. Code § 1613 (at pp. 99–100): "Under this section impossibility of ascertaining the price by the contractual method does not preclude a court from giving effect to the contract, ascertaining the consideration in place of the arbitrators or appraisers. Determination of the value of the property is a common task of courts in condemnation, partition, and other proceedings."
  • Quoting Kaufmann v. Liggett (at p. 100): a court of equity "will in such case make an appraisement itself, or direct it to be done by its own officer, and will thereafter enforce specific performance of the contract upon the terms so found."

Petrolink, Inc. v. Lantel Enterprises (2018) 21 Cal.App.5th 375 — VERIFIED (read operative passages)

CL cluster 6239476, opinion 6106390 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/6239476/petrolink-inc-v-lantel-enters/); parallel cite 230 Cal.Rptr.3d 283. Panel includes Huffman, Acting P.J., and Guerrero, J. — Fourth District, Division One (CL's "5th District" label is wrong). Lease purchase option at fair market value; dueling party appraisals ($1,615,000 vs. $320,000).

Mechanism actually used — court-appointed expert under Evidence Code § 730, not § 1281.6 and not an order that a party employ an appraiser:

"At trial, both of the appraisers that had been hired by the parties testified, as did an independent appraiser whom the trial court had appointed as a court expert pursuant to Evidence Code section 730."

The trial court adopted a value based on the court expert's appraisal ($789,000 plus "bonus rent," total $889,845) and decreed specific performance. Disposition on appeal: "The judgment of the trial court is reversed. The trial court is directed to determine the reasonable date on which the contract for purchase and sale should have been performed, and is further directed to consider what financial adjustments must be made in order to relate the parties' performance back to the date that the contract should have been performed." The valuation methodology itself was left intact; reversal concerned relation-back financial adjustments for the delayed performance. (A 2022 unpublished follow-up appeal exists: CL cluster 6623657.)

Civ. Code § 3390(b)/(d) applied to compel hiring a specific professional — NOT-FOUND; closest authority is adverse-adjacent

No California case was located applying § 3390 (or its subdivisions on personal service / procuring the act of a third person) to an order compelling a party to employ or retain a named professional. The closest verified authority points the other way:

Woolley v. Embassy Suites, Inc. (1991) 227 Cal.App.3d 1520 — VERIFIED (read operative passages) (CL cluster/opinion 2142292):

"it is a fundamental rule that specific performance cannot be decreed to enforce a contract for personal services, regardless of which party seeks enforcement. (Civ. Code, § 3390, subds. (1) & (2); Barndt v. County of Los Angeles (1989) 211 Cal.App.3d 397, 403.)"

and, quoting Corbin, the rule covers "contracts for the rendition of a performance that is of a distinctly personal and non-delegable character … [including] managers, sales agents …" — "The rule is statutory (Civ. Code, § 3390)." (Note: older cases cite subds. (1) & (2); the current lettered subdivisions must be confirmed on Westlaw.) Drafting implication: the safer prayer, squarely supported by Bewick and Petrolink, is for the court to determine value (itself, by reference, or via an Evid. Code § 730 expert) — not an order that defendants "employ" Correia-Xavier and Moss Adams.

CCP § 1281.6 / appraisal-as-arbitration — insurance context verified; non-insurance NOT-FOUND

Khorsand v. Liberty Mutual Fire Ins. Co. (2018) 20 Cal.App.5th 1028 — VERIFIED (read operative passage) (CL cluster 6239462, opinion 6106376):

"Because appraisals are agreement-based arbitration proceedings subject to the statutory scheme regulating nonjudicial arbitration (Code Civ. Proc., § 1280 et seq.), we look to that scheme to establish the meaning of the term 'arbitrator.' The sole statutory regulation within the scheme concerning the selection of arbitrators is Code of Civil Procedure section 1281.6, which provides that courts must enforce the method of selecting arbitrators set forth in the agreement."

That is an insurance-policy appraisal case. No published California case was located in this pass treating a non-insurance appraisal clause as an arbitration agreement and using § 1281.6 to appoint the appraiser. Note the tension to brief carefully: Bewick (1945) held the parties' appraisal provision was not arbitration under the then-current statutes, but the modern § 1280(a) definition (quoted in memo R2 from Legislative Counsel text) includes "valuations, appraisals and similar proceedings." Banwait v. Hernandez (1988) 205 Cal.App.3d 823 (EXISTS–NOT-READ) appeared in the § 1281.6 search results and may address court appointment when the agreed method fails; read before citing.

PRIORITY 4 — Existence + one-line-holding sweep

Authority Tag Verified holding (read in this session)
Purdy v. Johnson (1917) 174 Cal. 521 (CL cluster 3302219) VERIFIED (read operative passages) Beneficiary's action to surcharge trustees; judgment for trustees reversed and "[t]he case must be remanded for the taking of a new account in accordance with the established principles of equity. The court may either take the account itself or make a reference for that purpose. … it is the duty of the trustees to support every item of their account, and … wherever they fail to support the correctness of a charge or a credit by satisfactory evidence, the item must be disallowed." (at p. 531.)
Uzyel v. Kadisha (2010) 188 Cal.App.4th 866 (CL cluster 2278013) VERIFIED (read operative passages) Trustee-liability under Prob. Code § 16440(a), holdings enumerated in the opinion's introduction: "(1) tracing is not required for the disgorgement of profits made by the trustee 'through the breach of trust' under section 16440, subdivision (a)(2); (2) … liability for appreciation damages as lost profits under section 16440, subdivision (a)(3); (3) the determination as to which of the statutory measures of liability 'is appropriate under the circumstances' … is reviewed for abuse of discretion; … (5) prejudgment interest is mandatory on an award of damages under section 16440, subdivision (a)(1); and (6) the absence of an express provision for prejudgment interest under section 16440, subdivision (a)(3) does not preclude an award … under Civil Code section 3287, subdivision (a)." § 16440 quoted in full at p. 889.
Levin v. Winston-Levin (2019) 39 Cal.App.5th 1025 (CL cluster 4660932; CL lacks the reporter cite; date 9/13/2019 consistent) VERIFIED (read operative passages) Prob. Code §§ 850/859: return of trust property ordered for undue influence as to the 2012 amendment, but double damages under § 859 require bad faith: "the court correctly interpreted that section to apply only where the undue influence was exerted in bad faith"; "We do not believe the Legislature intended to provide double damages for undue influence without bad faith … First, it said so: 'by the use of undue influence in bad faith.' (Prob. Code, § 859.)"
Estate of Kraus (2010) 184 Cal.App.4th 103 (CL cluster 2255381, indexed as "Regents of the University of California v. Kraus" — same case; the § 850/859 petition was brought by the Regents and Make-A-Wish as residuary trust beneficiaries) VERIFIED (read operative passages) Affirms order that Kraus return $197,402 and pay "statutory double damages of $394,804. (Prob. Code, §§ 850 et seq., 859.)" "Section 859 provides for recovery of twice the value of property taken in bad faith. … The section 859 penalty is imposed when an interested party establishes both that the property in question is recoverable under section 850 and that there was a bad faith taking of the property." (at p. 112.) Probate court has power to grant relief without a personal-representative claimant; scheme exists "to prevent looting of decedent's estates."
Calcor Space Facility, Inc. v. Superior Court (1997) 53 Cal.App.4th 216 (CL cluster 2284385) VERIFIED (read operative passage) Nonparty document subpoenas: reads § 2031's good-cause standard into § 2020 — the proponent must "'set forth specific facts showing good cause justifying the discovery sought by the inspection demand,'" because "it is unlikely the Legislature intended to place greater burdens on a nonparty than on a party to the litigation." (at pp. 223–224.)
Obregon v. Superior Court (1998) 67 Cal.App.4th 424 (CL cluster 2301614) VERIFIED (read operative passages) Meet-and-confer: "The level of effort at informal resolution which satisfies the 'reasonable and good faith attempt' standard depends upon the circumstances. In a larger, more complex discovery context, a greater effort … may be warranted. … The history of the litigation, the nature of the interaction between counsel, the nature of the issues, the type and scope of discovery requested, the prospects for success and other similar factors can be relevant." Also: "A single letter, followed by a response which refuses concessions, might in some instances be an adequate attempt …" (pin pages not captured in this pass — confirm exact pages, approx. pp. 431–433, on Westlaw).
Williams v. Superior Court (2017) 3 Cal.5th 531 (CL cluster 4408734) VERIFIED (read operative passages) Discovery/privacy: rejects any blanket "compelling need" requirement — "To the extent prior cases require a party seeking discovery of private information to always establish a compelling interest or compelling need, without regard to the other considerations articulated in Hill v. National Collegiate Athletic Assn. …, they are disapproved." (at p. 557 & fn. 8.) Under Hill, "[o]nly obvious invasions of interests fundamental to personal autonomy must be supported by a compelling interest." (at pp. 556–557.)

(a) CORRECTIONS — what R1–R4 (and the verification tasking) got wrong or can now be fixed

  1. M. Lowenstein & Sons is real — lift R1's "do not cite" flag (¶¶ 189, 287). 80 Cal.App.3d 762 (3d Dist. 1978) exists; the "Davidson" name in R1's search was the real party in interest. It supports precisely the fact-of-service vs. proof-of-service proposition R1 wanted (quotes and pins above). It is a summons-service case; do not describe it as § 998 authority.
  2. Poster ambiguity resolved (R1 ¶ 36). The "§ 1013 does not apply" statement was the Court of Appeal's holding; the Supreme Court reversed it. Holding pin: 52 Cal.3d at p. 275 (35-day window for mailed offers). Licudine (2019) applies the same rule post-amendments.
  3. § 16601 subdivision number (R4 ¶¶ 44, 186, 287, 384 and the verification tasking). Per the published Han v. Hallberg opinion, the trust clause ("distribution of the trust's entire transferable interest … but not merely by reason of the substitution of a successor trustee") is § 16601, subd. (8); subd. (7)(A) is death of an individual partner. R4's substance is confirmed verbatim; its subdivision cite "(7)" should be corrected to "(8)" (and re-checked against the current official code, since paragraph numbering is exactly the kind of thing unofficial sources garble).
  4. Han v. Hallberg cannot be cited yet. Review was granted, S256659 (Aug. 21, 2019; 446 P.3d 234). Final disposition not verifiable in CourtListener. KeyCite before any use.
  5. Gorobets confirmed in full (R1 ¶¶ 38, 121, 211–217, 249, 253, 269). S287946, filed 8/6/2026, Corrigan, J., unanimous; below: 105 Cal.App.5th 913. R1's "reported" holding language was accurate; the verified opinion adds two load-bearing sentences R1 lacked: the offer "must delineate the specific terms attributable to each choice … and provide that the offeree must affirmatively choose one or the other set of terms by way of acceptance," and "[t]he rebuffed offeror seeking cost shifting bears the burden of showing its 998 offer was valid." Still no official reporter cite.
  6. Barella is broader than R1/R2 used it for. Beyond non-monetary-term valuation, it squarely holds (p. 799) the offeror bears the burden of demonstrating validity and the offer is strictly construed against the offeror — both directly useful against our own offer's defects, and both worth owning in the memo rather than discovering from opposing counsel.
  7. Petrolink's mechanism. The appraiser was a court-appointed Evidence Code § 730 expert; nothing in the opinion orders a party to hire an appraiser. R2's structural-analogy framing is right; any draft that cites Petrolink for compelling defendants to employ our named appraisers overreads it. Also note: judgment was reversed/remanded on delayed-performance adjustments (valuation approach intact).
  8. Licudine's court. 2d Dist. Div. 2 — CL's district metadata (which says 5th) is wrong; same error on Petrolink (actually 4th Dist. Div. 1). Never copy CL court labels into a brief.
  9. "Estate of Kraus" caption. CL indexes it as "Regents of the University of California v. Kraus"; same case, 184 Cal.App.4th 103. An automated citator name-mismatch warning on this cite is a false positive.

(b) REMAINING GAPS — needs Westlaw / CoCounsel

  1. Corp. Code § 16603 (effect of dissociation): no California appellate opinion quoting it was found. Statutory text still rests on an unofficial web source. Pull official text.
  2. Corp. Code § 16103(b) (nonwaivable provisions): no opinion quoting the nonwaivable list found; only the § 16103(a) default-rule principle is case-verified (Rappaport, p. 1225). If the partnership agreement purports to waive buyout/information rights, § 16103(b) must be pulled and parsed.
  3. Corp. Code § 16701(e), (g), (h), (i) full text: case-verified only in the fragments quoted above (Jones v. Goodman quotes (i) and part of (g); Mar recites (a)/(e) demand mechanics; R2 pulled text from Legislative Counsel data). Confirm official text of the 120-day tender and deferred-payment provisions.
  4. Subsequent-history / citator checks were NOT performed and cannot be done reliably in CourtListener. Priority items: Han v. Hallberg (S256659 — dispositive); Gorobets (12 days old — rehearing/modification window; no official cite yet); Corrales (any later criticism of the two-person rule); Bewick (1945) and Purdy (1917) (age; continued vitality); Poster (vitality under the post-2005 § 998(b)(2) — Licudine's 2019 application is a good sign, not a citator result); Mostafavi, Puerta, Barella, Licudine (routine KeyCite).
  5. Reporter citations to confirm on Westlaw (absent from CourtListener): Gorobets (Cal.5th, none yet); Mostafavi (61 Cal.App.5th 614); Jones v. Goodman (memo sources: 57 Cal.App.5th 620); Mar v. Perkins (102 Cal.App.5th 201); Levin v. Winston-Levin (39 Cal.App.5th 1025); Han v. Hallberg (35 Cal.App.5th 621 — plus review-grant history).
  6. Cover-letter question: no square holding located either way; read Berg v. Darden (2004) 120 Cal.App.4th 721 directly and run a targeted Westlaw search (e.g., "998" /s "cover letter" or "transmittal") before briefing.
  7. § 1281.6 outside insurance / § 3390(b),(d) compelling retention of a named professional: nothing found; Banwait v. Hernandez (1988) 205 Cal.App.3d 823 unread; the Woolley/Barndt personal-services line should be researched as the likely defense argument against our prayer.
  8. Obregon pin cites for the two quoted passages were not captured (approx. pp. 431–433); confirm before filing.

This pass verifies existence, text, and holdings as of the opinions' filing dates only. It does NOT substitute for KeyCite/Shepard's: no negative-treatment, depublication, review-grant (except Han, found incidentally), or amendment checking was or could be performed in CourtListener.

C. INCONSISTENCIES WITH CURRENT POSITIONS (key deliverable)

Current positions (per tasking): buyout $5,705,257.43 offered 7/2/2026 ($4,700,000 principal

  • $327,427.02 Bypass income + $677,830.41 interest at 4%); minority discount 25–30%; post-death compensation = 4% interest, not profits; offsets $262,592 + $194,353; $850,894.54 (2015–21 profit) agreed 8/30/2022; partnership value agreed ~$1,162,613.

C-1. Our own numbers moved five times — and the last move was DOWN. $3,950,565.28 (3/3/2025 offer, per chronology) → $4,900,000 + $658,345.21 interest (Jan 2026 drafts) → $5,000,000 / $5,671,780.82 total (5/1) → $4,700,000 / $5,705,257.43 total (5/1–5/4) → $5,750,000 flat lump sum (5/18 letters, one fully addressed to Cunningham and signed Ormonde) → $5,705,257.43 (7/2/2026, current). If the May 18 letter was served, the operative 7/2/2026 offer is $44,742.57 LOWER than a prior formal 998 — fatal to a "consistent contractual math" narrative and awkward for 998 cost-shifting (which baseline governs?). If it was NOT served, the drafts still document that we internally priced the same "strict contractual baseline" at $4.9M, $5.0M, $4.7M and $5.75M within 16 weeks. Action: establish definitively whether the 5/18/2026 letter and any $5.75M 998 went out.

C-2. Post-death profits: our own drafts undercut "4% interest, not profits."

  • "Trust Profits Discussion" concedes the § 16407 election ("the Trust generally has a choice: … profits … OR … legal interest").
  • The Timeline doc calls the accrued interest "mandated by RUPA."
  • Settlement V2 §2.6 and the 5/4 998 admit the Partnership kept paying the Trust parties' draws and personal expenses (insurance, utilities, maintenance) from dissociation to closing — conduct consistent with continued partner-like treatment, not a frozen creditor claim (and consistent with the partnership's own FY2023–24 books allocating 37.5% of income to the Estate, which the 5/18 letters call "unsupportable as a matter of law").
  • "Buyout Proposal without interest" offered zero interest — if 4% is contractually mandatory compensation, our own draft violated our own theory.
  • The drafts DO admit one category of income is owed: $327,427.02 "earned but undistributed income from the Manuel C. Leal Bypass Trust" — which concedes the general proposition that undistributed income survives the "everything-was-reinvested / double-counting" argument in the January docs.

C-3. The $850,894.54 agreed profit figure is contradicted, not managed. Every January draft "formally reject[s]" ALL historical unpaid profits ("Any profits generated prior to 2017 are barred by the 2017 Settlement Agreement"; releases waive "unpaid profits … March 25, 2015 through … closing"), and no draft anywhere pays, reserves, or even mentions the $850,894.54 for 2015–2021 that our current position treats as agreed on 8/30/2022 (agreed to by Esraelian "per YOUR calculation," i.e., ours). The drafts' "2017 bar" theory also conflicts with our own chronology's reading that the 12/7/2017 release is NARROW (¶13/15 — real-property division only). An examiner will put the January drafts next to the 8/30/2022 email and ask which position is ours.

C-4. Offsets: three incompatible schemas in our own papers.

  • Current position (and 3/3/2025 offer): $262,592 + $194,352.65 (post-death distributions to Hazel's trust).
  • Jan–May 1 drafts: $262,592 + $56,463 ("additional draws 1/15/2025–1/31/2026", marked "Needs verification" three separate times) = $319,055. These drafts SKIP the 9/23/2022–1/14/2025 post-death draw category entirely (the $194,352.65).
  • 5/4 drafts: $332,606.12 total "through May 4, 2026" (implied post-1/15/25 additional draws of $70,014.12; +$13,551.12 in the three days since the $319,055 version).
  • The $262,592 itself is labeled BOTH "reconciliation through September 22, 2022" and "as of January 15, 2025" within the same wave, and is derived as $591,965 (Hazel's gross excess draws at 9/22/2022 vs the 37.5/55/7.5 split) − $329,373 (Bypass Trust surplus credit). Either $262,592 is lifetime-only (and the May drafts under-deducted by ~$194K), or it absorbs post-death draws (and the current $262,592 + $194,353 double-counts). The near-twin figures $329,373 (Bypass offset) and $327,427.02 (Bypass income paid) also demand a Frazer-level reconciliation to prove we are not crediting ourselves and paying the same Bypass money once each way. This must be reconciled before any verified pleading or discovery response repeats either set.

C-5. Discount story drift. January: $4.9M as "full fair market value," no discount mentioned. 5/1: "(90% per 2017 Agmt)" on both components. 5/4 letter: "90% contractual buyout discount AND a 25% minority interest discount on the real property." 5/18: minority "interest-level adjustments" justified under Article XIII, Section B.2 of the 2018 Amended and Restated Partnership Agreement (not the 2017 Settlement). Current position: 25–30%. Prior record (chronology): Complaint 20–30%; 3/2025 offer 30%; defendants 15%. Also governing-document drift: Jan–May 4 drafts hang the 10%-down/20-yr/2-yr/10-yr/4% financing on "2017 Settlement Agreement Section 7"; the 5/18 letters and the record hang the 90% + 4% note on the 2018 Partnership Agreement Art. XIII (chronology cites Sec. J / B.2). Verify which instrument actually contains which term before the CMC statement.

C-6. Partnership value: $1,046,351 vs $1,046,587.50. Both sides' correspondence agreed the partnership at $1,162,875 → 90% = $1,046,587.50 (3/3/2025 offer; defendants' 6/19/2025 counter). The 5/1–5/4 drafts and the $4.7M principal instead use $1,046,351 (→ implies $1,162,612.22, the "~$1,162,613" in our current position). The two gross values differ by ~$263 and the 90% values by $236.50 — trivial in dollars, but it means the current position's "~$1,162,613" tracks an unexplained draft number rather than the mutually-corresponded $1,162,875, and $1,046,351 + $3,653,649 = $4,700,000.00 exactly — the components visibly reverse-engineer a round principal. Expect cross on "where did $1,046,351 come from?"

C-7. Interest arithmetic is stale/reused. $658,345.21 is exact-day math on $4.9M through 1/31/2026 (1,226 days at $536.9863/day) and $671,780.82 is the same math on $5.0M — but $677,830.41 (exact for $4.7M through 5/1/2026, 1,316 days at $515.07/day) is reused verbatim "through May 4, 2026" (5/4 drafts), inside the 5/18 "baseline," and in the 7/2/2026 offer — by which date true 4% interest would be ≈ $709,700 (+$31,900). Our "contractual" interest number stopped accruing the day the draft was written; an examiner will use that to argue the figure is negotiated garnish, not contract math (and the Trust was SHORTED interest under our own theory).

C-8. 998 structure risks are visible in the drafting history. Every 5/1–5/4 998 draft embeds non-monetary conditions precedent (offeree-funded LLA, well drilling, easement abandonment, life estate, cessation-of-expenses) inside the offer, and the drafts carry the $5,705,257.43 figure INSIDE the 998 while the final served 998 reportedly states no total (the number lives only in the 7/2 cover letter, per verified_facts_memo §6.7). The folder also shows a 72-hour ultimatum (Jan) morphing into 30-day 998s. All of this feeds the R1 998-validity analysis: the conditions were integral from inception, and the total-sum figure was consciously moved out of the offer document between May and July.

C-9. Hazel's capital account characterizations. Our drafts state, in our voice: Hazel's account showed $591,965 excess draws at 9/22/2022 against the 37.5/55/7.5 split; releases recite a "Net Excess" position of −$262,592 "reflect[ing] the offset of the Bypass Trust surplus against Hazel Leal's excess draws"; V2 §2.6 admits partnership payment of her side's personal expenses continued post-death. Note tension with 2018 Agreement Art. VI.E (chronology): a debit drawing balance is "a liability of that Partner to the Partnership" and "shall NOT reduce his [capital]" — i.e., our own governing document arguably treats excess draws as a receivable, not a price offset, which is not how any draft (or the current offset position) structures it.

C-10. 1983 note / $350,000 — the silence. No draft mentions the 1983 note ($212,035 at 9%) or the $350,000 payment due 6/7/2018 that defendants assert was never made. But every draft demands a mutual general release with a 1542 waiver "from the beginning of time," which would extinguish that Trust-side claim without pricing it. If a draft release had been signed, we would have obtained a silent discharge of a known disputed obligation of Steve and Marla — optics an adverse examiner (and a probate court reviewing trustee conduct) will exploit. Flag to counsel before any release language is reused.

C-11. Bypass Trust dissolution / 7.5%. The drafts use the Bypass in three ways — the 7.5% slot in the 37.5/55/7.5 split, the $329,373 surplus offset, and the $327,427.02 income payment "to the Estate of Hazel J. Leal" — but never mention that the Bypass Trust was dissolved and its 7.5% partnership interest ($821,249 of capital) moved to Steve on 1/1/2023. Paying Bypass income to Hazel's ESTATE while having taken the Bypass capital by transfer is a characterization choice the drafts adopt without support; discovery into the dissolution/ transfer will test both the offset and the payee designation.

C-12. Party/name/address drift (clean-up before anything is served). Co-trustee named "Ashley Susan Anderson" (5/1) vs "Ashley Susan Garabedian" (5/4–) vs "Ashley Anderson Garabedian" (160-acre doc) vs "Susan Garabedian, Ashley Garabedian" (5/18 #20); trust styled "The Hazel J Leal Rev Trust" vs the pleaded "Hazel J. Leal Revocable Trust dated November 3, 2008"; life-estate residence flips between 21127 and 21161 Road 68 (the 5/1 $4.7M draft grants the life estate at 21127; all others at 21161); the Release draft calls it the "January 2017" settlement (actual: 12/7/2017); the $5M drafts allocate partnership at $1,067,500 vs $1,046,351 everywhere else.

The brief's "partnership ~$1,162,613" appears nowhere in these files — closest figures are Steve's 1/1/2015 book capital $1,171,439 and 9/30/22 herd-line balance $1,026,048; reconcile before using.
  5. Discount drift. LOM rose 15% (2017–21) → 20% (9/23/22) → 30% (2024–26 snapshots); LOC constant 12.5%. Combined discount is thus 25.6% → 30% → 38.75% across the client's own worksheets — relevant to the stated 25–30% position.

Hazel's capital account (client's own numbers) shows her side UNDER-drawn by $719,809 through 12/31/22 relative to fixed 37.5/55/7.5 — supports the "due to Hazel $1,033,717" tally on the same sheet; cuts against any "excess draws by Hazel" theory but confirms unequal draws (Steve +617,285, Bypass +102,523).

ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT — PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL.

Gmail Sweep — jaceleal@gmail.com (OI-66)

Leal v. Garabedian et al., Tulare County Superior Court No. VCU327028 — prepared for plaintiff's counsel, 9/26/2026

0. Scope, method, and limits

  • Mailbox: jaceleal@gmail.com only. It was read through the Gmail connector using search and read tools only. Nothing was sent, replied to, forwarded, drafted, labeled, archived, trashed, untrashed or otherwise changed. Nothing went to any party.
  • Citation key: Gmail thread ID, plus the message date and sender. Dates are the sender's local date as shown in the message header or quote line; UTC header timestamps can fall a day later.
  • Read status: FULL means the body of every message was read, either directly or through a complete quoted chain. PARTIAL means only some messages were read in full, or only the Gmail snippets (about the first 200 characters) were read. A statement drawn from a PARTIAL thread quotes only the snippet text.
  • Privilege tags: [PRIV] marks client-side (Jace, Steve, Jordan) communications with Ormonde's office (Ormonde, Vieira, Lallas). The same tag is applied, as a presumption, to communications with prior counsel Griswold LaSalle (Johnson, Waite, Askins, Kapheim). This report does not treat privilege as waived. Possible waiver issues are flagged for counsel in §5.
  • Grading: every finding is marked [HELPS], [HURTS] or [BOTH] from the plaintiff's point of view. Adverse items get the same treatment as helpful ones.
  • Already read, cross-referenced only: 1827e17104001f86, 19e2d918e69961b7, 19ed33e5a03baa31 and 19faef5ef5a7be1a, plus the rest of gmail-extract.md. Their content is not repeated here.
  • Not covered:
    • (a) The second mailbox (lealdairy@gmail.com / "Leal Dairy") was not searched. Many 2017–2021 settlement messages were addressed to it, and this mailbox holds only the copies sent to jaceleal.
    • (b) Attachments were not opened. The connector cannot extract them, so figures that live only in PDF or XLSX files (for example $194,352.65, $327,427.02 and $329,373) could not be checked.
    • (c) Some keyword searches were reviewed only to snippet level on their first page (noted where it happens).
    • (d) Pre-2018 threads with Gin and Childs (2016) and a small set of pre-2022 Griswold LaSalle and Frazer threads were listed but not read (§1b).
  • Credential/PII rule: no password, full account number or SSN appears in this report. Only last-4 digits are given, marked "credential present — rotate" where a credential is involved.

2. Findings by topic (graded; verbatim; cited)

2.1 The 2017 dispute and pre-settlement conduct

  • [BOTH] Hazel's side conditioned partner signatures on financial reporting (2017). 11/9/2017, Esraelian to Johnson, lealdairy, Thompson and Cunningham (then McCormick Barstow) and TGG (15fa1ce3b9f72277): "Hazel will agree to sign this request at this time; 2. Hazel will not sign future requests … in the event Steve fails to provide the information requested … Hazel is willing to perform her duties as a partner … so long as Steve is willing to perform his duties as a partner and provide the financial information."
    • The same day, lealdairy (Jace) replied "Here is the response to your request. I have written my notes in red. I have attached canceled checks…". Johnson called it an "Excellent response." That is a same-day production, which helps us.
  • [HURTS] Caregiver-payment friction. 11/9/2017, lealdairy (Jace): "I will not be able to make checks for the home care nurses until the funds are in the business checking account." Esraelian: "Your continued threats to take away or to stop paying Hazel's caregivers is causing Hazel severe emotional distress." (15fa1ce3b9f72277)
    • [PRIV] Jace to Johnson: "My Dad just isn't too excited about loaning the partnership to pay for nurses." Johnson: "Remember Judge Broadman wants your hands clean … Let me be the bad guy."
  • [BOTH] Monthly reporting position (precursor to ¶8). 3/30/2017, Jace to Bekedam (Frazer), cc Gin (15b21082e5e451e6, snippet): "I am fine with sending a monthly QuickBooks backup if David thinks it is appropriate. I'm not going to send copies of invoices/receipts as I see it as an unnecessary burden."
    • 11/29/2017, Jace to Esraelian (16009327354a253c): "I will send the updated monthly statements for November on Friday."
  • [CONTEXT — not graded] Counsel continuity. Tim Thompson and Niki Cunningham represented Hazel's side in 2017 at McCormick Barstow (15fa1ce3b9f72277, cc line). Thompson (tthompson@wtjlaw.com) was receiving Johnson's settlement-implementation proposals in 2019 (168ed79bc0e71f61). The Trust side's CPA in 2017 was TGG (Aaron and Dale Garabedian). Lauren Garabedian Ruff signs from the same TGG address in 2021 (17687a1d2514e969). No relationship to Ashley Garabedian is established in any email read.

2.2 Settlement implementation, 2018–2021 (¶5 Morgan Stanley; ¶6 note; ¶8 accountings; deeds; retains; profits)

(a) ¶5, the Morgan Stanley account: actively fought 2018–2020, and the reimbursement was performed as modified by 12/2020.

  • 7/19/2018, Johnson to Steve and Jace (164b3f272e8d6737): MS staff are "working through all the necessary paperwork to take the $838,000 account out of your dad's name … Next she will determine the income due to your mother from March 25, 2015 through May 31, 2018. She will then cut a check from Morgan Stanley to the Dairy for reimbursement. The remaining money will be placed in a new account and will be subject to the division we agreed to in the settlement agreement."
    • Johnson to Esraelian (embedded): "We have made clear that both sides want this done."
    • 7/25/2018, Esraelian: "I met with quite a bit of resistance and bad attitude with both Doug and Veronica [MS]."
  • 1/17/2019, Johnson's proposal to Thompson and Esraelian (1685cc57cc4f8485; 1685d8f08355cec2):
    • MS value at 3/25/2015 was $610,699.71.
    • $101,140.67 to go to the partnership, and the remaining $509,559.04 to be halved: $254,779.52 to Hazel and $254,779.52 to the Bypass.
    • "Hazel will also receive a check from the partnership for about $60,000 for the income generated by the dairy for the by-pass trust."
  • [BOTH] Esraelian refused, 1/17/2019 1:04 PM. It helps attribution, because their counsel held up the ¶5 reimbursement. It hurts, because her stated reason was that our backup for the trust expenses was incomplete. Quoted in 1685d8f08355cec2: "NO, you cannot instruct Morgan Stanley to reimburse the Dairy $101,140.67. I have been asking for months for the Dairy to provide proof and back up of the Trust expenses … I sent you an email on July 20, 2018 … I have since requested this information on at least 3 occasions … we DO NOT AGREE TO THE DAIRY REIMBURSEMENT OF $101,140.67, WITHOUT PROOF AND BACK UP INFORMATION."
    • Johnson replied: "We have provided to you all the information. We remain at a stand still waiting for you to approve."
    • [PRIV] Johnson to the client: "Robyn is an impediment to progress. Why she would hold up $500,000 to her client is beyond me."
  • [HELPS] Our side's accuracy check. [PRIV] 1/17/2019, Jace caught that Johnson's income figure was wrong: Hazel is entitled to "the dividends and interest … not the capital gains," which gave $97,872.92. On 2/7/2019 Johnson sent corrected income of $100,465.89, broken down by year from 2015 to 2018, with checks proposed of $101,140.67 to the Dairy and $355,245.41 to Hazel (16d2665617dc84cf).
    • 2/14/2019 Johnson to Thompson and Esraelian: "We are awaiting your instructions." Thompson on 2/25: "out of the office in an arbitration." Jace on 2/27: "Any updates?" (168ed79bc0e71f61)
  • [BOTH] Pace, 2019–2020.
    • 10/1/2019: GL sent "2019.09.30 ltr to R. Esraelian re settlement.pdf" with Dropbox exhibits (16d89407f3ea0c79). [PRIV] Johnson: "getting close … I do have some concern about the request to distribute her individual profits."
    • 12/23/2019: Esraelian marked up the MS letter (16f34d336af6d5b2). 3/3/2020, Jace: "Has there been any updates…"
    • 8/10/2020: Esraelian updated the MS letter and attached her "March 2020 letter" (173d8f06cebf81db). Hazel signed on 8/12/2020 (173dab69613e5e17, snippet).
    • [HURTS, our prior counsel] 9/23/2020, Esraelian: Johnson "hasn't been available for my last 3 phone calls and hasn't called back" (174bb381422b450b). 9/10/2020: Jace's house deed was never prepared — "Michael Johnson's office dropped the ball" (1747888a1f62859a).
  • [HELPS] The ¶5 reimbursement was performed, modified to $80,000.
    • 11/9/2020, Edwards: "$80,000 of deductible professional fees should be deducted from $146,060.79 of income for a net of $66,060.79."
    • 11/10/2020, Jace proposed simply splitting the account. Esraelian: "your recommendation doesn't comply with the settlement agreement." Steve signed the MS letter on 11/11/2020 (1759e34185f40af4).
    • 11/24/2020, Esraelian: "The Morgan Stanley letter is in Veronica's hands as of last Friday."
    • 12/3/2020: "VERONICA TOLD ME LAST WEEK THE CHECK WAS ISSUED AND SHE WAS MAILING IT TO THE DAIRY ADDRESS" (175fb40be8a79e2f).
    • 2/17/2021, Edwards to Lauren Ruff, cc Esraelian: "the Bypass Trust reimbursed Manuel Leal and Son Dairy $80,000 to cover expenses" (17687a1d2514e969).
    • Not confirmed in this mailbox: that the account was actually split between Hazel's trust and the Bypass after the letter reached MS. No post-2020 MS statement or division confirmation was located.
  • [BOTH] Susan dealing directly with MS in 2021. 5/18/2021, Susan: "Veronica from Morgan Stanley is issuing a check today," to reimburse a $1,295 trust-accounting bill the Dairy had paid (177da1447b500f27, snippet). Which MS account the check came from is not shown.

(d) Retains and profits (pre-death). [BOTH, leaning HURTS on the promise]

  • 11/24/2020, Esraelian demanded retains ($3,000/yr, "not been paid since the settlement") and "Hazel … share of the Dairy profit … and the Bypass share … from 2015 through 2019" (175fb40be8a79e2f).
  • 12/2/2020, Jace: retains "Correct, These have not been paid. I will set up an ACH in the amount of $15,000"; Bypass income 2015–2019 "$224,101, or $240,172 if you exclude the loss from 2016"; "I don't believe the partnership agreement requires the distribution of partner profits."
  • 12/16/2020, Esraelian: "Article VII, paragraph A. The language of the paragraph is 'shall'."

(e) Deeds, TIC and title. [HURTS, a risk item]

  • 7/27/2018, Johnson: "We will record the appropriate documents" (164ddd3d35e2d82e).
  • [PRIV] 12/4/2024, Jace to Ormonde: "I'm assuming this deed got recorded … I believe that once Hazel passed away, all bypass trust assets including land are supposed to transfer over to Steve."
  • 12/16/2024, Jace to Johnson: "I am having a hard time confirming whether or not these documents were recorded."

06-counsel-transition/transition-checklist-and-counsel-selection.md · 5,866 characters

COUNSEL TRANSITION — CHECKLIST AND SELECTION CRITERIA

ATTORNEY WORK-PRODUCT SUPPORT — NOT LEGAL ADVICE — the mechanics below are practical notes; substitution procedure and file-ownership rules must be confirmed by the incoming attorney. Prepared August 18, 2026 · CMC October 13, 2026

A. Sequence — do these IN ORDER

  1. Say nothing to anyone yet. Not to current counsel, not to opposing counsel, not to Ashley or Susan. A visible gap between lawyers is leverage for the other side.
  2. Secure what only prior counsel's file contains — BEFORE any substitution conversation:
    • Stan Xavier's 5/8/2023 email (the joint-call/scope email — quoted in Ex. K, never produced)
    • the as-served § 998 proof of service, mail log, and any WTJ acknowledgment (OI-1)
    • the full email archive with Esraelian 2022–2025 (the 133-hit mailbox search)
    • any response ever sent to the 9/26/2023 $850,894.54 demand
    • engagement letter and billing file (shows retention date — relevant to A-6 and to any later questions about the § 998 package) The client file belongs to the client; a courteous written request for a complete copy of the file is normal and does not require announcing a substitution. Frame it as case organization.
  3. Interview candidates now (Section C). Conflicts check FIRST, using the names list below.
  4. Engage the new attorney, then file the Substitution of Attorney (Judicial Council form; client + outgoing + incoming sign; serve and file). Deadlines do NOT pause: the Sept 15 package date and Oct 13 CMC stand regardless.
  5. Timing options (decide with the new attorney, not before):
    • Substitute promptly: new counsel owns the CMC statement, the amendment, the discovery launch, and any fresh § 998. Cleanest if engaged by early–mid September.
    • Substitute after the CMC: avoids a scramble but lets prior counsel set the schedule and positions at the CMC that the new attorney inherits. Generally the worse option if the goal is speed.
  6. Preserve everything. All files, emails, drafts — including prior counsel's work. The new attorney may need the record of the § 998 service facts for the substantial-compliance argument, and preservation is simply required. Do not editorialize about prior counsel in writing anywhere.
  7. Do not sign anything with the other side, and send nothing to them, during the gap.

B. Conflicts list to give every candidate BEFORE any substantive discussion

Parties/counsel: Ashley Garabedian; Hazel Susan (Susan) Leal; Whitney Thompson & Jeffcoach (T. Thompson, N. Cunningham); Richardson Jones & Esraelian (R. Esraelian); Ormonde Rascon; Griswold LaSalle Cobb Dowd & Gin. Neutrals/experts: Correia-Xavier (S. Xavier); J. Hower & Associates; Moss Adams / Baker Tilly (S. Klett, D. Snyder); Frazer LLP (M. Edwards); Reddington (dec'd); T. Cardoza; JAMS (Hon. T. Volkmann, ret.). Entities: Manuel C. Leal & Son Dairy; the Manuel C. Leal Living/Bypass Trusts; the Hazel J. Leal Revocable Trust; Steve & Marla Leal Living Trust; AgWest Farm Credit; Citizens Business Bank; Land O'Lakes.

C. What to look for — keyed to THIS case, not generic

  1. A business/trust litigator who tries cases in Tulare/Fresno/Kings courts — the case is a partnership-buyout contract fight wearing probate clothes. Estate-and-trust specialization (State Bar certified specialist) is a plus, but contract/valuation trial chops matter more.
  2. Fluency test (use in the interview): hand them the two-page issue sheet below and ask how they'd handle (a) Han v. Hallberg + § 16601(8) vs. an express "Dissociating Events" clause; (b) a § 998 with a misdated POS; (c) a broken jointly-appointed-appraiser mechanism (Bewick / Evid. Code § 730 vs. ordering someone to "employ" an appraiser). Good candidates will see the § 3390 problem and the § 664.6 shortcut without prompting.
  3. Valuation-literate — comfortable running a CPA (Frazer) and appraisers, and willing to use the settlement model rather than round numbers.
  4. Capacity now — must be able to own an October 13 CMC on a September engagement.
  5. Referral channels that actually work here: the client's CPA network (Frazer sees the local litigation bar's work product), Tulare County and Fresno County bar referral services, the State Bar's certified-specialist directory (Estate Planning, Trust & Probate), and asking any respected transactional attorney you trust "who do you least want across the table in a partnership buyout fight in Visalia?" Interview at least three. No specific attorney is named here by design — names should come from live referrals and conflict checks, not from this workspace.
  6. Fee structure: this is a documents-and-valuation case with a finished evidence base — push for a budget tied to phases (pleading cleanup → CMC → dispositive/settlement window), and give every candidate the incoming-counsel briefing AFTER engagement (conflicts first, engagement second, file third).

D. Two-page issue sheet for interviews (safe to hand pre-engagement, no privileged detail)
